Almighty God I Our Heavenly Father! We reverently come to
Thee this morning, asking that Thy divine blessing rest upon those
uaembled here in Thy presence. Bless and prosper the Institution of
Masonry, which has been dedicated to Thy holy name for the uplifting
•>f ·mankind. We ask Thee to remember and bless those of our number
who are unable to be with us today on account of trouble, sickness, or
any other adversity. M'ay they feel that Thy benediction rests upon
them always, . and enable them .to say from the fullness of their hearts,
"Thy will be done." Especially we ask Thee to bless those of our
number who have worked in the vineyard of this fraternity early and
late; those whose heads have grown gray with the weight of years;
nnd may their reward be the priceless jewels of Patience and Content.
And, Heavenly Father, we ask The'e to guide and direct the young
inen of this Institution in the paths of rectitude and virtue. Enable
them to build pure and upright !!haracters, the noblest attribute of mart:
prepare them for the day that must come when the responsibiHties of
this great fraternity shall rest upon them.
We ask Thee, Almighty God, to be with Thy servant whose duty
it is to preside over this asseml;ily. Enable him to do momentarily that
which deliberation would impel him to do. And when our pilgrimage
here upon earth is ended, and the hour of probation has drawn to a
close, may it be our happy lot to assemble in that Grand Lodge on
high, whose doors shall never close-in that "house not made with
hands, eternal in the heavens."
All thes·e blessings we ask in Thy name, Almighty God ; and to
Thee we ascribe all honor and glory, now and forever. Amen.

The Grand Lodge of the Jurisdiction of California has been opened
in Ample Form for its Sixty-third ~nnual Communication. In obedience to our Constitution, this written message is now presented to you,
thereby setting forth 'all my official acts during the year, exhibiting the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

For the fitis.t time since the organization of the Grand Lodge, one
of its Annual Communications is being held in the city of Los Angeles.
Our new Masonic Temple in San Francisco is uncompleted. ·The Craft
of the State h;ave been glad to ho)d this Communication in this splendid .
metropolis of Southern California. Los Angeles is a city whose moral
and civic life is clean and in h·a rmony with Masonic i.deals. It is a city
of many Masonic Lodgesi. During my visits· in Southern California
last June and July, a citizen of this city declared to the National
Municipal League, assembled here, that Los Angeles has no slum or
red light district. That was a proud boast. It could not be made of
any other ci•y of equal population in the United States. This city is,
therefore, a fit place for the annual meeting of the great fraternity that
"has for its fotindatio.n the practice of the moral and social virtues."

CORNER-STONE OF OAKLAND CITY HALL.

After installation on Friday, October 13, 1911, the Grand Lodge was
·called off and the offioens and members of the Grand Lodge proceeded
to the city of Oakland. There, in the presence of the largest gathering
ever assembled in Oakland, including thousands of Masons, the cornerstone of the new City Hall was laid. Brother William H . Taft, President of the United States, was present as the guest of Oakland, and
delivered the address. The Grand Master, in accepting the invitation
from the Mayor of Oakland, remarked that it had been i;:ustomary from
time immemorial for the Cra£,t to lay corner-ston~ of public buildings ;
that it had the approval of no less a character than President Washington, who as a Master Mason laid the corner-stone ·o f the Capitol at
Washington. After laying this corner-stone, the Grand Lodge was
duly closed in San Francisco.

MASONIC HOMES.

I report that at the Masonic Home at Decoto everything is progressing satisfactorily. Under the able direction of the Board of Trustees,
s.econded by · the conscientious and capable Superintendent, Brother
F. B. Hartman, the Home is managed well. Every,thing is done that
can be done for the contentment, comfort and happiness of the aged
men and women who find :shelter there in their declining years. The
Trustees one and all are .deeply interested in making the Home a witness to the practice of that Masonic charity and brotherly love which
should distinguish Masons everywhere, ,and which gives dignity and
reputation to our noble fraternity.
I had the great ple:asure in July to spend some hours at the San
Gabriel Home, where are kept the boys and girls who are under our

11

'.

To visit this Home and see the well-behaved, healthy, happy and
contented children of our deceased brothers, who might otherwise be
thrown on the cold charity of the wor1d; to see them being guided into
paths of usefulness and virtue; to feel that they will be a credit to the
Home which sheltered them, is to be entirely convinced that the results attained at this Home are worth again and ·again all of the cost in
money and personal sacrifice to maintain it. The administration of the
Hoihe is well organized and its affairs economically administered. A
well-ltept giatden, chickens arid dairy cows are features that help to keep
down expenses. The boys a.nd girls are taught to work and be helpful
in and about the Home. The watchful care of the Trustees follow them
into the outer world to guard, advise and help them. The Trustees find
positions fot those who leave the Home, where they can learn a trade
or vocation. Brother Spencer took me to places where three of
"our" boys were employed in Los Angeles. They were contented and
happy. Sev-en boys, and three girls have left the Home and are doing
well.
I commend ,the work of the Home at San Gabriel. All honor to the
and Masons who maintain and admin~ster this Home. Their highest reward Is in the cotisdousness of
inestimable service to some of their fellow beings. The noblest and
greatest service that man can give to man is ,that which uplifts and
ennobles another. All who contribute in service or support to this
Home are entitled to credit. Their work is not on "tll.e canvas that shall
perish, or the marble that shall crumble into dust, but upon mihd, upon
spirit, which is to last forever, and which is to bear, for good or evil,
throughout eternity, the impress of a teacher's plastic hand."

The Special Committee on Mas,onic Home1 in its report to the

Master appoint a permanent committee of nine members of the Grand
Lodge, to be known as "The Endowrtl.eht Fund Committee of the
Masonic Homes of Califorrliai" who should devise ways and means to
taise an endowment fund of $1,00Q,000 for the homes. (Pro. 1909, page

168.) This recommendation wa.-; adopted. (Id., page 159.) Our lamented M.". W:. Brother Pierce stated in his annual address that
M.". W .;. Brother Lawlor ·had appointed him chairman of that committee, with power .to appoint other members to fill it. Owing to• failing health and other reasons, M.". w:. Brother Pierce did not appoint
the other members of the committee. (Pro. 1910, p. 15.) At our Annual
Communication in 1911 M.". w:. Brother Weller appointed as such
permanent committee w:. Brother Edward S. Valentine (chairman),
w:. Brothers James H. McLafferty, Edward Coleman, William P . Filmer, Charles W. Norton, Motley H. Flint, Edward Strasburg, William
E. J. Baughman and George M. Perine.
The progress made by this permanent committee will appear when
their annual report is read. Br-0thers, the object of this committee is
one of the noblest that can appeal to the heart -0f a Mason. The
brethren of California should raise this endowment fund. If our 50,000
Masons would give $1 a year for five years on the average the fund
would have a quarter of a million dollars. And that money would
continue its work of beneficence in caring for aged and helpless Masons
and their widows and -0rphans when the fleeting desires and vanities of
this time have passed into oblivion.
Any Mason who would take this matter in hand earnestly could
raise an average of $1 per capita from his Lodge for this fund. Our
glorious new Masonic Temple will soon be completed. When it is dedicated, what gratifying achievement to have made substantial advance
in raising this fund? Would any say "impossible"? To him let Carlyle reply: "Know that 'impossible,' where truth and mercy and the
everlasting voice of nature order, has no place in the brave man's dictionary. That when all men have said 'impossible' and tumbled noisily
elsewhither, and thou alone art left; then first thy time and possibility
have come. It is for thee now; do thou that, and ask no man's counsel, but thine own only and God's."

NJlW CONSTITUTION, ANNOTATJlD.

At the last Annual Communication M.". w:. Charles L. Patton,
for the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented an Annotated Constituc
tion, practically eliminating all Decisions and Regulations. The former
Regulations and many Decisions are now incorporated as part of the
Constitution. The Decisions not so incorporated are referred to in
notes under the appropriate sections of the Constitution. Of the 91
Regulati-Ons then existing all but one have either been placed in the
new Constitution or repealed. This new Constitution enacts in constitutional form the former Constitution and practically all other legislation
down to the date of its adoption properly included in a Constitution.
This new Constitution as annotated and with cross referencelSI will
be of . immense benefit to the whole Craft. Heretofore the body of
Masonic law was contained in so many different volumes of Proceedings, in Resolutions, Regulations, Recommendations of Grand Officers
Adopted, and Decisions by Grand Masters, .that it was often difficult
. for Mai~ers of Lodges to ascertain what the existing law was. These
difficulties are now re~oved. For the first time there is an index to
the Constitution. By its use nearly every question of Masonic law and
procedure can be decided.
The work of ·revising the old Constitution and including the Regulations and Decisions and Annotations has been immense. I understand that we are indebted principally to M.". W:. Brother Patton for
this great work, which cost him a vast amount of time and labor. His
great work entitles him .to the fullest gratitude of the Craft. It will
stand as a monument to his zeal, ability and useful labor for the fraternity.
Besides the index, the book as publi°shed contains in the beginning
a complete table showing the sections of the old Constitution and Regulations which correspond with the sections of the new Constitution.
The Manual as now published by the G!"and Secretary contains the
Uniform Code of By-laws and the various ceremonies of the fraternity.
The Grand Secretary has also published in this volume a table of the
Anci~nt Landmarks, and certtain of the ancient written Charges, Regulations and Constitution.s. The readings of these will be instructive

VISITATIONS.

During the past year visits were made to Lodges in more than forty
of the Masonic districts. On very many of these· visits V:. W:.
Brother Baker's presence added greatly to the gratification of the occasion. Great pleasure was received in meeting the mem~rs and installing the officers of sixteen Lodges. The third degree of Masonry
was conferred by, me twice during official visits. Once in Eel River
Lodge and the other time in Richmond Lodge, San Francisco, where
R:. w:. Brother Filmer acted as Senior Warden, v:. w:. Bl'other
Baker as Senior Deacon, the other positiQ{IS being filled by Grand Officers and Inspectors. On a visit to Nievada City I installed w:.
Brother Meservey Senior Grand Steward. These official visits covered
territory from Humboldt county to San Diego. Everywhere the greatest hospitality and protherly courtesy was shown the Grand Master.
"The deepesit feelings have no words at all." I can but feebly express
to my brethren who showed me as Grand ?>faster so much brotherly
kindness my profound thanks iand sincere appreciation. My Pasadena
brethren presented me with a beautiful gold-mounted trowel, suitably .
engraved, which shall be kept as a prized memento of the delightful
visit to their Lodge.
With the v:. w:. Brother Baker, a visit was made to Rising Star
Lodge No. 83, at Forest Hill, in Placer county, in the Sierra Nevada
Mountains. In that old mining town we stood on the spot where on
August 25, 1859, Colonel E. D. Baker, in addressing 3,(X() miners, uttered these immortal words :
"When yo·u speak to the poet of freedom, his lip quivers with inspiration, his heart glows, and the numbers break out as the stream
dashes from the mountain top to seek the valley below-bright, clear,
sparkling, FREE. I love freedom; I will speak her words ; I will listen to
her music; I will acknowledge her impulses; I will stand beneath her

"There is no death ! The stars go down

In regard to the foregoing, the profane who have been made Master Masons in Douglas Lodge No. 12 of Nevada, and who at the time
.residing in California, are irregular Masons under the laws of California. They can be made regular Masons in two ways:
1. If still residing in Catifornia, by applying to the nearest place of
residence for the three degrees of Masonry and thereupon receiving
the same; or,
2. By applying to such Lodge in California to waive jurisdiction
in favor of the Nevada Lodge, and upon the same being granted being
"healed" in the Nevada Lodge.
If any of such irregular Masons have removed from the State, then
by either "of said methods in the Lodge in California which was nearest
their residence in this State when their petitions were received in said
Nevada Lodge.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

23

In the event that application is made for waiver from the California
Lodge to join a Lodge in Nevada, the California Lodge granting the
waiver is · entitled to be paid its regular fees. It has the right to waive
such fees. The determination of the waiver of · such fees rests with the
subordinate Lodge. I would suggest, in this case, but not to establish
any precedent, that the California Lodge or Lodges which might grant
such waivers, if applied for, might either waive such fees, or part thereof, or divide the same with the Nevada Lodge according to the circumstances and the particular residence in each case. This is only a
suggestion and the . matter is presented to the Grand Lodge for such
action as it may see fit to .take.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

STATE OF THE CRAFT.

l. It is gratifying to report that during the past year our beloved
institution has been making constant advance. Many men have offered
themselves as candidates for the mysteries of Freemasonry and have
been received into our fraternity. We now have nearly 50,000 Masons
in this Grand Jurisdiction. Eleven new Lodges have been granted dispensations and all are doing well. This means that eleven new altars
have been erected to Masonry; that upon them the fire of truth is ever
shining, diffusing light to all within its circle. Around these altars these
bands of friends and brethren meet, to renew their vows, to strengthen
their virtues, to increase their patriotism, and quicken their sense of
duty.
·
"Is aught so fair,
As virtue's friends·h lp; as the honored roof
Whither from highest heaven, immortal love
His torch ethereal and his golden bow
Propitious brings, and there a temple holds?"
But more gratifying than our material progress is the constant
growth and development of our Masonic ideals and obligations; for in
this respect also there is continual advance. Masons are more and more
exerting their influence and efforts for the improvement of the moral
and social conditions where they have their homes.
2. The work of building the new Masonic Temple at &m Francisco
is prooeeding with satisfying speed. Stone upon stone and arch upon
arch, it is rising to completion. The superintendent in charge of the
work promises that it will be finished in the coming May. The concrete .
work is now finished to the top. The stone arches are in place up to
the second story. The partitions of the various rooms are being laid.
Further subscriptions are needed as .the work progresses. To our good
brothers who have given so much time and thought and effort and support to the building of this mighty edifice are due the thanks and appreciation of the entire Craft May the Great Architect assi.st them in their
labors, as He did our ancient brethren at the building of the first Temple
on M/ount Moriah. An account of the progress of the work will appear
in the report of the President of the Trustees of the Masonic Temple.
AMENDMENT TO THE CONSTITUTION.

At our last Communication an amendment was proposed to the Constitution providing that Lodges shall not receive petitions for the degrees, or for affiliation, from men engaged in the saloon business; also,
making it a Masonic offense for Masons hereafter to enter upon that
. business. This proposed amendment is to be voted upon at this Annual Communication. To obtain information for the Craft as to what

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

25

legislation along this line has been enacted in ?ther Grand Jurisdic~io~s,
I sent a circular letter to the Grand Secretaries of the Grand Junsd1~­
tions of the United States and Canada, asking for a statement of their
laws on that subject These Grand Secretaries have made courteo~s
and prompt replies. A statement of such replies is appende~ to this
report. Exercising the power you have so generously vested 1~ me to
"recommend .such legislation as I may deem necessary or expedient for
the welfare of the Craft," I now recommend the passage of that Constitutional amendment. In the address delivered by me as Grand Orator
in 1904 to this Grand Lodge these words were spoken : "M~sonic i~­
stitutions were framed for the elevation of men. Masonry with all its
poWJer is arrayed against this evil." Also, "May t~e d~y come soon
when Masons everywhere and at all times may proclaim without a blush,
without hesitation or misgiving, that temperance is a cardinal virtue )
practised by Masons; when Masonry shall be a bulwark and a force in
the struggle against this mighty evil."
To-day I repeat those words. Abraham Lincoln, in life the great,
the humble, the just, the forgiving, now the immortal, sai~ in 1853, in an
address in Illinois : "The open saloon, or grog shop, ~s the greatest
tragedy of civilization." If his words are true, t~e~. it is just an~ ;i.ght
to declare that men who livie and fatten on this tragedy of c1v1hzation" shall not be allowed to participate in our privileges. I believe that,
though the saloon may be legalized by men, it is outlawed by the teachings of Masonry.
And if we shall by this amendment say to the man behind the bar,
or who owns the bar, "You cannot enter here," what of the man in
front of the bar? For the man in front of the bar pays the money that
induces the man to stand behind the bar. If no men stood in front of
the bar, there could be no man behind the bar; in fact, saloon bars
would cease to exist.
"Lest we forget," let us realize that when we condem.n the man behind the bar we cannot be just without blaming the man m front of the
bar.

CONCLUSION.

I want to thank V.'. W.'. Brother John Whicher for his everwilling help, his unceasing solicitude in the work, and his advice and information. It aided greatly in many difficult places. Thanks also to
his Assistant Secretary, w. ·. Brother Johnson, for many courtesies.
To V.'. W.' · Brother Baker I am especially indebted. Together we
made many visits throughout the State. His intimate knowledge of the
affairs of the different Lodges, his acquaintance with means of travel
his untiring zeal and ever-present tact, contributed to make our visita~
tions satisfactory and gratifying to all. So many courtesies were received from so many good brothers that I must thank them collectively
for the pleasure and happiness they gave.
The present year of Masonry is near its close. In performing the
duties of his office the Gmnd Master is brbught into constant intercourse and close relations wlth many of his brethren. Together we have
ap.plied tl:e !de.1Is of Masonry to the affair; of life. It ltas been a gratifying experience. I humbly acknowledge that my constant association
with the high ideals of our great fraternity and tire endeavor to iricrea~e .regard for them among our brethren has given me a higher apprec1at1on of the worth and beauty of Masonic character. The ideals of
Masonry are so lofty that, though advancement be continually made towards their attainment, yet that very advancement, by giving a larger
vision and truer outlook, shows they are almost as distant as before.
As we rise nearer to our ideals by surmounting the obstructions in our
path, the height to which we attain reveals to our view and enables us
to behold the unknown heights of attainment that lie farther on. And
so, as we progress in Masonic character with the deeper insight and ·
larger view come new duties and obligations not seen or felt before.
And thus Masonry, sublime and moral in its nature, is a constantly augmenting force in the elevation of man.

27

After the reading of this address we proceed with the work berore
us. In a few days we will return again to the several homes from
which we came. Again, as in the past, we will assemble around the
altars in our respective Lodges, not for selfish ends, not to gra.tify appetite or passion, but that we may "reason of righteousness, and temperance, and the judgment to come." We will meet to renew our strength
and quicken our zeal for the performance of the high duties of life. We
will assist one another to rise neairer to the full height of Masonic
character. As. we came to our Temples in the first place "uninfluenced
by meroenary motives and with a sincere desire to be serviceable to our
fellow creatures," and to learn to subdue our passions, so we wlll hope
a111d strive to continue.
·· · ·
· At our altars ·we:wiiI seek the humility and reverent spirit that is
vouchsded us through prayer. To those we admit to our brotherhood
we will present the lambskin apron as an emblem of innocence and the
badge of a Miason, the greatest distinction that men can bestow, and
which should consecrate him who wears it to the highest purpose of man
on earth, the elevation of his character. In our fraternal intercourse
with our brethren and the world we will strive in our lives to ex•emplify
the manly virtues of temperance, fortitude, prudence a111d justice; and
we will endeavor to obey the injunction given by King David on his
deathbed to his son Solomon, afterwards our first Grand Master, "Be
ye therefor strong and show yourself a man."
In our Lodges new friendships will be formed and old ones cemented by indissoluble ties. The friendships formed with our brother
Masons will, when purified by virtue, ennobled by tempera.nee and justice, quickened by giving help to others, supported by a firm belief in immortality and blessed by the Author. of our being, be among the most
priceless and cherished possessions that life can give. For while "the
friendships of the world are often conspiracies of vice or leagues of
pleasure, ours have for their object severest virtue ; and such friendships can end only with death." We will meet with our brethren on the
level as we always have before. We will know no distinction of rank
or fortune. Only that which is within and part of the character of our
brothers will be regarded. To the brother who has least of worldly
goods or honor, but who liV'es as a just and upright Mason, we will
say :

"True, w~lth thou hast not; 'tis but dust ;
Nor place, uncertain as the wind;
But that thou hast which with thy crust and water
Can despise the best of both, a noble mind."

3. COLORADO. Constitution, Art. XIX, Sec. 4.
,..Intemperance and Liquor Traffic.-It is hereby made the imperative duty of all Lodges to restrain, as far as possible, the Masonic crime .
of intemperance by trial and punishment, as the case may require, and
to exclude from Lodge and ante-room all intoxicating liquors; and for
the faithful performance of these duties they will be held strictly accountable to the Grand Lodge. It shall be unlawful to initiate or affiliate any person engaged in the sale of intoxicating liquors to be used as
a beverage. · All Masons are, therefore, prohibited from engaging in the
liquor traffic."

those engaged in it when they apply for admission to our order. 1899.

"It is no more the duty of a Master to order an information filed

Masonic offense of like magnitude and importance.-Proceedings 1908,
page 108."

"Intoxicating Liquors.-One who is the agent of a non-resident
brewing company, and as such is in charg·e of the warehouse and sale
department of his employer, and either directly or indirectly superintends and directs the sale of beer and other intoxicating liquors, in violation of the State laws, cannot lawfully receive the degrees of Masonry
in this State.-Coleman, 1897."
"Intoxicating Liquors.-It is a Masonic offense for any Mason to

intoxicating liquors as a beverage; and I believe the Grand Lodge of
Kansas will sustain any of its Lodges should they suspend or expel any
of their members for such offense.-Brown, 1870."
"Intoxicating Liquors.-It is a Masonic offense for any Mason to
keep a dram-shop or to sell intoxicating liquors as a beverage.Adopted 1873."

"Intoxicating Liquors.-This Grand Lodge, by its approval of the
decisions of its Grand Masters and the adoption of standing regulations
relating to the sale of intoxicating liquors, gives no uncertain sound on
the subject, and hereby reaffirms its previous declarations and declares
that the sale of intoxicating liquors as a beverage, or the aiding and
abetting the sale of the same, directly or indirectly, by the renting of
buildings, or furnishing means for the conduct of such business, with
or without license, shall be deemed an offense against the body of Masonry, and all persons violating this regulation are ineligible to receive
the degrees of Masonry or to membership in any lodge within this
Grand Jurisdiction.-Adopted 1903. R,ecommended by Dewey, G. M."

"c. A brother whose Lodge has surrendered its charter, and who

9. KENTUCKY. Regulations.
"Section 117.-Manufacture or Sale of Liquors. No Lodge shall
receive the petition of anyone who is engaged in the manufacture or
sale of spirituous, vinous or malt liquors as a beverage. Any Lodge
guilty of violating this provision shall be dealt with."
"Regulation 388.-The retailing of spirituous liquors has been so
abused as to become a great evil in the social life of our country. The
prosecution of such business by a Master Mason is inconsistent with his
profession of moral character, and is calculated to bring the Order into
public disrepute. This Grand Lodge disapproves the conducting ~£ such
business by a Master Mason."
"Regulation 240.-Manufacture or Sale of Liquors. By the words
'anyone who is ,engaged in the manufacture or sale of spirituous, vinous
or malt liquors,' in Section 117 of the Constitution, is meant the person,
firm or stockholder of a corporation, or a salesman, engaged in such
business, and not one who may be employed as gauger, bookkeeper, stenographer, porter, driver of a wagon, watchman or laborer, who does not
actually sell the liquor, by sample or otherwise, or participate in the distributive profits of the business of making or selling such liquors
as a beverage."

12. MONTANA. Standing Resolutions.
"Art. VIII.-Resolved, That it is the determined sense of th1s
Grand Lodge that the indulgence in the vices of intemperance, gambling,
licentiousness, or profanity, or either of them, by Masons in this }urisdiction, should be promptly suppressed by the Lodges ; and it is enjoined as a constant and special duty of all Masons to counsel, caution
and admonish the Craft in this respect, and in case of wilful persistence
the Lodge shall punish those found guilty of such indulgence by the infliction of adequate penalties."
"Art. XXL-Resolved, That it is the sense of this Grand Lodge
that it is unwise for any Lodge or collection of Lodges to use spirituous,
malt or vinous liquors as a part of the refreshments provided at any
banquet or other Masonic function, and the use of the same is hereby
prohibited.-Adopted October 5, 1904."
"Art. XXIV.-Resolved, That any member of a Lodge in this jurisc
diction who shall engage in the saloon business or act as a barkeeper in
a saloon shall be considered guilty of unmasonic conduct, and it shall be
the duty of the Junior Warden of such Lodge to prefer charges against
any such member; but .it is understood that this. resolution shall not be
retroactive.-A.dopted September 16, 1908."

"In this State, where we have constitutional prohibition of the manufacture and sale of liquor as a beverage, we have sometimes had difficulty in the matter of the illegal sale of liquor through the medium of
drug stores, so-called, and we have a ruling that where a druggist so
far forgets himself as to dispose of liquors in quantities as a beverage
he becomes ineligible for the degrees. The Grand Lodge has likewise sustained the suspension of members who, after receiving their
degrees, have engaged in the saloon business in other States. Consequently the attitude of this Grand Lodge is very clear and strict."

The Grand Secretary read his annual report, as follows :
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Herewith my annual report:
In accordance with a resolution of Grand Lodge, adopted in October, 1911, and following the orders of the Special Committee appointed for the purpose, I have begun the work of indexing the names
of all members of Lodges in the jurisdiction,. based on the membership
a1s reported July 31, 1912. In this work the office of the Grand Secretary has been materially assisted by the cordial co-operation of Secretaries of Lodges, and to them my thanks are hereby extended. The·
report of the Special Committee will .explain in sufficient detail the
plan and scope of the work.
One thousand copies, paper bound, of the Annotalted Constitution
adopted at the last Annual Communication, were printed and distributed
pursuant to your resolution, to-wit: One copy to each Lodge, Grand
Officer and Inspector. I also caused to be printed and bourid in cloth,
fifteen hundred copies of said Annotated Constitution, the book being
called "Constitution and Ceremonies," the publication including the Uniform Code of By-Laws, the Installation Ceremony for Lodges, the
Funeral Service as revised by Past Grand Master Well er pursuant to
your order, the "Record Book of Example Lodge,'' the Ceremony for
Laying Corner Stones, the Ceremony for Constituting Masonic Lodges,
the Ceremony for Dedicating Halls, Procedure for Consolidation of
Lodges, the Monitoria·I Work, and the Ancient Laws of Masonry. The
labor of compiling all tMs was no small task, but the book has proved
to be a success, and although rohe cost was considerable-$1,694.50--the
copies sold up oo July 31 brought revenue to the amount of $853, with
576 bound books in stock and a goodly lot of paper-covered Constitutions.
Five hundred copies of the valuable "List of Regular Lodges" were
purchased, and one copy thereof mailed to each Lodge in the jurisdic. tion. Very few extra copies we!'le sold, which is disappointing. It is
quite important that the larger Lodges should have an extra copy, so
that one could remain with the Tyler and the other on the Secreta•ry's
desk.

"No Lodge shall receive an application for the degrees of Masonry,
or for affiHation, from any orte who is engaged, either as principa·l,
agent or employee, in the saloon bu'Siness (except in connection with,
and as part of, the operation of a bona fide hotel or restaurant) , or
who is a. barkeeper; and any Mason who may hereafter enter upon and
engage in the saloon business, either as owner, agent, or employee, except in connection with and as part of the operation of a bona fide hotel
or restaurant, or who shall become a barkeeper, shall be deemed guilty
of unmasonic conduct, and shall, upon due trial and conviction of said
offense, forfeit all Masonic rights and privileges, including membership
in any Lodge.''
The a·bove is Unfinished Business, and requires a two-thirds vote to
carry.

Some of the older Lodges appear to have By-Laws not authorized
by Grand Lodge, and their attention is directed to the Uniform Code
as found at page 227 of the "Constitution and Ceremonies." These
should be copied in the book of By-Laws of each Lodge, the blanks,
of course, to be filled pursuant to the will of the Lodge and approval
of the Grand Master.

The Masonic Board of Relief of the City of San Francisco presents .the following report for the year beginning September 1, 1911,
and ending August 26, 1912, both da.tes inclusive.
Since our last report this Board has· been augmented by the admission of San :Jl4ateo Lodge No. 226 into the compact, the Board now
consisting of twenty-six Lodges, who have been represented during the
year by their Masters or Representatives.
During the year the question of finding employment for sojourning
Brethren and their widows has become vuy important, and one which
will require the combined effort and co-operation of all the Brethren
of San Francisco to even partially solve. ·

60

61

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

EMPLOYMENT.

The coming Exposition of 1915 has brought a great many unemployed to this city, who have been disappointed in not finding the
amount of work the extensive advertising 'in the East had let them to
believe could be found here, and although not conducting a separate
employment bureau, positions have been secured for a great many, by
the Secretary, without incurring any additional expense to the Board.
IMPOSTORS.

Impostors are as plentiful as ever, and some of them seem to be
successful in working the ·whole Pacific Coast. A closer affiliation of
the various Boards of the whole coast and a system of inter-communication could be established which would tend to eliminate .this evil
to a great extent, and with that end in view a meeting of the Secretaries of all these Boards in the near future, to discuss matters of common interest, is greatly to be desired.
We are glad to note that many Lodges throughout the country,
when appealed to by this Board in cases requiring relief, respond
promptly by leaving the matter in our hands to act as we see fit. This
shows a confidence which we think we .deserve, as all cases are handled
to the best of our ability, the utmost economy being observed, as we
fully appreciate' the trust imposed.
In view of these facts, a telegram like the following from a Lodge
in . our own jurisdiction, showing a lack of confidence, by limiting
expenditures which are beyond our . control, is greatly to be deplored:
"Bro. L........ dead at ............ , . . . Street. Extend
courtesies. If financial assistance needed for funeral, limit
expense $75."
The two following telegrams are self-explanatory:
"S. F., July 26, 1912.
"Secretary .............. , Lodge No....... , Connecticut.
"Brother A. A. dead. Family wants Masonic funeral. Wire
instructions.
"Masonic Board of Relief, S. F."
" .......... , ., Connecticut, July 27, 1912.
"Masonic Board of Relief, San Francisco, Cal:
"Accede .to family request, but incur no expense to us
·
"Blank Lodge, No. Blank."

A WORD OF WARNING.

The large corporations and business houses req~ire their employes to pass a physical examination before a~cepttng them-and
rest assured the physicians who 1pake those examinations are honest
a~d give their employers the benefit of t~e doubt. Forty years of age
·
is also the limit.
The year just closed has been one calling f?r the greate7t amount
of relief in the history of this Board of Relief. In looking for a
cause I can only suggest that the widespread popularity of Southern
California has brought to our section many people who were unable
to maintain themselves after arriving in our midst. The low rates
of travel from the East to the West brought many craftsmen who,
being unable to obtain work and receive Master Ma~ons'· wages immediately upon their arrival, were forced to seek rehef at the ha~ds
of their brethren. Also a vast number of invalids-people suffering
from tuberculosis nervous prostration, rheumatism· or asthma, seek
the more genial ciimate of Southern California, after having expended
their money seeking health in their own state, vainly endeavor to regain their strength in the West. These must be given as the chief
causes for the excessive calls for relief.
Again look at the number of burials which have been supervised
by this Board of Relief, and the wonder is that our expe.nses have ~ot
been greater. However, it has been our ple~sur~ to contnbute our mite
to relieve the distress of our Brethren, their widows and orphans.

Past Grand Master William S. Wells, President of the
Board of Trustees of the Masoi:ic Homes of California, preiented a report of the stewardship of the Board for the past
} ear, as follows:

To TH1' M.". W:. GRAND LoooE oF CAtIF01tNIA :
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California herewith submits for your consideration and approval its annual report · for
the yea.r ending August 31, 1912.
The M.". w:. Grand Master having appointed W.". Elmer E. Stone
to the vacancy caused by the expiration of his term, the Board held its
annual meeting at the office of the Grand Secretary on October 14, 1911,
re-elected William S. Wells President, Motley H. Flint Vice-President
and Elmer E. Stone Secretary, and has during the year held regular and
1pccial meetings at both Decoto and San Gabriel. Reports of the Superintendent and Secretary and accountants arc made a part of this
report and show in detail the financial and general condition of both
Homes.
The improvements made at Decoto consist of remodeling the old
laundry building, making it into a comfortable five-room cottage for
the farm help; the painting of roofs and outbuildings, fences and stairways, and making of a croquet ground for outdoor exercise and the
usual necessary repairs and improvements to fences and buildings.
The improvements made at San Gabriel consist of painting the entire exterior of the building, the dormitory ftoors, remodeling of the
kitchen and changing all outside •entrances to make them suitable for
the use of the children. A plant for the sanitary disposal of sewage
has been installed, and grading of grounds to straighten the course
of a wash which threatened much damage last winter. The Board made
n most fortunate exchange of properties in transferring the property
listed in our last report as "Hadley lots" and securing approximately two
and one-half acres adjoining the Home, which through the kindness of
the Scottish Rite Bodies of Los Angeles are now being improved with
play-ground equipment. This ground was stony and sandy, but ":'hen
grading was done, with heavy soil covering it, it packed well and
proved particularly valuable for the purpose. From a real estate point
of view it is worth three times its cost, although we inventory it at
the cost figure. The general grounds have been much improved the
past year through the constant care of Brother Bettes, many of the
new plants and ftowers being propagated by himself in our own
green-house.

The vineyard and orchard are virtually producing nothing this
year on account of the dry season. The vineyard is deteriorating and
we fear that it will be necessary to take it up entirely, as it does
not pay for the labor expended on it. A new orchard will have to
be set out to provide for the future needs of the Home. We have
some two hundred and sixty-eight (268) acres of land in our tract,
much too large for our needs, and it is the opinion of the Board .that
it would be well to dispose of a portion of it, say the westerly end,
where the vineyard now is, and use the money for other purposes.
We could dispose of an hundred acre strip on the westerly end without injury to the balance of the property, leaving ample for all future
requirements, and we recommend the authorization for the Board to
sell when in their judgment the time and price justifies.
The general health of the residents has been good. While the
deaths have been on the increase it is owing to old age and general
natural conditions. We have had no epidemics of sickness at Decoto

pleasant and happy, and . we want to thank the fraternity and our

We desire to express our sincere thanks to all of those. who so
kindly contributed to our Christmas fund and .~ade d~nattons and
gifts and to those who have entertained our families durmg the rear. .
The' efforts and la.h ors of the Superintendent and matrons have been .

Decoto, Alameda County, Cal., September 1, 1912.
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California :

Brethren: The undersigned presents the fourteenth annual report
ns Superintendent of the Masonic Homes of California,
During the past year the work at the Decoto and San Gabriel
Homes has been carried on along the same lines as previously. Many
changes in the details of management ha-..:e been made to secure a
higher standard of service in the several departments to the end
that while those who are no longer active will enjoy the peace and
comfort that only a home can give. The younger wards of the fraternity are being carefully prepared for the responsible duties of
life. All are encouraged to render assistance however small it may
be for the well being of the homes, and the families at both homes are
loyally assisting the efforts made by the fraternity for their care and
protection. A good spirit prevails and every effort is being made to
realize the ideals for which the home stands. A further development
of the social side of the family life has been made this year. Recrear
tion grounds have been provided with proper equipment which furnish
wholesome outside exercis'e for all who are able to enjoy them. The
reading tables have been well supplied with daily papers and maga.zines and several donations of books have been placed on the library
shelves.
There are now at the Decoto home sev·enty-one men and thirtysix women. Every room is now occupied and admission from now
on can only be made as vacancies occur. The urgent need for additional room to accommodate those now on the waiting list is respectfully presented for your consideration. During the past fiscal year
there have been nineteen admissions and twelve deaths.
The generous gift · of Islam Temple A. A. 0 . N . M. S. in presenting to the Home an up-to-date moving picture machine with a
stereopticon attachment marks an important advance in the social side
of our family life. It has been permanently installed ·in the organ
loft of Siminoff Temple, and we are now able to give weekly entertainments of moving pictures and with the stereopticon illustrated
songs and lectures can be given. They are not only entertaining but
educational in their influence. The films and slides are easily obta.ined
of great variety and will be a continual source of pleasure to the
residents. Salinas Lodge No. 204 kindly furnished the curtain, ropes,
tools and slides which complete the moving picture equipment.

PROCEEDINGS OF '.rHE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

A croquet and quoit ground has been also provided, together with
croquet and quoit sds, the gift of Occidental Lodge No. 22.
The carpenter shop has in addition to minor improvements and
general repairs made several pieces of furniture, among which are two
large music recor!l cabinets, six dressers, two bookcases and twenty- .
five ta hies.
The roofs of all the buildings and reservoirs have been put in
repair and painted ; the fence fronting the home, about a mile in
length has been painted, also all posts and benches on the grounds.·
The barn a.nd employees' cottage have been painted, and the interior
of the stables, dairy barn, chicken and hog ranch has been whitewashed. The laundry building has been remodeled and repaired a,,d
is now used as a cottage for employees. A tailor shop has been
opened up in the annex where men's clothing can be cleaned and
pressed.
The residents are encouraged to assist in the routine work of the ·
home. The spirit of service so far shown has made it possible to
operate the shoe shop, tailor shop, work the chicken and hog ranch,
vegetable garden · and carpenter shop. The mending of household linen
and making of table cloths, sheets, etc., is done by the valuable help
of the ladies, and with their assistance twenty-four hundred quarts
of fruit have been preirerved and are now stored in the fruit room for
winter use.
Owing to the scarcity of rain last winer, the Home springs failed
to give the usual supply of water. It has been necessary to haul wa,t er·
for general use ; the small supply of the springs has been conserved
for special household purposes.
The returns of the orchards and vineyard, also the ve11:etable garden, have not been good this year, and the walks, flower beds, roads,
etc.... have been given but little · attention on account of the dry season.
All holidays have been observed in keeping with the day and in
the usual manner; Memorial Day with exercises at the Home after
which the Home plot in the cemetery was visited and floral tributes
placed upon all graves.
During the year entertainments consisting of musicals, vaudeville
and moving pictures have been given by individuals, lodges and members of lodges with their. ladies, all of which have been much enjoyed and aippreciated by all. The following is a list of those so
entertaining : Prof. H . B. Pasmore and the Pasmore Sisters ; Sequoia
Lodge No. 349 ; members of Sequoia Lodge No. 349 ·with their ladies;
members of Oakland 'Lodge No. 188 with their ladies; members of
Golden Gate Lodge No. 30 with their ladies; quartet from student~
of H. B. Pasmore; San Francisco Normal School Glee Club; Mr.

l i W. Perdy and five members of "Hizz Fun Makers;" J ewe! Lodgr
No. 374 and Jewel Chapter No. 238 0. E. S., with band of thirtJ
pieces under the leadership of Prof. Cassassa; members of Occidental
l,odge No. 22 with their ladies. In addition to these there have been
many little entertainments among the residents of the Home, the men
1ntertaining the ladies in their club room and card parties given by
the !~dies in the assembly room, etc.

SAN GABRIEL.
Our home for the orphans at San Gabriel grows in interest with
the fraternity as each year develops new features in the care and
training of our little men and women. Partly through heritage, of
course, these children are refined in manner and bright in mental
and physical action, but the comfortable surroundings and daily influfnce and discipline the Masons of California provide for them in
this home will mold their lives fot tnuch greater future usefulness.
N cw children received soon adapt themselves to the atmosphere of
the home so that little interrui>tion of any kind disturbs the real
fireside relationship of this large but happy family.
The health of the children is now perfect, the hospital rooms in
each dormitory are the least used of any in the building. In all
cases of epidemic careful quarantine rules were adopted for the time
nnd all means of prevention exercised. At the time infantile paralysis
was threatened, we closed the Home to visitors for about three weeks
as a matter of precaution. No case reached the Home. The only
other contagion met was diphtheria, which brought us four cases, and
mumps kept several pairs of jaws quiet for a while last spring. We
must report one death, the first to come to our family. Little Leonard
Stone, aged four years, was afflicted with a: throat trouble and unfortunately was one of those taken with diphtheria. The same treatment was given him as the others, but the complication of the throat
trouble and the diphtheria was too much for him to master.
The number of visits of Lodges and Eastern Star Chapters were
greater this year. · The children enjoyed the visits and delighted to
furnish some little program on these occasions. New drills by boys
and girls were given, new songs prepared, and the music haa. shown
1plendid progress.
All holidays have been suitably observed with exercises appropriate
to the occasion. The Christmas exercises held in the assembly room
on December 25 were particularly interesting. The decorations made
by the children were exceptionally beautiful. The generous fund subscribed by the several lodges made this occasion the best of any holiday season that we had experienced. A number of local Lodges at
Christmas added some special features to the program.

Special mention must be made here of. the thoughtful and conscientious interest shown by Dr. J. M. Dunsmoor. The high standard
of health among the children is due largely to his watchfulness of
every sanitary condition and prompt action in cases of contagion.
We desire to express our sincerest gratitude also. to Dr. Nannie C.
Dunsmoor and Dr. Frank D. Bullard, who, with Dr. J. M. Dunsmoor, ·
operated upon a number of the children for adenoids and · enlarged
tonsils. They were assisted by Robert Dunsmoor, a senior medical
student, an~ Mrs. Harriet Warfield and Miss D. Renney, who volun·
· teered their services as nurses.
Mrs. Ola Taylor by her frequent visits at the home and her ready
and willing assistance in emergency and her cheery and hearty participation on all occasions with the children has endeared herself to
them by most affectionate ties. She is loved by all and brings more
sunshine in the home than any other visitor on our register.
We desire to acknowledge the faithfulness and interest displayed
by Miss E. L. Olcott and Mrs. Lela Buckham, who are practically
donating .their services in the musical instruction of the children. They
accept little more than their expenses of the trip to the Home, but
have rendered a most valuable service in this important and most
delightful branch of our Home work for the children.

Brother Edward S. Valentine, Chairman of the Special
Committee appointed last year to devise an index system·for
the membership of the Grand Lodge, presented the following report:
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Special Committee to whom was referred the task of devising and installing an i!1dex system of registration in the office of
the Grand Secretary, whereby the name and Masonic history of each
member in the jurisdiction could be readily found, beg to report : That
with the co-operation of the Grand Secretary we collected data from
many jurisdictions using index systems, and after carefully studying
all' of them-and they were all meritorious-we adopted a modified
form of the system in vogue in the State of New York, the Lodges
of which State have a membership now of 175,(XX). The system was
formally started on the first of August, 1912, and although the Grand
Secretary has had -but two months' actual experience with it, it is
apparent that our choice was wise, and that by the expi~ation of
another year it will be possible to find the name and Masonic record
of every member at a moment's notice.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

103

The scheme of indexing adopted consists of cards, each bearing
n number and the name and Lodge of a member. These cards are
filed in a steel filing case, arranged in alphabetical order with one
thousand subdivisions of the alphabet. Books have been p~ovided of
heavy linen paper, with ruled lines, each line bearing a numbe; to
<orrespond with a card number, with headings for name date of
nffiliation, Lodge of which last a member, age at initiatio~, occupation, w~~re born, residence (city or tow.n), dates of initiation, passing
nnd ra1smg'. ~ates when dimitted, suspended, expelled, restored, died,
nnd an add1t1onal column for remarks. A oopy of all the above information is k~pt in sheet fonri, arranged by' Lodges, and filed in a
1teel document-filing case, and in the event of a Lodge losing its
rtcords by fire or -otherwise, the Grand Secretary can supply the
1 ecord of members.
. The installation of this system has already done away with the
tl'd1ous labor heretofore required of Secretaries in copying the entire
li~t of i:iembership on the annual returns, as the only report now necruary ts to show the losses and gains for the year.
Our membership as reported July 31, 1902-ten years ago-was
?4,735. T he number of names on the list July 31, 1912, was 48,315,
n tremendous gain not only in numbers but in the work of the Grand
Stcr~tary's office. It is evident that our membership in 1922 will approximate nearly 90,!XX>, and the annual printing of a roster will
i~1 a few years be a burden, the benefits of which would not be justified by the expense. We recommend, however, that the Roster be
1 ontinued in printed form as usual until the index system is completely worked up as to current membership. This is a matter that
can well be considered next year.
Last year Grand Lodge appropriated $1,000.00 for the installation
o>f the index system. This was nearly exhausted in the purchase
,lf steel furniture, books, cards and blanks necessary. The work
hns. been carefully planned, iand it was considered the part of good
business to encourage the purchase of steel rather than wood cases
thereby lessening- materially the danger of loss by fire.
'
We recommend that the necessary expenses of clerk hire, stationuy and postag.e for the ensuing year be paid as are other bills against
the Grand Lodge, after being duly audited by the Committee on Accounts.
Respectfully submitted,
Hl!NRY Ascaon.

Brother Edward S. Valentine, Chairman of the Committee on Endowment of the Masonic Homes of California,
presented the following report:
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
We, the Endowment Fund Committee of the Masonic Homes of
California, beg to present this, a partial report of our labors during
the past year.
Shortly after the close of the last annual communication of the .
Grand Lodge this Committee met in the offices of the Grand Secretary,
a majority of the Committee being present. After consideration of the
duties of the Committee, the work necessary to be performed, etc., it
was deemed best to request ideas and suggestions from well informed
Masons in the Grand Jurisdiction, as to the best method of procedure
in accomplishing the desired result. Accordingly, a circular letter (a
copy of which ·is attached to and made part of this report), was
formulated and addressed to two hundred and fifty prominent and
representative brethren. This letter contained a request for their assistance in the way of idea~ and suggestions as to how best to reach
and arouse an enthusiastic sentiment in favor of the Endowment idea
-in formulating a plan which would in a measure bring about concerted thought and action by the great body of Masonic brethren in
California. Your Committee regrets to report that there came an immediate response from but fifteen out of the two hundred and fifty
addressed, but we are proud of those fifteen good brethren who did
reply, for from them came splendid ideas and suggestions which have
been of great assistance to this Committee in formulating its plans.
Undoubtedly the other two hundred and thirty-five br-ethren are in
hearty accord with the aims and ideas of the Grand Lodge, but like
us feel keenly the magnitude of the undertaking and will "ask for

further time."
We believe that it is but just and proper that the Masons of this
jurisdiction should be fully informed as to what has already been
accomplished with the means at the disposal of .the Board of Trustees
of the Masonic Homes of California; also what is desired to be .
accomplished. We have prepared a brief summary or history of the
Homes. This we purpose using in such manner as may be considered
wisest by this Grand Lodge in furtherance of the work of the Endowment Fund Committee, and which is respectfully submitted for consideration.
In view of the financial situation, your Committee has refrained
from making any specific appeal to the fraternity for donations up to
the present time, but has utilized the time in making preparations.
Notwithstanding no specific appeals have been made, we are pleased

am?ums. This 1s very gratifying and encourages us in the belief of
ultimate success in securing the attention of the fraternity to th
needs. of those. noble institutions, our Homes, a-nd the endowment
s~ffic1ent ~agmtude to place them beyond the possibility of failure or
?indrance in the good work now being accomplished through the medium of the Homes.
~ong other suggestions received by your Committee, was that all
Subo~dinate lod~es take up the work of creating within their membership a fund to be known as "The Endowment Fund for Masonic

this Grand Lodge and recommend their adoption:
First: The Grand Lodge consent to the creation .of a separate
fund in each subordinate lodge of this jurisdiction, said fund to ~e
known -as "The Endowment Fund for the benefit of the Masomc
Homes of California."
Second : Said fund shall be created solely from the voluntary
contributions of its members--of cash or property-and shall be continued for a period of five years.
Third : The Master shall appoint a Committee of t.hree members
.of the lodge, whose duty it shall be to do any and all thmgs necessary
to be done to create and promote the interests of the Perma~ent Endo~­
ment Fund of the Masonic Homes, receive all contribut10ns to said
fund and pay same to the Secretary of the lodge when collected. The
Secretary shall remit same to the Grand Secretary of the Grand
Lodge for the benefit of the Masonic Homes.
Fourth: No compensation shall be paid to any person at any
time for services rendered in creating and maintaining the Permanent
Endowment Fund.
Fifth: Immediate action by subordinate lodges in the creation of
the Fund to be appreciated and duly recognized by the Board of Trustees of the .Masonic Homes of California in such manner as may be
deemed appropriate by them.
Sixth: Such portion or portions of this Committee's ;eport .be
embodied in pamphlet form together with any other informat10n .which
may be deemed of importance, and said pamphlet be placed m the
hands of every Mason on the Roster of this Grand Lodge so far as
practicable to do so, at as early date as possible, preferably at sa~e
time instructions are promulgated to lodges rel~tive to the cr~ation
of the Permanent Endowment Fund referred to m these suggestions.
Seventh : That the , expense incurred in carrying out these suggestions is a proper charge, and be paid out of the ~eneral Fund ~f
this Grand Lodge, in same manner as other ex?enses incurred ~y this
Committee during the past year-as per special recommendation of
Finance Committee, page 205, proceedings 1911.

Copy of Circular :
ENDOWMENT FUND COMMITTEE MASONIC HOMES,
Grand Lo~ge, F. & A. M., of California.
Dear Sir and Bro. :The Special Committee on Masonic Homes in its report at session of 1909, which was adopted, recommended the establishment of a
Permanent Endowment Fund of at least One Million Dollars for the
maintenance and support of the Masonic Homes of California. At the
last session of the Grand Lodge this Committee was appointed, and
we have now begun our labors.
The Committee is keenly sensible of the many difficulti-es attending the performance of so great an undertaking, and appreciate the
labor necessary to arouse the interest of the Craft, but feel that with
the assistance of the zealous and unselfish Masons, leaders in the
noble work, by their valuable and wise suggestions our work must be a
success.
Knowing your love for the Order, and the great interest manifested in all things which make for the good of the Order, we a:re
writing this to enlist your assistance. We will greatly appreciate
any suggestions you may see fit to 1tive tQ this Committee as to the
best method of procedure to arouse the interest of the Craft in this
jurisdiction in the movement towards creating this Endowment Fund
by donations, endowments, provisions in wills or otherwise.
This is not a request for a donation; we only want your ideas,
which will be appreciated.
Please give this your attention at your very earliest convenience.
Yours fraternally,

for the Committee.

A BRIEF HISTORY OF THE MASONIC HOMES OF
CALIFORNIA.
It will possibly be news to many well informed Masons of the
State to learn that the proposal to found a Masonic Home in California was accepted by the First Grand Lodge, held in 1850. Vol. 1,
page 42, proceedings 1850, recites the donation of ten acres one mile
from Sacramento for a Masonic Home by Bro. A. M. Winn. This was
an unconditional offer and was accepted by the Gra~d Lodge. No

108

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND I,ODGE OF CALIFORNIA

action beyond the appointment of Trustees was taken at that time.
Proceedings were continued from year to year until 1859, when it
was discoV1ered tha..t the land donated by Bro. Winn was included in
the Sutter Grant, and no further steps were taken with that land.
The matter of Home was not raised again until the year 1876, when
it was again recommended by tpe Grand Master, but no action was
taken. In 1880 a Committee was appointed, but it appears that nothing was done by that Committee. Efforts were made at the sessions
of 1889, 1890 and 1891 to establish a Home which was finally in the
latter year successful and the project took on new life. The Committee was sucoessful in arousing the. Cra.ft to the necessity of a Home.
Subscriptions were asked for and a generous response came from all
sides. At the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of 1892, reports showed subscriptions to the amount of $25,359.50 from 154 lodges
-and $19,400 from other sturces, mainly allied Masonic Bodies; also
included two private subscriptions of $5,000 and $2,000, respectively.
The year following the fund was increased to $57,142.50, and the present site at the Home · at Decoto, consisting of 267.46 acres, was purchas·ed at a cost of $33,093.00, and plans for the main building were
adopted. Matters were allowed · to remain in abeyance for the next
three years owing to the financial condition of the country. On October 14th, 1896, the Corner Stone of the Masonic Home at Decoto
was laid by the Grand Lodge in full form, Grand Master ·Preston
officiating. Grand Lodge attended in a body, and after the ceremony
was entertained at luncheon as gue·sts of Alameda Lodge No. 167. Ori
October 12th, 1898, the Home at Decoto was dedicated with full ceremony by the Grand Lodge, M. W. Thos. Flint, Grand Master. The
Grand Lodge attended in a body, escorted by Golden Gate Commandery No. 16, Knights Templar. By this time considerable enthusiasm had been aroused and the donations from the va:rious Masonic
Bodies, individual Masons, and other sources (among others a Masonic
Fair held in the City of San Francisco during the year of 1898 which
yielded the magnificent sum of $39,000.00) , were of such magnitude
as to warrant the Board of Trustees in making extensive improvements in the plans-and although the sum of $125,550.00 had been expended in the erection of Horne and acquiring the land, only $30,000
had come from the Grand Lodge funds. The Home was turned over
to the Grand Lodge free of all incumbrance. March, 1899, the Home
at Decoto was opened for the reception of residents and while the original intention was to restrict the beneficiaries to Widows and Orphans,
the Board of Trustees decided to receive also aged Brethren, and there
wer-e accommodated and cared for the first year 16 men, 5 women,
IO boys and 6 girls, a total of 37. This number was gradually increased until in 1908 there were resident at the Home 138 people,

To the M.'. w:. Grand lodge of California:
I am very sorry I cannot · meet with you and the brethren at the ·
coming Annual Communication bo be held in the City of Los Angieles.
I am sure it will be an· occasion of much interest to the Craft, as
well as a great Joy to partake of the hospitality and good cheer
which await you in the far famed City of the South. But my doctor.·
advises me that it would not be prudent to "expend my strength
in the long journey and then join in the duties and business, as well
as the social activities which I know await the brethr,en in this, the
annual gathering of our Ancient Craft.
For these I'easons I deem it prudent to forego the pleasure · of
filling my alloted station among the Officers of the Grand Lodge.
But, be assured I shall be with you in spirit with the recollection of the '
friendships and fraternal greetings of many whose faces were once
familiar in our midst but are now enjoying the richer and more '
enduring companionship of those who, having completed their earthly
pilgrimage, are now resting from fheir labors where friendship continues forevermore.
Fraternally yours,
EDWARD CoU:MAN,

· The evidence was conflicting and covers some ninety pages of

followed in courts of law. If the accused · has had a fair opportunity

has no just cause for complaint.
·

ieels that he' is' disqualified as a member of this Board after using

To the M. '. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The Committee on Grievances to whom was referred a transcript

by order of the Grand Master tried by San Jose Lodge, No. 10, submit the following:
The charge against the accused,. in addition to unmasonic conduct,
is in brief that he, in his capacity as manager of various companies in
the Pajaro Valley, was guilty of financial irregularities and embezzlement.
The accused admitted some irregularities, but. denied any intent to
cheat, wrong or defraud, expressed sorrow for his irregularities, and
made complete financial restitution. The Commission, by some process
of reasoning too abstruse for us as a committee to follow, found him
not guilty upon specifications 1, 2 and 3, made no finding upon specification 4, but found him guilty of unmasonic conduct. On this finding
he was sentenced to suspension.
It has been, repeatedly held in this Grand Jurisdiction that unmasonic conduct is not a Masonic offense upon the finding of which
sentence can be imposed. It is a manifest absurdity to acquit the
accused of the acts alleged to constitute .unmasonic conduct and in the
same bre'ath to find him guilty of unmasonic conduct. If a man should
be accused of felony in that on a certain day and at a certain time
he committed the crime of burglary, it must follow, as a matter of
course; if they could not convict him on a specific act of burgfary
they could not convict him on the general charge of felony. It follows
then that the judgment should be reversed.

fraternity. We do feel, however, that a wanton and deliberate disrciard and neglect of an admittedly just bill is a Masonic offense and

charge is unsatisfactory and inconclusiv,e, and it appears therefrom that

the sum of $75.00 to go through insolven~y for the express purpose
of freeing himself from the legal obligation of this bill. It certainly
would appear that that sum might better have been applied to his
Indebtedness to the accus.er.
Your Committee is of the op1mon, taking into account all of the
circumstances of the case, that the brother probably acted as fairly
ns he deemed himself able to do, and that the judgment of the Commission in finding him guilty of unmasonic conduct is unwarranted.

To the M.'. w:. Grand'Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievan~s, to whom was referred a transcript
of Trial Record No. 121 of Sierra Madre Lodge, No. 408, upon charges
preferred against him by a brother of the same Lodge, submit the
following :
The charges themselves are extremely informal in character and
admittedly based upon a letter received by the accuser from a woman,
who charges the accused of being the father of her f.emale child born
out of wedlock, and that knowing her condition he had married another
w.oman.
No legal evidence was produced before the Commission to sustain
the charge. The woman in question was not called as a witness. Her
deposition was not taken. An abortive effort was made to obtain a
statement from her in something approaching a legal form, but even
that was not eventually done. A statement from the woman was received in evidence. The taking of this statement, however, was ex
parte and not attended with any legal formality. There was more or
less hearsay testimony tending to show that the accused admitted
having had relations with the woman in question, but also denying
that he was the father of her child.
The Commission seems to have been considerably incensed because
the accused apparently made no effort to appear before them, and is reported to have stated that he supposed "the Lodge would slip it to
him."
The accused brother appears to have been confined in the Los Angeles jail during the progress of the trial, although whether such confinement was upon this charge o r some other, does not appear. The
accused certainly does not seem a very promising member of the
fraternity, but in view of the extremely free and easy trial accorded
the accused, and realizing what a very dangerous precedent would be
established were Masons to be convicted of so grave an offense as this
charged, upon no evidence except that furnished by letters and hearsay
statements, we believe that the judgment should be reversed and the
matter remanded; and your Committee so advise.
Respectfully submitted,

H. M. OWENS,

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to whom was referred Trial Record No. 118, of
North East Lodge No. 266, having had the same under consideration, respectfully report as follows:
The charges preferred against this brother are set forth in the
following specifications: First-Habitual drunkenness; Second-Leading a dissolute life; Third-Exp<ising grip and signs in public places
while in an intoxicated condition. A verdict of guilty was rendered
on sp~ifications 1 and 2; and not guilty on specification 3, and
the penalty imposed was expulsion.
The record in this case comes before the Grand Lodge, both upon
the transcript of the proceedings had at the trial of the accused, and
also upon an appeal which is urged by the accused from the judgment
rendered. The appeal is urged on -three grounds, towit : Insufficiency
of evidence, errors of law, and failure to allow accused time to secure
witnesses. The appeal is supported by much evidence, otherwise competent were it not for the fact that the appeal itself was not made for
seven weeks subsequent to the time legally allowed for perfecting same,
(See Section 20, Constitution of Grand Lodge) This delay precludes
its consideration by your Committee.
However, we have examined with care the original transcript, and
find that in several respects the most elementary principles of evidence
have been · disregarded. Not only was hearsay evidence freely admitted at the trial, but witness after witness was permitted to draw his
own personal conclusions, instead of testifying as to facts within his
actual knowledge. We believe it to be an elementary principle of
Masonic law -that when a brother is charged with so seri~us an
offense as "habitual drunkenness" he has a right to demand that his
accusers produce facts and dates, and not ba·r e inferences or conclusions to support their charges. The charge of "habitual drunkenness"
involves such a continuous course of, or life of dissipation as to
naturally and necessarily inca·p acitate the accused from the transaction
of his ordinary business. The seriousness of the offense, viewed from
the Masonic standpoint, fully justifies the rule requiring the production
of sufficient legal and competent evidence substantiating such a charge,
before a Mason can be justly deprived of his character and standing
as a man and citizen.
In the opinion of your committee the transcript of testimony in this
case' 'fails to show sufficient legal evidence to sustain the verdict of
guilty_and judgment: .o f e:icpulsion, and we therefore .offer the following
resolution and. r~commen~ . its adoption:

Resolved That the action of Surprise Valley L odge No. 235 in the
matter of ch~rges preferred against Reco~d No. 266 be reversed, and
the case is hereby remanded for a new trial.
G!io. H. BURCHARD,
H. M. OwliNS,
A. B. W!iBS'l'ER,
FR!iD L. ARBOGAS'l',
GEO. E. CHURCH,

Committee.

The Grand Lodge refused to ·concur in the views o~ the
Committee, and the action of the Trial Lodge was sustained.

Your committee, to whom was referred Trial Record No. 123,

Charges were filed against the brother, charging him with unmasonic
conduct in five specifications, as follows:

the Master of his Lodge to "post" a brother, nearly always appeared
at the brother's house in a semi-intoxicated condition, much to the ·

Second-'f'hat said accused, while thus engaged in "posting" tht

Third- That about two years ago a brother, of Hermann Lodge,

Fourth_;That said accused was, on the 26th day of July, 1911,

F ifth- "That I, myself, have seen said accused within the last two
years at various times and at various public places, sometimes in a semiintoxicated and sometimes in an intoxicated state." For all of which,
etc. Signed by accuser.
The accused was tried before a Commission of seven and found
guilty of unmasonic conduct and expelled. He was found gui~ty of
specifications one, three and five upon the uncorr.oborated testimony
in each case of one witness. The a ccused denying the material testimony
relativ·e to the first and third specificati-ons, and admitting that he
had been intoxicated on different occasions, but that he had not taken
intoxicating liquors to excess since last January (ten months previous
to the trial), and that he has not been intoxicated since that. time.
It is obvious to your committee that the circumstance which precipitated the charges against defendant was the filing in the criminal
courts of a complaint charging him with rape.
.
The only evidence to sustain specification · ,f ourth. wa.s _the · introduction of a certified copy of the complaint from .t.he ,crmunal. c.ou,rt,
the accused testifying that he was not guilty of "the offense charged,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

140

141

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and that the action was dismissed on the testimony of the prosecutrix
herse.Jf.
No evidence was 'a.dduced to show that there was any truth in
the charge. On the contrary, it appears that there was no evidence
presented in court sufficient to justify even the filing of the complaint.
The presentation of a complaint or an indic;tment against a person
raises no presumption of his guilt. On the contrary, the law throws
around every person charged with crime the presumption of innotence,
which follows him throughout the ·trial, even to the finding of a
verdict by the jury.
A Masonic trial is strictly a criminal proceeding, and if the law
clothes a defendant in a criminal case with the presumption of innocence, should not the brother of a Lodge be more watchful and guard
well the rights which are so sacred to a Master Mason?
In the eyes of your committee, the only conclusive evidence
adduced which justifies the finding of guilty of a Masonic offense was
given respecting specification fifth, where a brother testified that he
had seen the accused int9xica:ted several times; and where the accused
admits that he has been intoxicated on different occasions, but that
he has not taken intoxicating liquors to excess since January, 1911,
and has not been intoxicated since that time.
The record shows that seven Commissioners tried the case, but
that only six subscribed to the same as required by Masonic law.
It appears to your committee that upon the filing of the criminal
complaint ag.a:inst the accused, which in itself is no Masonic offense,
the brdhren of the Lodge became at once aroused and endeavored
by the fine-toothed comb process, to find sufficient accusations against
him to expel him from the Lodge. We know nothing except what
the record discloses, and to us it appears that perhaps the Commission.
might have exercised more discretion and Masonic charity and endeavored to raise the brother by their counsel instead of excluding
him from the rights and privileges of a brother Mason..
We offer the following resolution end recommend its adoption :
Resolved, That ·the action of Hermann Lodge, No. 127, in the
matter of Trial Record No. 123, be, and the same is hereby reversed.

To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence submits the following report in
the matter of the decisions by the Grand Master on questions of
Masonic Law presented to him for determination.
As stated by the Grand Master in his address, he has followed the
commendable practice inaugurated by Grand Master Lawler in the
year 1909, of submitting such decisions as he deems it necessary to
report, to this Committee some weeks prior to the commencement of the
annual communication, to be reported by the Committee to the Grand

149

The following are the decisions submitted:
(References ar,e to Constitution adopted in 1911.)
Decision I: A request was made for a dispensation authorizing a
Masonic funeral, when he dies, for an old Mason 82 years old who
has dimitted many years ago. He had never made application for
affiliation, although ever since residing in this State.
This request was refused because the Grand Master is not authorized to issue a dispensation for such purpose. Also such a dimitted
Mason cannot be "the recipient of any of the rights, privileges, or
charities of the Order."
Secs 43, 165 Constitution.
The suggestion was made that the Lodge could admit the old
Mason to membership, if desired, and he would then be entitled to a
Ma.sonic burial. I am informed that this was done.
Committee: 'fihe ruling of the Grand Master refusing a dispensation was correct for the reasons stated by him. Section 165 of the
Constitution clearly defines the position of such a brother, and prescribes the only method by which he may be restored to Masonic rights.
We recommend that the decision be approved.
Decision 2: Can a Lodge refund a member who has paid dues
in advance, and rllen becomes a Life Member, any part of the dues
covering the time after such Life Membership begins?
Answer : It can. The part of such dues a Lodge may refund
should be oomputed from the end of the quarterly period during which
the Life Membership begins. Dues are payable quarterly in advance.
(Sec. 1, Art. IX, By-Laws.) Since dues are payable quarterly, it is
logical to compute from a quarterly period in refunding to a Life Memb.er dues paid in advance.
Committ11: This decision is correct. We recommend that it be
approved.
Decision 3: Is it possible for a member of a foreign Lodge, who
ia in arrears for dues and cannot afford to pay them, to petition a
California Lodge for the degrees?
Answer : It is not possible.

Committee: . This decision is correct. The same point was decided
by the Grand Lodge heretofore. (See Vol. 22,, Proc., pp. 18, 263.)
We have no right to accept as a. member one who belongs to a Lodge
in another Jurisdiction. We recommend that it be approved.
Decision 4: It is legal ·to install officers before St. John's day.
Officers are to be installed as soon as practicable after election. A
Master installed after Trial Commissioners elected, who is not otherwise disqualified, cari legally preside at the trial.
Committee: This decision is correct on both propositions. We
recommend that it be ·approved.

10 to do at a stated meeting,'' etc.
