1111' full moon regardless of the calender months, paying attention only
II• the lunar months. Am I right or wrong?"
1. Answer: It will not be necessary to cliilnge your By-Laws to
11111c stated day in the month. Many LodgeS' have provisions for stated
111n1 lnga similar to yours.
2. Sec. 78, Constitution, provides, "Each Lodge shall have not more
than one stated meeting in each lunar month, which shall be designated
11 such in its By-Laws."
By lunar month is meant from full moon to
lull moon. Sec. 1, Art. III of the By-Laws provides, "The stated
meetings of thiS' Lodge shall be holden on the . . . . . . in each month."
All the provisions of the Constitution of which the Uniform Code
..1 By-Laws are now a part must be read together to reconcile appar1•ntly conflicting provisions and ascertain the meaning of particular
provisions.
The words "in each month" in Sec. 1, Art. III, By-Laws, mean
In each calendar month, not each lunar month. So also the word
"months" in Sec. 2, Art. IV, By-Laws. Since "in each month" in the
Hy Laws means "in each calendar month," Sec. 78, Constitution, is only
11 limitation that stated meetings shall not be held oftener than once
tach lunar month.
Referring to foregoing table showing dates of full moon it appears
that Monday, March 25, is "before" full moon ' 1on" April 1. If no
regard is paid to calendar month there would be no way to determine
on which date the stated meeting should be held. But as the By-Laws
require a stated meeting "in each (calendar) month," and as there
could be no meeting in March except on March 25, that is the day of
meeting. As only one stated meeting could be held in the lunar month
ending April 1, the next meeting would be April 29.
Committee: We a.re of the opinion that the Grand Master solved
the somewhat complicated problem presented correctly. We recommend
that his decision be approved.

Decision 12: A Master of a California Lo\!ge requeated the Master
of another California Lodge to oonfef the Entered Apprentice degree
on a candidate duly received in the first named Lodge. This Wai c;lone.
The Lodge electing the candidate did not in any manner authori~
the Master to request the conferring of such degree PY t4~ othef
Lodge.

154

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Held, that the Master of a· Lodge cannot make such a request until
authorized so to do by his Lodge; that the Entered Apprentice was
an irregular Mason; that the first named Lodge should adopt a' motion
requesting the second named Lodge to confer the first degree upon the
candidate; that thereupon the Lodge that had conferred the degree
upon the request of the said Master should have the Entered Apprentice
brought before it and administer to him the obligation of an Entered
Apprentice and he then would be "healed." ·Or, that he should be
otherwise "healed" in his own Lodge.

Soe. 155, Constitution.
Committee: The Grand Master was correct in his conclusi,on that
the Constitution (Sec. 155) contemplates the conferring of a degree for
another Lodge only upon the request of such other Lodge, and that the
Master should not make such a request in the absence of action by
the Lodge authorizing him to do so.
However, the Entered Apprentice was not an irregular Mason. He had, in fa.ct, received the
first degree in a regular Lodge and was in all respect a regular Entered
Apprentice. Any possible irregularity in the proceedings would be fully
obviated by a subsequent ratifica.tion at a stated meeting by the Lodge
of the action of the Master, without going through the formality of requiring the degree to be conferred anew, in whole or in part. We
recommend the approval of the decision as thus modified.
Decision 13: The Grand Lodge lays corner stones "only of such
buildings as are either strictly Mas1Jnic in their character, or erected
exclusively for public purposes."

Decision 18: State of facts; The widow of a Mason, who was in
good standing at the time of his death, is taken sick at a plaoe different
from that where the Lodge to which her husband belonged is situated.
She goes to a hospital. She has a capital operation. She is without
means. She asks aid from a Board of Relief at the place where she is
sick. A member of the Board of Relief upon visiting her learns that
she is without means. He wires -the Lodge to which her husband had
belonged, asking "if the home Lodge had a~y objection to giving required aid?" The home · Lodge wired answer, "Give widow necessary
aid." The Board of Relief a few days aft>erwards paid hospital bills
of the widow amounting to $182.00.
Answer: The authority, "Give widow necessary aid" wa.s general,
unconditional, and authorized the Board of Relief to exercise discretion as to the manner and amount of the aid necessary to be given.
(See Sec. 90.) The duty of caring for the widow was on the home
Lodge. The Board of Relief in the place where the widow was sick
are presumed to have acted in accordance with their very best judgment.
as authorized by the home Lodge. The home Lodge should therefore
reimburse them what they expended for this widow. The Board of
Relief were acting as agents for the home Lodge, and if they made a
mistake of judgment that is no reason why the home Lodge should not
bear the burden of the expenses.
Committee: We are of the opinion that the authorization of the
Lodge was properly construed to warrant an expenditure in excess of
$25. It is important for all concerned that the officers of the Lodges
should be very explicit in their authorizations. We recommend that the
decision be approved.

Decision 20: Question: "Is it a Masonic offense for a Mason to
rent his property to be used for purposes of prostitution?"

158

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALl.li'ORNIA

Answer: Section 316 of our Penal Code makes it a crime to let
any tenement knowing that it is to be used for the purpose of prostitution. Our Supreme Court has declared that the renting of tenements
for purposes of prostitution is against public morals.
·
The renting of a house knowing that it is to be used for the purpose of prostitution \s not only a crime but a flagrant violation of the
moral law. It is therefore a Masonic offense.
Comrt1ittee: This decision is clearly correct. We recommend that
it be approved.

Decision 22: Complaint was made by the Senior Warden of a
Lodge that the Miaster opened his Lodge at 6 :40 p. m., when the hour··
fixed in the By-Laws was 7 :30 p. m. That before the hours for opening
a candidate was elected to receive the degrees of Masonry. I was
asked to restrain the Lodge from conferring the degrees of Masonry on
the candidate until it was decided whether he was legally elected.
Answer: Section 78, Constitution, is mandatory that the stated
meetings of a Lodge must be convened at the hour and on the day
fixed by the By-Laws; that the acts done before the hour of meeting
were irregular, ra.t best;" that the initiation of the candidate could be
stopped by simple objection if desired; that I would not be justified in
interfering with the Master simply on an ex parte statement by complainant; that the Miaster had a right to be heard; and that if desired I
would take the matter up with him, and that if a 'Master violated the law
in this regard, he would be subject to charges under Section 175, Constitution.
. Committee: This decision is· correct. We deem it proper to add
that we are of the opinion that a Master who convenes a stated meeting
of his Lodge prior to the time fixed by the By-Laws is guilty o( a
serious breach of duty, and that where such action is had for any improper purpose, charges should be preferred against him. We recommend its approval.
Decision 23 : Statement-A. Mr.· M., residing 'within the jurisdiction of a California Lodge applied for the degrees of Masonry to a

Sec. 124, note d, Constitution.

In a case like this there are two procedures, viz :
1. Mr. M. may petition the proper California Lodge to waive
jurisdiction in favor of the Nevada Lodge. His petition must be in
writing and state good cause and his request must lie over a month
and the Committee must be appointed and report at the next stated
meeting. (See Section 96, New Constitution.) In the case of a profane
seeking to join a Lodge in a foreign jurisdiction waiv.er can only be
granted by a unanimous vote as provided by Section 124 of the Constitution. His petition for waiver should be raccompanied by the fee
prescribed by the law of the California Lodge for the three degrees.
If your Lodge should grant the waiver they could retain the fee or
return it, as they decide.
2. The other method of· procedure is for Mr. M. to present a
petition to your Lodge for the degrees in the same manner that any
profane would do. Such petition would take the same course a.s any
ordinary petition. If the Investigating Committee report favorably and
he should be elected, the Secretary of the Nevada Lodge could certify
that he had received the first two degrees in that Lodge, which certificate should be attested by the hand and seal of the Grand Secretary of
the Grand Lodge of the State of Nevada. The third degree of Masonry
could then be conferred upon him by your Lodge, or by the Nevada
Lodge at your request, which request should be made through the
Grand Master of California to the Grand Mra.st·er of Nevada. The conferring of the third degree could be considered as ·having healed Mr.

All this was definitely decided by this Grand Lodge in the year

It has been decided that a California Lodge receiving an appli' ation from one situated as is Mr. M., may require the full fee
provided by its by-laws for the three degrees (Sec. 124, Constitution,
note "e" ). This amount, in the event of election or wiaiver, it may
deduct from the amount voluntarily paid to it by the Nevada Lodge,·
returning the balance to the applicant in the event that he is received
us a member, or to the Nevada Lodge in the e'V'ent of a waiver of
Jurisdiction. If Mr. M. be rejected on application, and a waiver of
Jurisdiction is not granted, the whole $75 shall be returned to the
Nevada lodge.
It should be added, in regard to the fees, that it is entirely within
the discr·etion ·of the California Lodge to require or to waive the
payment of fees for the degrees actually conferred by the Nevada
1,odge. Where a California Lodge receives such a person as a member it is bound to charge and receive the fee prescribed by its by-laws
for any degree it actually confers, or that is c-0nferred by another Lodge
for it, at i.ts request, and it is likewise bound to charge and receive
at 1east an amount equal to the sum prescribed by its by-laws for affiliation, when it receives as a member one who has received all the degrees in a Lodge of another state or country. In its discretion, it
may charge and receive a larger sum in all such cases, never, however,
exceeding in any case, the aggregate of the fee prescribed by its by-laws
for all the degrees. In the event of a waiver of jurisdiction in favor
of a foreign Lodge, it may grant such waiver without any payment
whatever, or it may charge and receive any sum n-0t exceeding the
full charge made by its by-laws for all the degrees. As was said
by the Committee on Jurisprudence in 1877 r·cgarding a waiver of
jurisdiction over a pers-0n not a Mason in favor of another Lodge
in this state (Vol. 13, Proc., p, 181), "the Lodge 'having the exclusive
right to receive the petition and the fees, may surrender its right as
to one or both, or may refuse as to either or both." · The same is true
as to a. waiver in favor of a foreign Lodge. But where it unconditionally waives jurisdiction, it ,loses all right to the fees and cannot
subsequently demand them (Proc. 1898, Vol. 23 Proc., p. 850).
We recommend ~hat the decision of the Grand Master be approved
in so far as it is in accord with · the views herein expr~sed, and
that in all other respects it be not approved.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California :

Brothers Wollenberg, Benton, Hammond and Griffith present the
following proposed amendment to our Constitution :
"Whereas, one of the principal .tenets of our Order is relief, and
we further are · obligated to properly aid and assist the stricken of
our craft; and
"Whereas; in furtherance thereof, we have provided ·homes for our
indigent and afflicted, but tlhe inadequate housing facilities and
generally inappropriate conditions of our homes, both at San Gabriel
and at Decoto, prohibit the proper carrying out of our duties as aforenamed; and
"Whereas, not less than fiffy thousand dollars will be required
immediately for the erection of new buildings to suitably fit said
homes for the purposes for whieh they are intended; and
"Whereas, the present general funds of the Grand Lodge are inadequate to ameliorate the aforenamed wants of said hoines, which
said wants are urgent and pressing :
"Now therefore be it Resolved, that Subdivision 2 of Section 41
(Sub. 2, Section 4, Ar.t. IX, P1art I) of the Constitution be amended
to read as follows :
"For each Master Mason borne upon its· roll at the date of its
annual report, the sum of seventy-five cents ; together with such sum as ··
the Grand Lodge shall appropriate at each Communication for the
support of the Masonic Homes of California; provi-ded, that in addition to the sums herein mentioned, each of said Lodges shall con·
tribute as annual dues the further sum of fifty cents for each Master
Mason borne upon its roll at the date of its annual report, the sum
thus raised to constitute a building fund for said homes."
The only change in our existing law proposed by this, is tlhe addltion of the proviso. Under the section as it now stands, each Lodge
pays to the Grand Lodge, annually, seventy-five cents for each Master
Mason borne upon its roll at the date . of its annual report, for
general expenses, and such additional sum as may be fixed by the
Grand Lodge for the 111aintenance of the Masonic Homes.
If this proposed amendment be adopted, each Lodge will continue to pay tlhese sums, and in addition will pay to the Grand
Lodge, annually, fifty cents for each Master Mason borne upon its

1ull

at the date of its annual report, the same to be used solely for

building purposes for the Miasonic Homes.
There is no legal objection to the proposed amendment.

1ho11ld be adopted.

maintenance of our Masonic Homes at Decato and San Gabriel, and
are of the opinion that, as heretofore, the tax of $1.00 per capita
should l>e continued. We are also of the opinion that the water
system at the Ma.sonic Home at Decato is wholly inadequate for its
present needs, and that prompt measures should be taken to install
a proper water system in said Home. We, therefore, offer the following resolution, and recommend its adoption :
Resolved, That the usual per capita tax of $1.00 be levied· on our
membership for the maintenance of said Decato and San Gabriel
Homes; and, further, that the sum of $5,000.00, and such additional
amount as in t:he opinion of the incoming M.'. W.'. Grand Master
may seem proper, be appropriated from the general fund of this
Grand Lodge for the purpose of developing and , installing a water
sys~em, and other necessary improvements in said Masonic Homes.
Your Committee on Finance has likewise considered the resolµtion referr·ed to it making an appropriation for the purpose of
defraying expenses to be incurred by the Endowment Committee of
the Masonic Homes of California in the discharge of its duties during

report as follows :
To the M.".

it is evident at the outset that the painstaking, efficient and enthusiastic labors of our v:. w:. Brother ha,v e continued to mark tht!
administration of his office.
No man whose heart was not in the work could continue without
varying the arduous duties of the office of Grand Lecturer. It is
apparent from !l11s report that, not only has there been no wearying,
but rather a fuller and deeper insight into Masonic problems as the
years have gone by, so that the office has become not alone the
fountain-head of ritualistic perfection, but the source of information,
counsel and guidance for those inexperienced in Masonic law and
tradition.
The Grand Lecturer makes timely and pithy comment on the
great care necessary in scrutinizing candidates for admission to the
Order. Now that Masonry has become popular, it well behooves us
to guard the outer door with peculiar care and discrimination.
Again, the Grand Lecturer has "hit :the nail on the head" in
his comment on the care to be taken in the selection of officers gen.
erally, and of Secretaries in particular.
We agree most hea.rtily wit'h the Grand Lecturer that the Annotated Constitution "fills a long-felt want," and that our deepest gratitude is due to its author.
That Brother Baker is ever on the alert to inaugurate some
pleasing and instructive custom which will increase interest in the
work is evidenced by the Inspector's degrees and his comments upon
them.
We note with pleasure· that the Grand Lecturer is able to report
a marked improvement in the ritualistic work, and that the Inspectors
have done their little to hold up the hands of their chief.
Brother Baker's report and comment on the third degree coaching lecture is both encouraging and instructive. Nothing has been
quite so painful in past years as the marked contrast between the
proficiency of initiates in the first and second degrees and their blissful
ignorance upon the third degree. Nothing but the reduction of the
sublime degree to systematic form could have solved this difficulty,
and it is only another evidence of the unwavering enthusiasm of
Brother Baker that the effort was made and the result attained, as

Brother Elmore M. Billings, Chairman of the Committee on Returns, reported as follows:
To the M.". W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
The growth of Masonry in our Grand Jurisdiction, as shown by the
returns herewith submitted, is splendid, and has no parallel.
All
Masons can study the returns and reports on this subject with pride,
and your Committee believe, as suggested by the Grand Secretary in
his report, that we will soon carry ninety thousand members on our
Grand Lodge Roster. And it is certain tha,t there are today within the
bqrders of our Grand Jurisdiction more than ninety thousand
good men and true who would honor our Lodges and !help us in the
great work we have to do if they were initiated into our mysteries and
became interested in our work of uplifting mankind. Still, Brethren, do
not forget tha.t not every man would make a valuable Masonic asset.
There are two conditions to which we desire to call your attention: A
brief study of our Masonic charities and the vast sums we so cheerfully expend in that behalf points with certainty to the fact that we
should look well to this side of the subject before receiving a petition

170

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and be convinced that he who would enter our gates must be able, as
well as willing, to extend his opportunities to do good to his fellow
men. A strong ~uspicion that mercenary motives are not entirely absent
may well arise where the petitioner has not sought fellowship in our
institution until the vigor of youth and manhood is frosted with "the
snows of winters that never melt." Then, Brethren, in the all important and sacredly secret consultation as to the advisabmty of receiving
a petition, let us never forget tpe duty we owe to our members, our
Lodges and to Masonry in general ; and that the common multitude
has no value to be compared with "the chosen few."
We have examined the returns of the Lodges for the current
year, with the assistance of the Grand Secretary, and take pleasure
in repor.t ing that the returns of all Lodges have been received by that
officer; that most of them were prepared correctly; that those that were
erroneous have since been corrected by the Secretaries, upon notice
thereof; that the dues in nearly every instance have accompanied the
reports, and that all dues have now been paid.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Afternoon Se.s·sion.
Thursday, October 10, A. L. 5912.
The Grand Lodge was called on at 1 :45 o'clock, the
Grand Mast·e r presiding.
M.". W.". James A. Foshay in a finis.bed, scholarly address, delivered to the pleasure and instruction and uplifting of his Brethren the annual oration, as follows:
M:. w:. Grand Master, Wardens and Brethreti of the Grand Lodge:
T:his has been a year of astounding prosperity. The Great Author
of nature, the Grand Master of the universe as well as of our5elves, has
dealt with us ri'chly and bountifully. It .has been a yea.r of wonderful
development in all the sciences and in all that goes to make up the sum
· total of happiness; and to prepare humanity for the great achievements
to come.
We are pleased to have this session of the Grand Lodge in our
sunny southland, where nature so lavishly bestows upon us ·everything
for our comfort and happiness. You are welcome to our hearts, to our
homes. May your coming bring to you no less of pleasure than to us

~~~~
.
.
This afternoon I would be to you a Spencer, of far-reaching phi·
losophy, and a Xenophon, intensely practical, but my wish, I know, is
vain,"I am no orator as Brutus is,
For I have neither wit nor words nor worth,
Action nor utterance nor the power of speech,
To stir men's blood."
Yet I am proud to occupy this station, so greatly honored by men who
have held it before me, and who have left to us a rich inheritance of
wisdom and of grace.
'!'EMPLE AND CHARAC'I'E:R BUILDING.

We rea.d in the Holy Writings that it was decreed in the wisdom ·
and counsels of Deity aforetime that a house should be built, erected
to God and dedicated to His holy name. "And Solomon selected 70,000
men to bear burdens, and 80,000 men to hew in the mountains, and
3,300 men to oversee them." This vast army of workmen of more than

181

153,000 was divided into companies, a.s best fitted their special qualifications. "And Solomon sent to Hiram, King of Tyre, saying, 'Send me
now, therefore, a man cunning to work in gold and in silver, and in
brass and in iron, and in purple and crimson and blue. Send me also
cedar trees and fir trees and algum trees out of Lebanon.' Then the
King of Tyre sent a cunning man; and cut the wood out of Lebanon,
which was brought in floats by sea to Joppa.'' This account marks the
beginning of a great structure, at a time held by many as -t he date of
the beginning cif what is now known as the Order of Free and
Accepted Masons.
This structure, perhaps the most wonderful in the world's history,
was known as King Solomon's Temple, and to it Masons have turned
for many ages for examples in operativ·e masonry. We are told that
the stones were hewn, squared, marked, and numbered in the quarries;
that the trees were felled and prepared in the foriests, and ihat the work
was so carefully planned by the architects and builders that the building was put together without sound of axe; hammer or any tool of iron.
What a wonderful description is this of silent yet marvelous workings
with most stupendous results, yet without nois.e or confusion I
The material was so carefully planned and finished that every part
fitted into its place with exact nicety. The material of which Masonry
is composed should be selected and prepared as carefully. As the Temple was a wonderful scientific and mechanical structure, such should be
in the moral world the body of the teachings of the institution of
Masonry, whose tenets have been transmitted through the ages, and
which for ages shall continue to endure. The wisdom which brought
into being our great fraternity is beyond our power to fathom, and
may we not believe that the Great Architect of the Universe ever has
had in mind the welfare and best interests of Masonry? The same
wisdom which designed our moral and spiritual edifice will maintain
it to bless mankind.
Masonry always has been synonymous with building. It is true
righteousness built into character, which is the grandest and best of
structures. The work of the initiate is that of a builder-he is building
a great temple of human character. It does not have to deal with bad
men and endeavor to make such good, for they are supposed to be good
at the beginning, but it makes good men better.
In art and symmetry, the Temple was a triumph of the human
mind. It stood unrivaled, an inspiration to every beholder. So must ·
the spiritual temple stand in its moral beauty and adornment as the
mystic creation of Him whom we all delight to serve.
In selecting material for our Spiritual Temple we must see that •
we are not misled by title, position, wealth or profession. We must .demand something higher, nobler and better than these. A man to fill a

183

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

place in the Temple of Masonry should be intelligent, that he may
understand its teachings; he should be iwcial and fraternal, that he
may enjoy the companionship of his brethren; he should be unselfish,
that he may practise charity; he should be scrupulously honest; he
should be broad-minded, ready to appreciate the deep lessons taught in
the several degrees. Perhaps one of the greatest deficiencies in the material from which we build the moral, Masonic edifice is ignorance of
the high moral ground which should be occupied by every Mason.
Craftsmen must be able not only to read the designs on the trestle
board but they must be able to carry them into effect. They must
have 'the efficient knowledge before they·can attempt to teach it to
others.
The first lesson taught in Masonry is "To be good and true,'' and
this fundamental principle is emphasized in every stage of the progress
of the initiate, It is the foundation upon which Masonry is established,
and upon which its stability and perpetuity depend. In Masonry is no
place for contention, but always there is room for emulation among
"who best can work and best agree"; where a· mild and beautiful influence for good reaches out into the world and betters all mankind, hy
making all nations purer and all life sweeter.
The building of King Solomon's Temple is emblemaitic of the formation of character. Man's character is being formed daily and hourly;
silently, unobserved by himself and others, yet surely. Much of this
silent upbuilding takes place in the home, where the child from infancy receives the shaping that determines his character and makes him
the true man. Th.en there is ·t he silent influence of the school, marvelous in its effects. There is the bible school and the church, influences
woven and interwoven until at last the beautiful Temple of Manhood
comes into existence, and the man so formed in silence becomes a
tower of strength in the world, and in his world-the community in
which he lives.
It is the duty of the Master Mason to see that the first impressions
of the entered apprentice are correct; that he is admonished to act
honorably and decently, to deal honestly by, and justly with, all mankind. Yet notwithstanding these admonitions, Masons may find competition similar in the lodge to that found in the general business world.
Masonry cannot be properly understood or appreciated without
necessary proficiency in the degrees as the candidate advances, and
this should involve knowledge of more than the Ritual; it should include the divine .truths and precepts of Masonry, its history and the
purposes for which it was instituted and has been maintained for all
t~se centuries. Intimately connected with the different branches of
equipment should be the provision of a Masonic library, where the

Muson can ha.ve opportunity to ·e nlarge his m~ntal culture and secure
the knowledge necessary for advancement and accomplishment.
We live in a jurisdiction whose outlook for the future is very
bright. With the completion of the Panama Cana~ bringing to us a
muss of foreigners who must be made true American citizens, and with
the peace policies of President Taft influencing our line of thought, a
1reat commercial growth necessarily wilt' come to this State. It should
be guided by those who fully realize that a national growth must be
founded upon morality, and they themselves should be willing to render
the services of citizenship.
In_ the ea.rly history of our country, conditions were different;
cities and great corporations and the fierce competition which has
tmnsformed commerce into industrial warfare, were unknown. Now,
one of the greatest questions before us is, How shall we care for the
hundreds of thousands-aye, millions of people who come to ?ur
8 hores from foreign lands? In many cases these people know nothmg

it is the silent influence which must aid in giving to them a training
in true American citizenship. There must be developed in ·them something more than a proper sense of responsibility and .obedience t?. authority-an esprit de corps of the highest order, which shall m1htate
for civic righteousness and moral culture.
If we are to meet the demands of California, our responsibilities are
stupendous. There must be a unification of all moral forces to counternct the movement of evil in our country. Our Order has helped to
produce many great men, who have done their part and left their inspiration to those who are now on the scene of action. Let it be known
to all forever · that Masonry stands for the development of the individuai. of his' integrity and personal worth, and that it will meet its
responsibilities to the full.
As the wonderful temple was reared silently but systematically,
nnd when it was. perfect in its completeness was dedicated to the w.orship of God, so Masonry at that time, while operative, was symbohcal

that we shall build into character that which is for the highest, noblest

the lodge room greatly helps toward the formation of character. In
the building of character, let us take care to see that material and

In harmony with the laws of nature, and the moral environment which

"In the elder days of Art
Builders wrought with greatest care
Each minute and unseen part;
For the gods see everywhere."
It is our duty ·to take the rough ashlar-the entered apprentice~to
note his possibilities and capabilities, and to assist him quietly and steadily to overcome self, to govern his appetites and passions, to realize that
he is a moral being, fit to attain his highest ambitions if he obey the
dictates of his better conscience, and thus to become an exemplar of ·
one of the greatest of institutions, whose noble influences and noble
deeds have merited the admiration of .the world.
It is our duty to teach carefully the seeker after truth as he passes
through the several stages and receives the degrees, and to unfold to
him the deep, underlying principles and truths of Masonry. We must
not think that the work is accomplished when a member receives his
full initiation, but we should assist in training him toward the highest
ideals which it is our privilege to have. It is the silent force which
makes for good citizenship and leads man to fulfil his highest and best
mission. If our work does not make the brother stronger and better,
and more fully prepare him to face the world, we have failed.
All men look forward to a ripe old age, in full possession of their
powers. We are admonished to be temperate and properly to care for ·
our bodies- to be temperate in eating and drinking, in work and
recreation, but more especially to avoid strong drink. The great literary
master says :
"Though I look old, yet am I strong and lusty,
For in my youth I never did apply
Hot and rebellious liquors in my blood;
Nor did not with unabashed forehead woo
The means of weakness and debility;
Therefore my age is as a lusty winter,
Frosty but kindly."
Masonry makes for character by precept and example. Each
Mason should build in himself a temple of imperishable character by
living the lessons that are taught in the lodge room. As the entered
apprentice is placed in the northeast corner of the lodge ready to begin
his work of preparation, so in life should he be placed in a moral environment, under the teachings of the Holy Bible and the guidance of
divine leadership, and so s'hould his character be formed. By working

1urrounds him, a Mason grows into a true, upright, moral man, and
fulfils his duty to be a strong, living force, and to exert a power for
1ood in the world.
Think, if you please, of the silent influences which are woven into
the characters of men through music, decorative art, beautiful archi·
lecture-all silently working together to make true men. The standard
»f beauty and truth set for us in the Holy Writings inspires the beautiful works and s~blime melodies of the musician, and we are lifted
out of ourselves in the comprehension of the beautiful symphonies and
oratorios of the great masters.
In the cities of the Old World civic administrators realize the necessity of positive ·t raining in morality and the rights and duties of'
citizenship. These can be taught to some degree in the schools and
colleges, but the teaching must be forwarded in such organizations and
societies as our own. The emphasis placed upon such teachings by
this fraternity compares, in some instances, to the zeal shown in parts
of the world by religious enthusiasts. Men who are leaders are beginning so to vitalize the subject of moral growth and training that
the people receive inspiration, and are assisted to grow into true manhood. Formal instruction in ethics and mora.!ity, URless vitalized and
humanized, is of little value; we must see to it that this vitalizing and
humanizing is a part of our accomplishment.
In some of the countries of the Old World, especially in England,
France and Germany, associations of men of wealt'h and education are
devoting themselves to the unfolding of the deep mysteries of Masonry.
It matters little, however, what further revelation the future may have
in store, for we already well know the fundamental truths, the strength
and support of Masonry, the foundation upon which stands the everlasting Temple.
We are unable to trace the descent of our Order from the original
temples of Egypt, Asia, and Europe, but we can safely assume that
Masonic- teachings, as given us today, are perpetuated in symbols and
characters which have been recorded from time immemorial. The
great Masonic library in the Temple of the Supreme Council of the
Southern Jurisdiction of Scottish Rite Masons, with more than 10,000
volumes on Masonic subjects and history, gives to us some idea of
the immense amount of labor and thought which have been devoted
by men of education, culture, and refinement to the production of
Masonic literature. Books, though silent, speak with the tongues of
~en and the learning of the great philosophers. We are permitted to
enjoy the society of the brilliant intellects of other ages, and to profit
by the results of their labors. ·

In the formation of character, much depends upon the influence of
environment. It, therefore, is the duty of intelligent, moral men to
assist in making Masonic environment for the community such, that it
shall fill this ideal purpose.
. Soci:ty exists because men always have realized that security comes
from union, and that each must give to the collective body something
from himself as an individual. The silent influences of our temple
should so enforce this principle that our citizenship shall rise high and
higher in the moral, social, and intellectual scale. Macaulay said
"Logicians may reason about abstractions, but the great mass of me~
must have images." Then let us see that every stimulus to the imagination shall serve the highest purpose.
One reason why the general tone of our citizenship is not higher is
because our people have not seriously attempted the proper training of
our young men, so that they may enter upon life with clean bodies and
clean minds. We well may look back to take lessons from Sparta,
Athens and Rome, and accept from them the ideals which they held in
regard to their young men.
Ian MacLaren, in his "Young Barbarians," gives this prayer:
"Lord, keep the laddies before Thee from cheating, lying and cowardice-which are of the devil. Be pleased to put common sense in
their heads and Thy fear in their hearts, and give them to be honest all
the days of their lives.;' This well may be adopted as the prayer of
our active men, because it sums up much of the teachings which have
come to us through Masonry.
1_1asonry represents altruism and Qptimism; its philosophy and
teachings cause us to see with prophetic eye into the future. But we
are living in a world of commercialism, of chance and change of materialism and utilita.rianism, and because of this we should emphasize the
finer teachings of this institution, and point our young men to their
opportunities of forwarding in quiet and helpfulness the work of our
society. Masonry should be synonymous with civic righteousness and
good citizenship. When lessons are taught and charges given, let
them ever carry with them the great import which the authors ·intended.
Our nation, our government, our social fabric depend in a very
large degree upon the protection and chastity of women. We, as
Masons, ever should stand ready to protect our wives, sisters and
daughters, and we should go. farther and defend woman because she
is a woman. To be honest in this we must maintain that purity of life
ourselves that will commend us to our brethren and to the community
in which we live.
·
. Mason;y should offer aid and leadership to the study of the questions of sex education and sex hygiene now engaging the attention

not only of the people in general, but of the schools as well; a study
that I believe is destined to revolutionize conditions and make for man's
future welfare and happiness.
Prostitution is not only seriously affecting men in the lower scale
of life-those we term wicked-but it is contaminating innocent people
as well, by causing paralysis, deformed children, insanity and mental
decay. It is time that we, as intelligent, stalwart, moral men should
lend support in some way to fhis movement to prevent moral and
physical degeneration. Statistics show that syphilis and gonorrhea, two
great venereal evils, are responsible for the threatening decay of our
people, while according to the statement of Dr. Morrow, of New York,
"Social tradition holds that it is a greater violation of conventional propriety publicly to mention this infection (gonorrhea) than privately to
contract it and carry it home to the family.''
I have seen the statement that the greatest contributing factor to
the social evil is men, and while we are spending large sums on rescue
homes, or endea.voring to check the vices by bringing the girls into
juvenile courts, we seem to lose sight of the fact that the remedy of
this great evil lies with men. By dealing with men and not with
women, we can settle this great problem.
Man must b.e true. His duty to his friends, his family, himself and
his God demands that he keep his body clean and pure. The call is to
right living, the formation of true character, and all should be enabled
to say,"My strength is as the strength of ten
Because my heart is pure."
We shall reach the high moral plane which is just before us because
it is our ideal and our inheritance. The members of our great fraternity, that grand army of noble men, should stand by its counsels and
reflect its teachings in their deportment and conversation-to extend the
true fraternal spirit and to be honest in their dealings.
It means much to a young Mason when he realizes that the officers
and leaders of his lodge stand well in the community; tha.t they are
men who can be trusted; that they do not lie and cheat; and that no
charge of chicanery, graft, or mismanagement is ever laid at their
doors. If young Masons find that those whom they are supposed to
obey as their leaders are not honest and do not exemplify true courtesy
and right living, they are likely to become cynical and skeptical regarding our loved so~iety. Let us, as men and Masons, ever be jealous of
the good name and seek to promote the best interests of Ma.sonry.
Where devotion to its ideals exists, Masonry greatly promotes true
moral character. One of its lessons that we must learn is to commit

ourselves to the ends of benevolence, not in impulsive acts or spasmodic displays of generosity, but in those which come from the growth
which generous impulses build into true manhood. The great work of
our institution is to train its members towa.rd the ends of benevolence.
For there is much of selfis'hness jn the world, encouraged by our·
general acceptance of the competitive idea in our efforts for achievement. The spirit of mankind seems to favor the tearing down of one
to build up another; but we as Masons should say to the community
by our actions that we believe in a nobler policy, in seeking to elevate
the whole body of our people, and in helping to make them all useful
citizens. How much harm has beert done in the world because of selfish
ambition! Let us help to develop that type of man who will not prey
upon his fellows for his own advanta.ge. What is needed today, in and
out of Masonry, is a vision of a spiritual ideal and strength for the
accomplishment of great things in the moral world. History shows
us that whenever moral ideals are not emphasized civilization suffe~s,
and while we ponder the maxims of philosophers and psychologists let
us not forget that the highest text book of ethics is the Great Book
which ever is open on the altar when a Masonic lodge is in session. Le;
co-operation take the pla.ce of competition, and let all work together for
that which is highest, noblest and best: We, as a nation, must build
for a stronger race of men, physically, morally and intellectually, but
above all we must establish cha.racter, the result of education and train~
jng, as the foundation of our Temple.
The ever-increasing complexity of our economic conditions, and
the race to get rich, makes it more and more difficult for thinking .
men, who realize the necessity, to build for the future that which shall
a~sist in creating a mora.l environment and in emphasizing the principles of right living, so that the integrity and prosperity of our country may be properly safeguarded. The influence of the love of money
has reached those who have been honored with positions of confidence
and power, and even in these days of prosperity, in practically all parts
of the world, it t'hreatens to destroy our civil liberty and undermine our
institutions. It seems to push aside our higher, purer and better
motives. But, brethren, let u~ see to it that there shall be 352 altars in
this jurisdiction alone, and more in the coming years, from which
brotherly love, relief and truth shall be exalted far above the love
of money.
We all seem bent on becoming rich, not realizing that wealth of
itself, has no moral or intellectual value or uplifting influence: I~ is
beneficial to. ~s only as it serves high ideals and noble purposes, as it·
makes conditions better for the individual and for society. If used to
improve physical conditions and the general environment of our people

In State and Nation, the possession of it should be encouraged, otherwise not. When it is use<i to lift up the fallen, and to bring all mankind into one vast fraternity, then it shows us that there is
"One God, one law, one element,

The tongue is an vnruly member, often used in repeating that
which is derogatory to the good name of a brother or a fellow man.
We must not be content simply to confer degrees, to permit men to go
out with no teaching except that which they receive when the degrees
are conferred. They must be taught the true, deep, underlying principles of Masonry. We must emphasize the cultivation of self-control in
our members, so that each one ma.y have an independence and individuality of character that will never accept for himself false or arbitrary
standards.
As our institution has hitherto flourished because of the results it
has brought about in promoting the general good of mankind, so should
we of today continue to share with the world that light which we receive
in the lodge room. A Master Mason should be thoroughly impressed
.
with the responsibility of high station and deep knowledge.
Masonry often has been misunderstood and misrepi::esented because
it has been confused with religion. It is religious in its teachings, but
does not profess to be a religion. It never has claimed to be a religion,
and it is very unfortunate that occasionally a Mason says, "It is a good
enough religion for me." Religion has been defined as "a belief binding
the spiritual nature of man to a Supernatural Being upon whom he is
conscious he is dependent, and the practice and duties growing out
of such belief." The Christian church, in general, sustains a very
friendly attitude toward Masonry. Masonry in no way assumes the
functions or takes the place of the church, and none of its ceremonies
suggests the supplanting of any of the sacraments of the church. The
church is waging a great battle against all sorts of dishonesty, wrong, injustice, and infidelity, and so is Masonry. The quiet, steady, active
influences of Masonry are needed to aid the church and assist in fighting
wrong-doing and in building up character. The church and Masonry
are doing parallel work. They are as the rails of the railway, running
side by side; they bridge the same rivers. and chasms; they tunnel the
same rugged mount;iins ; they extend side by side across .the broad
plains; they ascend t'he same heights; and at last may they together
enter the beautiful city that hath foundations and whose Maker and
Builder is God.
God ever has revealed Himself more powerfully and clearly through
the symbols of natur.e than through the works of man. With us con-

stantly are the examples of the wonderful works of God-our own
world, with its myriads of stars, its golden clouds, its beautiful flora
and interesting fauna, its magnificent mountains and delightful valleysthese numberless wonders speak to us silently, emphatically and reverently of Him who hold~ all things in His care and keeping.
The improvement of character, the systematic fraternal work, the
promotion of virtue, all should be results of Masonry. The invisible ·
part of Masonry is the spirit which animates and pervades the lodge
rooms, in manifestation of the vital, active principles that have been
emphasized through the ages. Let us realize that the ritualistic work,
the forms, ceremonies, signs and lectures, the visible part of Masonry,
are simply for the purpose of teaching and developing these very principles, that secret of vitality and power that has made Masonry what
it is through all the generations past, and shall maintain it for generations to come.
We are proud of our country and of the patriotism of our people,
but let us not forget that the highest patriotism is that men shall live
for their country as well as die for it. It is the daily living of a devoted
life that makes the patriot and the hero. We, as men, must cherish high
ideals, believe in them, and act them. As King Solomon first dreamed
of his wonderful temple and afterward builr it, so should we dream of
that which is morally elevating and spiritually uplifting, and then build
it into our noble Masonic edifice.
We are in.the midst of an unexampled political campaign. We are
hearing daily conflicting statements as to the conditions of our country,
its finances and its outlook. Orators draw us first one way and then
another. Each party endeavors to show that whatever it does is i:ight,
and whatever its opponents do is wrong. There necessarily is confusion in the affairs of the outside world because of the conflict of convictions. But if we follow our God-given model, the Temple, in building the character of ourselves and our fraternity, there can be no differences of opinion among us, for the standard set in the building of
the great Temple, the standard which should be our own, is the perfect
standard set by Him who sees and understands all conditions, to whom
is no possipility of error or of wrong.

M.'. W.'. Frank M. Angellotti, Chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence, reported as to the proposed Constitutional Amendment relating to concurrent jurisdiction,
as follows:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

213

' o the M.". W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
In his address last year Grand Master Weller recommended a
change in our Constitutional provisions relating to jurisdiction of
l;odges not having concurrent jurisdiction with other Lodges, owing
1 the fact that the "air line method" of determining jurisdiction is, "in
these days of trolley car and other means of rapid conveyance," not
nlways satisfactory. The matter was referred to this Committee with
Instructions to devise and report such changes as are deemed advisable.
After full consideration, we are satisfied that the law now in force
1hould prevail as the general rule. We are of the opinion that no
other method can l:>e devised that would be practicable. We realize,
however, that in rare cases, special circumstances may absolutely ;equire that a particular Lodge should have a special jurisdiction. We
think that where any such special jurisdiction is given, it should be given
only after notice to all Lodges interested and after full consideration
by the Grand Lodge, and that the boundaries of the territory of such
1,odge should be made a matter of record in our proceedings. This is
nhsolutely essential to prevent confusion and complaints of excess of
jurisdiction. We have prepared a Constitutional amendment along these
lines, providing for such cases.
We recommend that our Constitution be amended by adding thereto
n new section, to be know as 92a (Sec. 13, Art. II, Part III), to
read as follows :
"If it be made to appear to the Grand Lodge that special circumstances require that in the case of any particular Lodge or Lodges
the general rules as to the territory over which such Lodge or Lodges
fthall have jurisdiction should not apply, the Grand Lodge may by
resolution define the territory over which such Lodge or Lodges shall
liave jurisdiction. When such a resolution is adopted, the Lodge o.r
l,odges therein named shall thenceforth have exclusive jurisdiction over
the territory therein described, and shall have no jurisdiction, exclusive
•>r concurrent, over any other territory, or over any Mason, not a
member of said Lodge or Lodges, residing outside of such territory.
The provisions of Section 6, Article II, Part III (Section 82), shall no
longer be applicable to such Lodge or Lodges. No such resolution
1hall be adopted except upon the recommendation of the Grand Master,
and after reference to the Committee on Jurisprudence and report
!'hereon. Notice of the application for any such resolution, with a
precise statement of the poundaries of the proposed territory, shall
be given by the applicant Lodge or Lodges at least 30 days prior to the
commencement of the annual Communication of the Grand Lodge at
which the same is to be made, to each Lodge whose. jurisdiction
will be affected by the proposed resolution. Such resolution may be
repealed or 'modified at any subsequent annual communication of the

214

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Grand Lodge; provided t'hat no modification enlarging the territory included shall be adopted except upon compliance with all the conditions
prescribed for an original resolution. As long as such resolution continues in force, the provisions of this section shall, as to such Lodge or
Lodges, be paramount to all other provisions of this Constitution in
the matter of jurisdiction."

The report was adopted, and the Constitution amended
as above by unanimous vote.

AMENDMENTSTOCONSTITUTIOK
Adopted October, 1912.
\ 28.

Standing Committees.

The following standing .committees, to consist of five members
each, shall be appointed by the Grand Master at each Annual Communication, just before the close, viz: On Jurisprudence, on Finances,
on Accounts, on Grievances, on Correspondence, on Returns, on Pay of
Members, on Credentials, and on Library, the duties of which committees shall continue during the year thereafter, and shall cease at the
close of the next succeeding Annual Communication.
32a.

Committee on Library (New).

All members of the Committee on Library shall be residents of
t'he Bay counties, and it shall be their duty to meet at the Library of
the Grand Lodge once each month and on the call of the Chairman.
They shall have general supervision over the library, make and enforce
all rules relative to the care and loaning of books, and they shall have
the power to incur the necessary incidental expenditures with the
permission of the Grand Master.
41. Contributions, What Shall Be Levied.

2d. For each Master Mason borne upon its roll at the date of its
annual report, the sum of seventy-five cents; together with such sum as
the Grand Lodge shall appropriate at each Communication for the
support of the Masonic Homes of California; provided, that in addition to the sums herein mentioned, each of said Lodges shall contribute as annual dues the. further sum of fifty cents for each Master
Mason borne upon its roll at the date of its annual report, the sum
thus raised to constitute a building fond for said homes.
92a.

Jurisdiction of Lodges (New).

If it be made to appear to the Grand Lodge that special circumstances require that in the case of any particular Lodge ol' Lodges
the general rules as to the territory over which such Lodge or Lodge$
shall have jurisdiction should not apply, the Grand Lodge may by
resolution define · the territory over which such Lodge or Lodges shall
have jurisdiction. When such a resolution is adopted, the Lodge or
Lodges therein named shall thenceforth have exclusive jurisdiction
over the territory therein described, and shall have no jurisdiction,
exclusive or concurrent, over any other territory, or over any Mason
not a member of said Lodge or Lodges, residing outside of such
territory. The provisions of Section 6, Article II, Part III (Section

No such
•>lution shall be adopted except upon the recommendation of the
I.rand Mast<:r, and after reference to the Committee on Jurisprudence
nnd report thereon. Notice of the application for any such resolution
with a pr:cise statement ~f the boundaries of the proposed territory:
1h~ll be given by the applicant Lodge or Lodges at least thirty days
Pl 1or to the commencement of the annual communication of the Grand
I. ld.ge at .which the same is to be made, to each Lodge whose jurischct10n will be affected by the proposed resolution. Such resolution
inny be repealed or modified at any subsequent annual communication
•>f ~he ~rand Lodge; provided, that no modification enlarging the
lcrntory included shall be adopted except upon compliance with all the
1 rmditions prescribed for an original resolution.
As Jong as such
resolution continues in force, the provisions of this section shall,
ns to such Lodge or Lodges, be paramount to all other provisions of
this Constitution in the matter of jurisdiction.
I·

I 29a.

Saloon-Keepers Ineligible (New).

No Lo~ge. shall receive an application for the degrees of Masonry,
or for affihation, from any one who is engaged, either as principal,
agent or employe, in the saloon business (except in connection with
and ~s part of, the operation of a bona fide hotel or restaurant), 0 ;
who is a barkeeper; and any Mason who may hereafter enter upon and
engage .in the sal.oon b.usiness, either as owner, agent, or employe,
except m connection with and as part of the operation of a bona
fide hotel or restaurant, or who shall become a barkeeper shall be
deemed guilty of unmasonic conduct, and shall, upon due' trial and
conviction of said offense, forfeit all Masonic rights and privileges,
including membership in any Lodge.

PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO THE CONSTITUTION
(To be called up at the annual communication in 1913.)
Resolved, That Section 129a of the Constitution be amended to read
as follows:
. Sec. 129a. No Lodge shall receive an application for the degrees
of Masonry, or for affiliation, from any one who is engaged either as
principal, agent or employe, in the saloon business; and any Mason
who may hereafter enter upon and engage in the saloon business, either
as owner, agent or eniploye, s'hall be deemed guilty of unmasonic conduct, and shall upon due trial and conviction of said offense forfeit all
Masonic rights and privileg.es, including membership in ~ny Lodge,
except when acting under order of any Court.

ALABAMA, 1911.
The Ninety-first Annual Communication was held in the Masonic
I cmple in the city of Montgomery, December 5 and 6, 1911-M.'. w:.
Brother Lawrence H. Lee, Grand Master, presiding.
The Grand Master, in opening his annual address, says :
"Considered only as an institution, Masonry may be said to be
n voluntary association of individuals for mutual benefit and mutual
Improvement, governed by laws, customs and obligations, self imposed,
lo secure justice, fraternity, mutual happiness, and the just government
11ntl perpetuity of the institution itself. In other words, we represent
1111 ideal republic where mutual obligation, mutual interest and mutual
1ervice secure fraternity and the greatest good to the whole.
"The bond -0f union which securts this permanency in so large
11 body of men, united in one common cause-men differing in nationality, religion, occupation, social and financial standing, ought to elicit
more than a mere passing interest.
"It was upon precisely this idea of our ideal republic that Washington and his associates (all of them Masons) , founded our governnu:nt. Perhaps no better Masonic document was ever penned than
the declaration of independence and the Federal Constitution.
"Here, then, exists an ideal republic within that conglomerate mass
constituting the nation, composed of a body of men representing
equity, .fraternity and · equality. A living germ within an outer
Mtructure, numbering between two and three million men.
"Hence arises an important question. Has this body of men, so
t"ndowed and so prepared for the duties of citizenship no function,
office or duty to the community, on the part of the institution they con1tltute and represent? The answer is found in the distinction existing
(I )

between our ideal republic and the real republic we 'call our common
country. Here no one is admitted, unless after ca;e~ul exan;ination,
he is found worthy and qualified to assume, and .w1llmg to discharge
all the obligations necessary to secure fraternal umon and permanency.
In the real republic no such requisition is made or seems possible.
There men clamor for their rights who habitually disregard their
.
.
duties and ignore all mutual obligations.
"Not only is this true, but today the irresponsible part of the
citizenship of this republic is being added to annually ~y . more than
a million of the ignorant, oppressed and revenge~ul y1chms of the
aristocracy and clericalism of the old world. It 1s time, therefore,
that we were awake to the meaning and transcendant importance of
the existence maintenance and mission of this ideal republic (which
Masonry is) 'in the midst of the competition, strife and confusion of
tongues which constitute our present real republic.
"If every one of us should carry into the world of politics, eco- ·
nomics and citizenship outside, the principles and usages he recognizes and conforms to in the Lodge, Masonry could do .no more .than
all other combined influences to convert our country mto an ideal
republic where justice, equity and fraternity would replace ignorance,

vice, po~erty, injustice, bitterness a~d strife: .
"If the institution has no higher m1ss1on than to mcrease its
membership, initiate its candidates and simply exist; if it can s.ecure a full attendance of its members only by a banquet or a frolic,
it must and should fall to pieces from sheer inanition.
.
"Let us, therefore, strive to do our whole duty to 9od, the nation
and the brethren, and we will stand, as we were designed to stand,
first among all human institutions in the onward and upward evolution of the individual and the race. Our past, present and future arch enemy is not asleep."
The Grand Master's address discloses a year of marked activity in
which dispensations were granted for the organization of thirteen new
Lodges.
Ten corner-stones also were laid under direction of the Grand
Lodge.

"Suspension must be for a definite period, to be fixed by the
verdict, or indefinite; susp,ension cannot be imposed until the happening of a particular event.'

rendered, and on the second day of the Communication the Grand
l,odge conducted the ceremony of laying the corner-stone of the Alabama
Masonic Home. An exceedingly interesting program was carried out
upon that occasion, and several able addresses were rendered by prominent members of the fraternity. The president of the Masonic Home
Board, M.". w:. Brother Ben M. Jacobs, gave an exhaustive history
of the "inception and struggle" of the Masonic Home idea, the "struggle"
covering a space of time from the "inception" in the year 1868, and
he Yeferred to the fact tha: many of the present members of the
<irand Lodge fully appreciated the bitter struggle and the heart-pangs
of defeat experienced during the many years of work before the Masonic
I lome became an assured fact.
Something like $110,000 has been contributed toward the Masonic
I lome Fund, and the expectation is cherished that within the year the
I lome will be completed ready for the reception of residents.

ARIZONA, 1912.
The M.". w:. Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
Arizona held its Thirtieth Annual Communication in the Masonic Hall
in the city of Prescott on February 13, 14 and 15, 1912.

In opening his annual address, the Grand Master says:
"In this spirit of closest unity I bid you welcome to our Annual
Session and as we work another space in the annals of our history, let
us pause, with bowed heads in recognition of the care of our Supreme
Grand Master during this period of time and with grateful hearts render thanks to Him for the lessons it has brought into our lives.
"Since our last meeting held in Tucson, great and momentous
events have transpired within our boundaries and beyond our borders.
The section wherein we labor has been advanced . to Statehood, while
in our sister Republic revolution and . bloodshed have stirred the people. All of these happenings give a greater field for the teachings of
our Order. The enlargement of our population, following the rights of
Statehood, will increase our ranks in Arizona, while the tragedies being
enacted across the line give those of our craft working there opportunity for instilling our principles of Brotherly Love and Relief."
The address of the Grand Master and the reports of the other
Grand Officers set forth the usual activities of the year, in which.
a substantial growth in membership is recorded and general Masonic
good work disclosed.
Commenting upon the Grand Master's address, the special committee to which it was referred uses the following language to express its
appreciation of the Grand Master's work during the preceding year:
"Your Committee appreciate the full presentation of the condition
of our Order throughout this Jurisdiction, as given in our Most
Worshipful Grand . Master's Address, and the evidence in it of his
devotion to the work during the past year in its every detail, and find
therein one very potent reason for the flattering progress we have
made during that time."
Perhaps the most delightful function which occurred during the
session of the Grand Lodge was the planting of a tree by invitation
~f the Prescott Chamber of Commerce, and the Yavapai County Board
of Supervisors in the Court House Square to commemorate the admission on that date of Arizona to statehood.
The Grand Lodge was called from Labor and a procession was
formed under the direction of the Grand Marshal, F .. G. Brecht, and in

5

Brother Past Grand Master Fletcher M. Doan made a felicitous
address, at the conclusion of which Brother Morris Goldwater, Mayor
of Prescott, spoke as follows :
"Fellow Citizens, Friends and Brethren:
"We have gathered to celebrate the birth of a new State. I have
not lived ·under State government long enough to have forgotten the
forty years spent in the Territory. In spite of what has been said by
politicians and others, looking back over the Territorial administration, fairness compels me to say that whether Republican or Democratic
it has not been such a bad government. I do not know what the
future may bring to the new State, I can not tell what Time may
hold in the hollow of his hand for Arizona. I can only hope that
s'he may grow in the nobleness of her citizenship, in population, in
wealth, until her Star shall shine the peer of any that is in the galaxy
that makes our nation's flag. But come weal or woe, nothing will ever
efface from my memory the joys and pleasures I have had in the Territory of Arizona. And so, as we say welcome, we say farewell.
"And now let everybody join in three cheers for the new State of
Arizona."
Brother Harry A. Drachman, Tucson, was elected Grand Master,
and on being installed as such addressed his brethren as follows:
"Mv I3ROTH:ERS: At this, the greatest moment of my life, I cannot find words to express my gratitude for the great honor bestowed
upon me, that of Grand Master of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge,
JI. & A. M. of Arizona.
"It is an honor of which any man may feel prouQ. Especially has
this honor been pleasing to me for the reason that, at the moment the
Grand Master declared me elected the whistles were blowing and
cannons were booming the glorious news of the admission of our commonwealth into the Sisterhood of States. f>.nother honor is that of
being the first nathoe born Arizonian .to become Grand Master. Still
another honor that of being installed by my God-Father, M.". w:.
P. G. M. Morris Goldwater. All these honors make me feel a keen
responsibility for the tasks before me. I can only turn to the Supreme
Grand Master above to assist and guide me in the right 'Path, and
I ask my brethren to be charitable in passing judgment upon my acts,
remembering that I am going to try and do the best I know how.
"I thank you again, my brothers, for this great honor. I pledge
to you my strength, my heart and my hands for t.he great responsibility that is before me."
Brot'her George J. Roskruge, Tucson, re-elected Grand ~ecretary.

unusual nature of the questions asked, we copy as follows:
"Can there be ahy penalty inflicted on a brother for non-attendance
when the Lodge is ma.k ing a Mason of a man whom the absent brother
deems unfit material for masonry?"
Answer. "No. But a brother who absents !himself for the
reasons named, does the Lodge wrong and himself an injustice."
Question. "Has a Lodge a right to elect a member Worshipful
Master who is in the habit of getting drunk and violating masonic law?"
Answer. "No, etc."
·
Question. "Is it proper or 'prudent at public installations and the
laying of corner-stones under the auspices of the Masonic Lodge, to
have or to approve of having speculative stands; such as shooting
matches, doll racks, knife boards, swings, and other devices for
speculative purposes?"
Answer. "No, etc."
It would seem that some of these are remarkable questions to be
pres.ented to a Grand Master, and even more remarkable that .these
questions and answers should be entered under the caption of "Decisions."
Arkansas has an Orphans' Home, of which the jurisdiction is no
doubt justly proud, and the Grand Master recommends that there be
established, in addition to the Orphans' Home, a Home for Widows
and Indigent Masons, and in anticipating the objections which will naturally be raised to such a project-that is, the cost and burden upon
the fraternity- he takes a look backward and sees that objections of
this character were raised when the project of a Masonic Temple for
the Grand Lodge was first agitated, and afterwaras when the project of
an Orphans' Home was considered, and concludes that, inasmuch as
these projects were realized and are now accomplished facts, without
having caused the fraternity any distress, so also may his recommendation of a Home for Widows and Indigent Masons in time become one
of the realized ideals of Arkansas Masonry.
The Committee on Jurisprudence apparently overruled the Grand
Master in his decision that "doll racks," "knife boards" and other devices for speculative purposes at corner-stone ceremonies were improper,
for it held "that these adjuncts were not unmasonic, and that probably'
none of them could be called immoral in character, thus giving its sanction, apparently, to the idea that the turning of the ceremony of
laying a corner-stone into a circus is in no wise out of place.

From the address of the R.".
Grand Orator, Brother J. J.
Miller,•we quote as follows:
"There is always something significant in the laying of a foundation stone. It signifies progress, advancement, development, pros_.
perity. We, here in this new country, live in this environment. Foundations are laid every day. We are engaged in the development <Jf a new
country and in laying the foundations of our own fortunes and those
who come after us. The building up of this Western Country is our
portion. We are all builders today, building up our respective businesses,
building our homes, building schools and churches, building universities
and colleges, building railways and shipyards. We each one play an
important part in the development which is going on all. around, and
we should all realize our own responsibilities.
"The same work of building has been going ·on all through the
ages. The advance of science is marked even in the building art~.
Great structures are now erected "o f steel and concrete, unknown until
recent years. Stone and timber were the principal materials used
through all time. At the erection of King Solomon's Temple, that
masterpiece of architectural construction, stone and timber were chiefly·
used. It was in connection with the erection of Solomon's Temple
that the traditional foundation stone of Masonry was laid. Some of
the conditions that prevailed in those ancient days are even much the
same today. History tells us that the stones were prepared in the
quarries, and the timber in the forests; the timber being placed in the
water from the forests of Lebanon and brought in by floats. The fleet
of tug boats on our local waters is to-day engaged in the same
work, bringing in by water the stone from the quarries and the
timber from the forests for the building of our towns and cities. 'The
glory of an old land is in its past, the glory of a new land is in its
future.' The glorious history of our own Nation is our heritage, the
builders of the British Nation have builded better than they knew.
Let us so lay the foundation of our future and so build upon it that
they who come after us may say the same of us.''

"When a body of Masons claiming to be a Grand Lodge asks for
fraternal recognition, it should accompany its application with reasonable
proof that it has been legitimately formed; that it practices the fundamental principles of craft Masonry; that it acknowledges dependence
upon the Great Architect of the Universe; that it places the 'Volume
of the Sacred Law upon its altars; that it is a sovereign and independent
body; and that it does not exist for political purposes. If it cannot do
this, it should not be recognized."

COLORADO, 1911.
The M:. w:. Grand Lodge, A. F. and A. Masons of Colorado, met
in its Fifty-first Annual Communication in the Masonic Temple in Denver, Colo., Tuesday, September 19, 1911-M,'. w:. Brother Albert D.
McGaffey, Grand Master, presiding.
Representatives were present from 119 of the 123 chartered Lodges,
and many of the representatives of other Grand Lodges were in attendance and were invited to the East, where they were received and welcomed by the Grand Master. w:. Brother William H. Esworthy, the
representative of the Grand Lodge of Victoria, spoke in behalf of the
representatives as follows :
"M,'. w:. Grand Master: In behalf of my brother representatives
and myself, I thank you for your kindly words of welcome and I
assure you that we deeply appreciate the honor of a seat in so splendid
a body as the Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of Colorado.
There is nothing within my knowledge that we need bring to your
attention at this time regarding the fraternal relationship existing between your jurisdiction and those of ours, save the assurance from us
of a cordial desire, that we trust is mutual, to maintain a· perfect
understanding, thereby insuring the perpetuity of peace and goodwill. We are here representing jurisdictions throughout the civilized world, and while some of them are only without the borders
of your own State others are in the far-off Antipode~. We are
taught in the Entered Apprentice Degree of the vast dimensions of a
Lodge, to impress upon our minds the idea that Masonry is universal.
Most Worshipful Grand Master, there is nothing that brings to my
mind more forcibly that fact than the presence of these. my brethren,
about your altar to-day. The jurisdictions which we rep~esent are to
be found, some beneath the North Star and ·others under the Southern
Cross, some in this Western hemisphere and others in the dista'nt
Orient. To some of our brethren your sunrise is their sunset, your day
is their night, and your summer may be their winter ; but, Most W orshipful Grand Master, our brethren kneel at the same altar, receive
their light from the same Great Source, and bow their heads to the
same God as do you in Colorado. Masons have ever been pioneers, in
discovery, exploration, settlement and development of new lands; and
whether traveling in hitherto unknown lands or sailing uncharted seas,
in the frozen fastnesses of the polar regions,. or the blistering heat of
the tropics, their conduct toward their fellowman has ever been such
as to characterize them as 'just and upright men and l\fasons,' and rec-

Grand Master McGaffey, in his annual address, disclosed a most
excellent administration of Masonic affairs during his year, The fol~
lowing paragraph, taken from his opening address, will -convey an idea
of his marked activity:
"I have tried to keep in close touch with Masonic affairs during the
past year. I have been present at over two hundred Masonic meetings,
have made forty-eight official visitations, have laid ten corner-stones
have installed the officers of thirteen Lodges, have constituted thre~
Lodges and dedicated four halls, I have traveled over the greater
part of the. State by rail, wagon and auto, and have enjoyed every
moment of 1t.
"I am pleased to be able to state that the condition of the .Lodges
in this jurisdiction, as a whole, is very good, indeed. There are a few
in which some things can be improved, but peace and harmony prevail and no contention exists. As a Grand Jurisdiction we are at
peace :with the world."
·
He .reports a total membership of 14,917, a gain over the preceding
year of 6_98. The .four Lodges. which received charters at the preceding
Annual Communication were duly constituted by him in the year.
One dispensation was gr;mted 'by him for a new Lodge to be located
at Hugo, Colo. He states that he has answered a great many questions of Masonic character during the year, but did not feel it necessary to render any ruling i.n regard to the fundamental law that could
be dignified by calling it a decision.
He reports his attendance as the representative of the Grand Lodge
of Colorado at the meeting of the George Washington Masonic Memorial Association, which was held in the city of Alexandria, Va., on Febn:ary 21 and 22, 1911. He states that this meeting was very enthusiastic
and was said to be the largest assemblage of Grand Masters ever congregated, thirty-three Grand Jurisdictions being represented.
The reports of the Grand Treasurer and the Grand Secretary reveal
a healt'hful and prosperous condition of the fraternity in Colorado,
Brother Charles H . Dudley, Grand Orator, delivered an exceedingly
interesting oration, which, by resolution of the Grand Lodge, was printed
in the Proceedings, and the thanks of the Grand Body were extended
to Brother Dudley,

The Custodian of the Work submitted a report, from which we
quote as follows:
"Due principally to the fact that we have among us so many
Masons who were made in other jurisdict.ions, and who sometimes intentionally and sometimes unconsciously introduce their original work
into ours, we have peculiar conditions to deal with in Colorado, and
there is not the uniformity of work that ought to exist Again, different interpretations of the work have been given by Colorado authorities in the past, which has led to confusion,
"It is to clarify the situation and to crystallize the work that this
report, embodying the result of two years' study of conditions on the
part of the Grand Lecturer at least, is presented to you.
"In the past year the Grand Lecturer has discussed this subject in
practically every Lodge in the State, and with hundreds of wellinformed Masons, and many sug¥estions have been received. In addition
he has spent much time in studying the work of other jurisdictions, particularly England and Scotland, from whom we are all descended,
in an effort to ascertain the origin of our work.
"These opinions and suggestions obtained have been grouped and
sifted, and by a process of elimination only the most worthy have
been given consideration, the desire being t'O get rid of any innovations our work may contain, ·and to get back to ancient words and
forms; taken from an operative craft. We do not propose any radical changes, the sole desire being to break off the rough corners of the
stone and thus secure a more polished and perfect ashlar.
