REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE
tell you of the prerogatives and powers that belong to the Grand Master .of the Grand Lodge of England. Their Grand Master is always
some one of the royal family, and they elect him as long as he will
take the position, which is usually as long as he lives. So that when
he dies they elect his successor and have no Past Grand Masters. They
enter over there in the precise order of their rank, and every one knows
his place and does not get out of it, and every one is placed according
to his rank. So that, according to their Masonic procedure, next to the
Grand Master of England would be Past Grand Masters, if they had
them. Therefore, when I received their invitation and notified the Grand
Lodge that I would be there as the proxy and representative of the
Grand Master of ·Ohio, as well as in my own capacity as Past Grand
Master, I found that I was up next to the head of the column and had
a seat on t'he left of the presiding officer, Lord Amthill, Pro Grand
Master, the left hand being the seat of honor for an invited guest. At the
dinner I received the same honors, and, when I looked around, I was
almost inclined to feel glad that there were no other Past Grand Masters
'
from the United States present.
"I found over there that Masonry was radically different from ours.
They divide themselves into small bodies. 1There are very few of them
that are one hundred or even one hundred and fifty strong. It is more
a social organization. Nearly all meetings are followed by a dinner.
No one visits a Lodge over there unless he is invited. They have
Lodges composed of only one class of men. Royal Life Lodge, to
which I was invited to witness the initiation of Prince Arthur of Connaught, the eldest son of the Duke of Connaught, never receives any
candidate save those of the royal family. Other Lodges are composed
exclusively of musicians or newspaper men, and so on. A man can
belong to just as many Lodges as he pleases. Of course, he is initiated in his mot'her Lodge, but he can be ·a member of as many
Lodges at one time as he pleases. Some belong to a· large number,
and pay as high as two and three hundred dollars a year in dues.
Their charities are magnificent. The Royal Institution for Boys is a
magnificent charity, and so is that for girls. I had the privilege of
attendinP", with Mrs. Melish, the annual festival of the Institution for
Girls. These charities are supported by contributions made by Lodges
and largely by i.ndividuals. At the annual festival, they selected a patron
and patroness and the amount of the contribution was some forty thousand pounds, or two hundred thousand dopars."

Brother Greenleafs conclusion is well worth perusal by all thoughtful Masons and is, therefore, quoted in full, as follows :
"Through sixty-four subdivisions of the Masonic tealm we have
jou-rneyed, gathering here and there specimens of the work of others,
and sometimes· 'curios' which we deemed would be of intetest and place
our own jurisdiction in touch with the great body of their fellow
craftsmen who are striving for the betteTment of humanity.
"As we have heretofore noted, the growth of the fraternity the
past. few years has been phenomenal and has awakened in the minds
of conservative brethren much anxiety as to whether it bodes strength
or weafcness. If the portals are well guarded there is no cause for
alarm, for we cannot have too many good men and true in the ranks
of Masonry. In this day and generation there are great evils menacing
the basic fot1ndation·s of all that is just, right and true, in government,
commerce and social life, and they must be met with firmness and
determination. It is a good sign that so many young men are joining
our Lodges and identifying themselves with the fraternity. It is remarked by Grand Masters, Grand Lecturers and others, who from
their visitations are qualified to judp;e, that the best men in every
community are Masons. It is through the lives and character of its
individual members that Masonry accomplishes its work. When the
lessons taught in the Lodp;e are absorbed by the mind and heart, and
influence the life and conduct, Masonry moves forward in all spheres
of activity, not as an organization, but through individual effort, thus
strivinlf to accomplish its divine purpose.
"College fraternities, to which reference was made in our 1909
report, have greatly multiplied, until at last advices there were some
· twenty-four chapters of what is known as 'The Acacia Fraternity' connected with our leading universities, there being one at the Unlvei:sity
of Colorado. Their purpose and outline of work is thus set forth in
its Constitution :
"We, students, faculty and alumni of various universities and colleges, being Master Masons, and believing that the principles of Freemasonry are worthy of the most careful cultivation among universities
and college brethren, do hereby adopt this constitution for the purpose
of uniting us in a closer friendship, the more effectually to inculcate
Masonic principles."
"From all that we learn, these fraternities, as auxiliaries to Masonry; are doing a good work, and there is no occasion for any misgivings as to their . beneficial results upon their members who are
among those who have attained the highest lionors in schofarship and
whose conduct is sans reproache.
"Masonic dubs, Grottoes and other attachments to the Lodge are
being formed in some jurisdictions, while in others they are discountenanced as detracting · from the interest and effort that should be

22

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

devoted to the work of the Lodge. There has doubtless, in many instances,. been too close application to the work of conferring degrees
and not enough time devoted to the social feature, which is an important part of the purpose of the fraternity. Brethren have thus grown
restive, and have sought through the organization of clubs to supply
that in which they felt their Lodges were deficient. It is a question ,
which requires careful consideration, and one in which there is much
diversity of opinion. There is a distinction between Masonic clubs and
organizations of Master Masons formed upon plans similar to the·
shrine. The former are for social purposes and intellectual improvement, while the latter are for fun and enjoyment, pure and simple. We
are not sufficiently informed to speak intelligently as to the mfiuence· ,
of the latter, good or bad, upon the prosperity of the Lodge.
•
"It will be noted that in our reports we never fail to record cornerstone layings, for the reason that it is the only ceremony in Masonry
where the Speculative feature comes in touch with the Operative, reminding us of the time when our ancient brethren wro ught in both
Speculative and Operative Masonry.
"It is claimed that a Lodge of Operative Masons is still in existence in London, England, and that it is in possession of the ritual
which was made use of by Dr. Anderson in forming the Speculative
system. We have not the time or inclination to discuss this question at
the present time."
H. W. Woodward, Leadville, Grand Master.
Chas. H . J aco~son, Denver, Grand Secretary.

There are about 3,000 Masons in the Grand Jurisdiction of Delawurc, considerably less than half of the number in either of the great
metropolitan districts of California.
The jurisdiction, however, is in a condition of sound and vigorous
hralth, showing a substantial growth of membership and financial re••>nrces. "T he Grand Master reported that he had made a number

Very little progress, so the Grand Master states, was made during
the year in the matter of the Masonic Home project, but we judge
that greater progress is likely to be accomplished in the near future
from the adoption of the report of the Committee on Masonic Hom~
which carried a recommendation of a per .capita tax for the benefit of
the. Home .of $1, .to be payable on rhe !st of July, 1912. If this per
capita tax is continued from year to year, progress in the future will
be comparatively rapid in bringing to a consummation this invaluable
adjunct to Masonic charity in the jurisdiction of Delaware.

"The action of the Grand Lodge of Scotland in granting charters
in the Canal Zone at Panama has been the .means of causing a peculiar ·
condition of affairs. They have ·established two Lodges there, Sojourqers No. 874 and Thistle No. 1013 both being at Colon.
''This province, while credited to the Republic of Panama, is in
the Canal Zone, practically United States territory, and the interesting
feature of this erection of a Masonic province in this territory lies in
the fact that the Grand Lodge of Scotland has thereby brought to American territory a dispute of two of her own Lodges and left them to
fight it out as best they can, viz.: The conundrum of wh\te and black
Lodges of legitimate Masonry, acknowledging the same paternity, under
the same jurisdiction, under warrants issued from the same Grand
Lodge, and yet two separate and distinct Lodges, neither acknowledges
the right of visitation to the other, and the existence of which may_
affect the fraternal relations Scotland now has with bodies believing '
that Masonry belongs only within the ·confines of the Caucasian race.
A. AND A. S. R. AND CLANDESTINISM.

"One of the incidents of the year which may have a far-reaching
effect upon Masonic conditions in the United States and which indicates ·
the position which will be taken by the regular A. and A. S. R. bodies
of the States on the matter of clandestine Lodges is the statement made
by Brother James D. Richardson, Sovereign Grand Commander of the
Supremr Council of the 33d Degree of the Southern Jurisdiction, in
his allor.ution at the biennial session at Washington, D.C., in October
last.
"He says that their relations with ·Spain remain as they were two
years ago. Most diligent efforts on his part to obtain information in
order that he might make proper recommendation which would be satisfactory has resulted in entire failure. Three attempts have been made •
to get the Sovereign Grand Commander to explain whether the Suprem~
Council upholds the Grand Orient in planting bodies of Masonry in
this country, but without result. He says that he does not see how
they (the Supreme Council) can restore relations of amity with the
Spanish Council and he does not recommend it. He says: 'I am unwilling to maintain relations of amity with any Supreme Council or
Grand Orient in Europe or elsewhere that undertakes to establish and
maintain subordinate bodies of Masonry in any State of the United
States.'"

Some of the finest specimens of Masonic literature that are yearly
current in · Grand Lodge reports are found in the annual addresses. of
the Grand Masters of Georgia, and that the high standard is maintained·
this year may be judged from the following conclusion of Grand Master Napier's address:
MASONRY IN OUR OWN LAND.

"In 1893, at the World's Exposition in the city of Chicago, thousands of our countrymen beheld the beautiful structure on the shore
of the Great Lake, called the Peristyle. On its colonnade stood heroic
figures of the pioneer races of America, and the crown of the watergate bore an inscription to the pioneers of-civil and religious liberty.
"But upon the very summit of the Peristyle were the masterful
words, 'Ye shall know the Truth, and the Truth shall make you free.'
"I remembered then that an English Freemason, Thomas Cromwell,
began the agitation which resulted in the migration to this land of a
band of patriots who considered freedom of conscience, and the right
to worship God in the manner dictated by their own convictions, dearer
than the ties of home and the scenes and associations of childhood ; and
my mind brought vividly before me a series of pictures pertaining to
this wonderful land, in which Masons were the chief actors."
"Out there, just off Cape Henry, Virginia, in 1607, a small boat left
the sailing vessel and put in to land. It bore Edward Maria Wingfield,
Bartholomew Gosnold and four others. They were among · the first
white men making a permanent settlement on this hemisphere. Two of
them were Masons; and thus did our brethren aforetime march in the
vanguard of human progress and human liberty!
.
"A few months later there we.re to be seen operative Masons layirig
the foundation of the first parliament house and of the little church at
amestown, and at the same time Craftsmen who had ventured chartess on the sea of storm-engendering liberty were organizing a Lodge
of Masons, to keep alive in the new country the 5acred flame which
had long illumined the old land.
"In June, 1776, Richard H enry Lee, in the Continental Congress,
moved that a committee be appointed to draft a Declaration of Independence. He was a Mason, and my heart thrills with fervor and pride
when I recall that this first bold step was taken by a Freemason. History records that there were named on that committee Roger Sherman,
John Adams, Robert R. Livingston and Thomas Jefferson. Livingston was Grand Master of New York, and it is said that Jefferson was
a Mason. Whether he was or not, he accepted the suggested verbiage
.of the Chancellor of New York, for the very words of the Declaration
of Independence are Masonic, and none other than a Mason could
have dictated them.

l

35

"When this im!11o~tal docum~nt . ha~ been. submitted. and adopted,
there was some hes1tat1on about s1gnmg 1t. With stentorian voice John
Hancock thundered the words, 'Sign, Sign!' And this great Mason led
the way to the desk :ind with flourishing rubric. a~fixed. his bold signature. Of t~e forty-six who eagerly followed his 11lustr1ous example it
has ?e~n said that all but four were Masons. This is hardly probable,
but 1t 1s undoubtedly true that not more than a half dozen of the signers were not members of our order. .
"When the Declaration had been signed, the Liberty Bell gave forth
a peal that resounded throughout the worfd. It was answered from
England by a peremptory order for the arrest of John Hancock and
John Adams. General Gage secretly dispatched 800 British troops to
Lexington at 10 o'clock at night to seize him: But a volunteer of intrepid daring crossed the river under the very guns of the English manof-war Somerset, looking back at the lantern signals from the tower of
Old North Church, which told him which way the troops had gone. lt
was a Mason, Robert Morris, who held the lantern that memorable night.
The Grand Lodge of Massachusetts erected a suitably inscribed stone
at his grave. It was a Mason who saw the sign-not of distress but
of love for country, a warning to be caught up by the Sons of Libe~ty­
and the young patriot took horse and galloped to Lexington shouting
at every door to arouse the Minute Men.
'
" 'A hurry of hoofs in a village street,
A shape in the moonlight, ·a bulk in the dark,
And beneath from the pebbles in passing a spark
Struck out by a steed flying fearless and fleet.'
'
"Such was the 'midnight ride' o.f the immortal patriot and Mason
later Grand Master of Massachusetts, Paul Revere!
'
"The Deputy Gi:and Master of Massachusetts was the engineer
who laid out the breast works of Breed's Hill and Bunker Hill· and
the then Grand Master, Joseph Warren, incarnadined the hi~toric
slopes of Bunker Hill with his lifeblood.
"And what a long roll of heroes of the Revolution who were
Masons : the fearless Israel Putnam, 'Light . Horse Harry Lee' 'Mad
Anthon:( Wayne, the Car?lina 'Swamp Fox,' Francis Mario'n, and
the Fabian General, Nathaniel Greene, whose body was given sepulture
in .Georgia soil. Indeed, virtually all the military leaders of the Revolution were Masons, from the noble Warren, who died Grand Master of

"The coinage of a country is looked to as significant in many ways.
In future ages, when the coins of this country are examined, they will
be found to show more than the mere dates. I hold in my hand coins
of both gold and of silver, and these, and indeed every coin of this
Republic, except the subsidiary coins, have stamped upon their face an
inscription significant to every Mason-'In God we trust.' A few years
since, when it was proposed to strike these words from the dies for our
coins, the American people, led by the Masons, protested so vehemently that Congress perpetuated this beautiful testimonial to our dependence upon the God of Nations for our help and for our national
guidance.

"The most famous public edifice in the world is the Congressional
Library Building in the city of Washington. It covers acres and cost

triumph of the decorator's art. Yet the most striking features of all
the mural faintings, carvings, statues, frescoes and friezes are the

"But, my brethren, this is an age of progress. Even a mighty force
like l< reemasonry must know the time of day and be alert to the process

allegiance to the great principles which have made Freemasonry perpetual. Yet, 'O tempora ! 0 Mores !' times and customs are changing,
and men are changing with them. All things seem to be set to the pace
of electricity. The macadmized highway, the automobiles, and the telephone have made of every man a neighbor. What space has not already
been anniliilated the airship will likely conquer.
"Withal new dangers have arisen to this Republic. The mad desire
for place and wealth stalks abroad with brazen front. The magic suddenness with which princely fortunes·were to be accumulated has caused
to be permanently established in our land the worship of the Golden
Calf. And its devotees are not alone the rich, hut men often drawn
from the ranks of those who are possessed of but a moderate living, yet
who, infected by the fever of avarice, or moved by envy of the rich
whose eyes stick out with fatness, burn incense to the god of Mammon.
Greed seems to be a modern germ, and a restive people, which sustains
a growing influx of new and foreign hlood, finds crime increasing and
nn ever-present effort to foist intemperance upon the body politic.
"Against these encroachments Masonry has· quietly inculcated her
noble teachings more zealously than ever, to raise the barrier of moral
suasion against the subtle influences which would degrade, weaken and
finally destroy the State.

The Grand Master makes this recommendation concerning the
proper channel of communication between Lodge~ of different grand
jurisdictions, viz., through the Grand Master of each State :
"Most Grand Lodges require that all communications between
Lodges of different States be sent through the Grand Master. The reason for this is obvious. In requesting Lodges in. other States to confer
degrees application might pe made to clandestine or irregular Lodges.
In asking waiver of jurisdiction the same care is needed. Lodges as
such should not invade other Grand Jurisdictions to visit or confer
degrees without consent . and approv:il of .Gran~ Ma~te;s, . w~o are responsible for the regularity of work m their various 1urisd1ct1ons.
" It ·has become necessary for Grand Masters to otter apologies to.
me for unwarranted action of Lodges in invading the jurisdiction of
Illinois. I have felt called upon to make similar amends to Grand Masters of other States.
"One of our Lodges asked a Lodge iri another State to confer the
2d and 3d Degrees upon ·a candidate, collect and send the fee . The
degrees were conferred and fee collected as requested. The foreign
Lodge not only kept the fee, but stole the candidate by having him sign
the by-laws of the Lodge and entering his name on their roll of membership. My attention was calle.d to the case. When I c:illed the attention of the Grand Master to this he very promptly reqmred the Lodge
to make a satisfactory adjustment. Had the matter gone throuih the
hands of the two .Grand Masters in the first place there would have been
no trouble. This is only one of the many cases I have been called upon
to adjust.
"Some of our Lodges have conferred degrees for Lodges in other
jurisdictions without the knowledge of either Grand Master. This is
not only wrong but dangerous.
"I recommend that all business ·o f our Lodges -with foreign jurisdictions be sent first of all to the Grand Master for approval and action,
when necessary. This will save time and sometimes complicatil>ns and
trouble. It also observes the courtesies due in such cases and conforms
to customs practiced in most Grand Lodges.','
And in accordance with his recommendation there was at this Communication of the Grand Lodge an amendment to the Constitution
offered which will lay over for one year and come up for adoption at
the Annual Communication of 1912.

The Grand Master-elect said:
"The M.'. W .'. Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge of
Illinois : I hardly know what to say to you at this time. I am deeply
sensible of the great honor that you have conferred upon me in electing me as your Grand Master. I once heard Brother Owen Scott say
that he would rather be Grand Master of Masons than to be Governor
of the State of Illinois. I have never been Governor of the State.
When a man like Brother Owen Scott says that it places a very high
standard upon the office of M.'. W.'. Grand 'Master. I realize, brethren,
that I am standing to-day where twenty-six years ago my father stood, ··
and there comes to me at this moment a feeling which almost prohibits
my speaking to you. I have taken an obligation, brethren, to administer
the affairs of this Grand Lodge according to its by-laws, its landmarks
and its regulations; I pledge you to do my very best to discharge that
trust. I have but one ambition in filling this office, and that is to be
of some small service to the great institution of Freemasonry, arid if I
shall have accomplished that I shall retire from the office amply satisfied."

pursuing the even tenor of their way. Differences are diminishing and
MHonic law and usage are becoming more uniform.
"There is ever present the evidence of healthy and national growth
In membership and influence. Owing to the existence of spurious
uul fraudulent bodies, assuming to be Mas.o!1ic, there is a stea~y in11 C'llSC in the number of Grand Lodges requmng documentary evidence
In addition to 'strict trial and due examination.' The written evidence
11quired is that the visitor be in good standing in his Lodge and that
the Grand Secretary.certify that his Lodge is regular. This wide growth
In the requirement for written proof will necessitate some form of
1eceipt for dues bearing the Grand Secretary's certificate of regularity.
ISrethren who would visit outside of their own Grand Lodge should fortlly themselves for this new requirement. A mere receipt for dues
'" not sufficient. The additional proof that the Lodge is not clandestine
but regular is more and more demanded.
WM . J, HUGHAN.

"An event of world-wide Masonic significance and sorrow was the
death of William J. Hughan, the distinguished English author and historian. He passed away May 20, 1911, at the age of seventy years, and
wns buried with Masonic honors. He was a Past Senior Gram:! Deacon
of the Grand Lodge of England. On account of the system in vogue
among our English brethren, a man, as an ordinary craftsman, can
1carcely reach the position of Grand Master. This is reserved for the
royal family. When Albert Edward, Prin~e of Wales, ascended the
British throne, it became necessary to find his successor as Grand Master. The new Prince of Wales, the present King George, not being a
Mason could not succeed his father as Grand Master of Masons. In
, onseq~ence, Arthur, King Edward's brother, the Duke of Connaught,
was made the head of English Masonry. He does not actually officiate
except on rare occasions. He chooses a pro Grand Master and a deputy. These are active in the affairs of the Grand Lodg~ of Englan?.
They are, like the Grand Master, royal personages. Plain workers in
the quarries, like Hughan, no matter how great by natur~I endowm~nt
or by acquisition through labor, cannot be called to the highest service
of the Craft. Gladly would .they be summoned by the workers, but
rank and station make their advancement impossible. Though Hughan
wrought in a somewhat different field from that of Robbins, yet they
were in the same distinguished class of Masonic writers and thinkers •
Masonry can ill affot'd to lose these giants.

A. ·resol~tion was adopted that the proposition of Clarke Lodge

Masonic Home in Indiana is assured.
We note in the Proceedings that w:. Brother Edward H. Wolfe
presented credentials as the authorized Grand Representative of the
Grand Lodge of California to the Grand Lodge of Indiana and he was
accordingly recognized and enrolled as such Grand Repr:sentative.
The matter of the endorsement of the proposed memorial to Washington, the Mason, at Alexandria, Va., received the consideration of a
special committee, whose recommendation,. which was approved by the
Grand Lodge, was to the effect that no action be taken at this time
by the Grand Lodge incurring any financial or other obligations until
more complete information is at hand as to the possible or probable
ultimate expense, etc.
The Order of the Eastern Star presented to the Grand Lodge a
request to be permitted to participate officially in the creation and
control of the proposed Masonic Home, and while the Grand Lodge
expressed its willingness to receive all possible aid from outside sources
in the establishment of a Home, yet it proposed that the Home should
be und~r the absolute charge, control and management of the M.". W:.
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of Indiana and therefore
declined the request made on behalf of the Grand Ch;pter 'of Easter~
Star to divide the control with that organization.
Our opinion upon the subject has not been invited, but if there is
anything connected with Masonry that the female adjunct of the order
may properly participate in it is in the administration, control and sup~
port of Masonic Homes, and we think, therefore, that the Grand Juris~
diction of Indiana should have been more than eager to welcome the
offer of the Eastern Star to assist in the creation and carrying forward
of the Masonic Home project.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The following are quoted from the "decisions" rendered by the
Grand Master during the year· and embodied in his report:
"AYOUC'hment-Lawful Information: Construing Section 239 of the
Code, I have held lhat it was not lawful for a brother to vouch for
another as a Mason whose knowledge of his being a Mason is derived
solely from his having sat with him in an open Chapter of Royal Arch
Masons, and is not derived from having sat in open lodge with him or
fro~, h,i~ havi~g examined him by authority of t.he Master of a Lodge.
C1hzensh1p: I have held that our Masonic law did not require
that a candidate for the degrees of Masonry should be a citizen of the
United States, provided he could comply with our statutory requirements as to the necessary time of residence within the territory of the
Lodge to which he applied.
"Unmasonic Conduct : I have held that the M'ason who holds criminal intercourse ~th the daughter of a Master Mason violates his obligation, whether the daughter be herself chaste or not, and -is subject to
trial and punislnnent as for the commission of a Masonic offense."
Iowa is one of the very few important States of the ' Union that
has not adopted the Masonic Home idea-although the Order of the
Eastern Star has a Home at Boone, la.-but the method employed by
the Grand Lodge of Iowa for the care of its 'aged and indigent members that cannot be proverly taken care of by the subordinate Lodges is
more in the nature of a system of pensioRs or annuities, a form of
Masonic charity approved by certain foreign Grand Jurisdictions, not-ably England, Scotland and some of the Australian Grand Lodges, and
the system seems to yield a large measure of satisfaction to the Grand
Lodge of Iowa, although it is not designated in that jurisdiction as an
annuity system. But concerning the administration of the Charity
Fund the Grand Master has this to say :
"The more experience I have with our Iowa idea of administering Masonic charity, the more satisfied I become with our present system. The Trustees of our Grand Lodge Charity Fund have certainly
done most excellent and effective work during the past year. Under
their most intelligent management and smoothly working organization,
our Grand Lodge has educated children, found employment for widows
and orphans, kept up the interest payments on mortgaged homes, paid
for business college scholarships, supplied food, clothing and school
books; has taken care of the sick in homes and hospitals, and has
administered substantial relief in a very effective way, without any
publicity whatever. It has done great work in helping the unfortunates
to help themselves, and has administered aid to them without causing
them to lose that personal pride and self-respect which are the strength ·
and SUPJ?Ort of every true man and woman. Our deeds of charity have.
been QUJetly done to those dependent upon us without tearing them
away from their old home ties and the circle of their life-long friends.
I have not heard of one single instance in which the Trustees were not .
quick to respond effectively and intelligently to the cry for relief
coming from a worthy sufferer.
"If there is one department of our Iowa Masonry that gives pro~
found satisfaction, it is that of our Masonic charity. We have great
reason to be proud of the work done by the Trustees of this fund, and

we owe them a great debt of gratitude_ for the splendid manner in
which each one of them has performed his. duty.
.
.
"Our present law limits the amount which can be contributed m any
one year to the relief of any one case to the sum of $200. I would recommend that this limit be increased to the sum of $300. From my
experience with this Board of Trustees., I have no ·fear whatever that
they will ever, in any case, waste or misapply our funds to u!lworthy
cases or will in the least degree abuse the trust we confide m them.
They' have a splendid system, which is effecth:e to the. min?test. detail,
and they keep in close and constant touch with the s1tuat1on m each
case.

"There is just one little finishing touch w~icry I bel.ie~e can be ad?ed
to perfect the system now in ,u~e. And that 1s 1!1 0~1ttmg t~e publication of the names of the recipients of our charity m the printed Proceedings of our Grand Lodge. I wo~ld recon:imend that these names
appear, for the purpose of reference, 1,n the. written record of our Pro7

in our published Proceedings. In this way we will absolutely keep from
the eyes of the world the names of those who have been forced to call
upon us for help. And I believe that they will be grateful to us for our
thoughtfulness in so doing."
.
The Grand Master manifested a degree of activity in placing of
comer-stones of public buildings; in the dedication of Masonic halls
and tempi~; in official visitations, etc. He is a believer in the doctrine
that it is the inner and not the outer qualifications which recommend a
man to be made a Mason, for he can see no reasonable objection to
receiving as a candidate a man with an artificial leg or a foot, on which
subject he makes the following comment:
"I believe that Section 285 of our Code should be so amended as
to allow the Grand Master to issue a dispensation pennitting of the
initiation of a candidate having an artificial leg or foot in such cases
as may meet with his entire a.pproval.
"Such an amendment would ena~le th~ Gran~ Master to ma~e
proper inquiry as to whether the candidate m question wer~ otherwise
sound and healthy, well able to support and take care of himself, .and
otherwise qualified to become a member of the order. ~nd h7 might
go a step further and require that in such cases the cand1date m qu~s­
tion should sign a statement that he w?uld never .acc~pt ~1:1bstant1al
relief from the order for any cause growmg out ?f his d1~ab1ht)!" ,,
"I recommend the subject to you for your serious ctms1deratton.
He also is a thorough believer· in Masons looking beneath the
surface to find the real meaning of mystic words an<l symbols.
"It is one thing," he remarks, "to be able to comment and recite
a ritual and quite another to know that the ritual has a meaning, ~nd to
know what that meaning is.
"Masonry has no use for a blind, stupid devotion, vouchsafed her
by wooden men, but what she loves is the intelligent loyalty of thinking
men, who have a reason for the faith that is in them."

The Report on Correspondence is by Brother C. C. Clark, of Burlington, in which report California, 1911, is considered.
He objects to the Uniform Code of By-Laws, such as is prescribed
by many Grand Lodges, including our own, and thinks that liberty
should be allowed to subordinate Lodges in the matter of adopting their
own By-Laws, and otherwise conceding to them local self-government.
We believe, however, that the Uniform Code is the better system.
He disagrees also with the California method of Masonic Home
charity and prefers the Iowa system, to which we have previously re- .
fer red.
As a money saver it must' be admitted that the Masonic Home J>YStem is not a pronounced success, but as an aid to character building,•
both for the recipients of Masonic aid and for those who contribute, it
possesses. elements of strength not embodied in the annuity or pension
system, or pure d~nation arrangement, and inasmuch as Masonry has
little, if anything, to do with successful finance, we may be excused
if we prefer the Masonic Home system as exemplified in Californ1a, to
the purely monetary administration. of charity as exemplified in certain
other American and foreign jurisdictions.

"The history of modern Masonry is traceable to England and Holland; it is there that we read of the first initiations into the order in .
modern times, and it is from England and Holland that our modern
world has learned all its great lessons of civil and religious liberty.
From them came bright beams of light, reaching across the Atlantic,
by which the earliest American settlers were guided in laying the foundations of the free government which is ours, and in whose effulgence we
have seen that nation grow, until it 'reaches from ocean to ocean, from

form of government established in the world since that time. And it
has often been asserted that the leaders of that early period found in

KENTUCKY, 1911.
The Grand Lodge of Kentucky, Free and Accepted M;isons, held its
One Hundred and Eleventh Annual Communication in the Masonic
Temple, Louisville, commencing Tuesday, October 17, 1911, and was
opened in Ample Form on the third degree at 10 o'clock a. m.-M.'.
w:. Robert R. Burnam, Grand Master.
.
·T he Grand Master reports having granted nine dispensations to
form new Lodges.
He visited in the year Alexandria, Va., to attend the meeting of
the George Washington Masonic Memorial Association. He is in
hearty sympat)1y with the project and pledged so far as possible the
·support of the Grand Lodge of Kentucky to the same.
Concerning this movement, he has this to say :
"For this whole movement I am in sympathy, and I pledged the
support of the Grand Lodi;re of Kentucky to the same. If the members
of this Grand Lodge could only have been there and have seen the
distinguished Americans who belong _to us, you would have been proud
indeed. Beginning with President Taft, came Senators, Congressmen:
judges and a host of distinguished private citizens from many States.
"For the purpose of pushing this work, I pledged $100 for this
Grand Body. I hope you will become a permanent member of .this
assoeiation.
"Hon. Thomas J. Shryock, who has been the Grand Master of
Maryland for more than a quarter of a century, was elected preside11t
of the association. This alone is a guarantee that all funds will be faithfully handled."
·
He speaks of numerous requests which have come to him to grant
permission to Lodges to initiate candidates who have serious phy$icai
imperfections. He states that he uniformly refused all such requests,
because of the belief entertained by him that a Mason should be physically qualified as well as spiritually. The following are his vi~ws as
.
he expresses them upon this subject:
"I recognize the great Masonic truth that it is the internal and
not the external qualifications which are so essential in Masonic character, but the internal are not all by any means.
"Regulations No. 343 says : 'A Lodge is the sole judge of its
petitioners' qualification.' This is true, but within certain bounds. An
irrelig-ious libertine, a madman or a fool are certainly not proper
subjects for initiation, but under said regulation the Lodge can elect
them. It seems to me that the Grand Lodge should rule that no petition. can be received from any candidate unable to comply with the
physical requirements, such as taking the steps on· the Master's carpet,

63

r.

ving perfectly the grips and signs. This has been· my own interpre1tlon and I believe it is that of the vast majority of our members.
Sometimes a Lodge becomes too anxious for new members.''

One of the incidents that occurred in the year that occasioned a
1reat deal of correspondence back and forth was the controversy with
ltennsylvania over the question of penal jurisdiction, Pennsylvania
111erting its right to .perpetual penal jurisdiction, and Kentucky making
the stand for territorial jurisdiction, claiming this right for itself and
' unceding' the same right to other Grand Jurisdictions.
The Grand Lodge of Kentucky in its regulations has declared :
"The doctrine of 'perpetual jurisdiction' over a rejected profane is
not held in Kentucky, which has always maintained the doctrme of territorial jurisdiction, and accorded to other Grand Lodges what it re1erves to itself-the right to pass upon the fitness of all candidates who
have been bona fide residents of the State for the requisite time. The
Grand Lodge has never claimed power to act outside of its own jurisdiction, nor will it allow its own action to be controlled by any other
body of Masons.''
Grand Master Burnam maintained in his correspondence with the
nrand Master of Pennsylvania that the doctrine of perpetual jurisdiction, Masonically speaking, was no more defensible than the doctrine
of perpetual jurisdiction over acquired citizenship by nations, and that
n foreign born resident of America who had foresworn his allegiance to
the mother country was just as effectually beyond the jurisdiction of
the mother country, and a citizen of our country, as a so-called "profnne" who had moved from one State into another and had acquired
citizenship in the latter State was beyond the jurisdiction of the State
In which he formerly resided.
Grand Master Burnam, in our opinion, had the best of the argument, and the principle involved is precisely the one involved in the
present controversy between the jurisdiction of Arkansas and that of
California, in which California has initiated a candidate over whom it
had acquired territorial jurisdiction, although the candidate was one
that had previously been rejected by Arkansas, and ov'er whom ArkanHS still claimed penal jurisdiction.
The Masonic Homes of Kentucky are reported to be in splendid
condition, and these charitable works are being carried forward by this
Jurisdiction in a most efficient and capable manner.

"Of course, the perpetual jurisdiction doctrine is, like the poor,
always with us, but it has passed the acrimonious stage, and when it
obtrudes itself into the sphere of controversy, as it occasionally does, is
being discussed dispassionately, as it should be.
"There is another question which, as to its rationals, is closely
111ied to it : The right to Masonic recognition of a brother who has
been regularly made a Mason by a Lodge of a jurisdiction other than
that in which he has a legal residence. The objection in these cases
founds itself on the alleged fact that the Lodge so making him a Mason
violated the jurisdiction of the Lodge within whose territory the candidate on whom it conferred the degrees had his domicile and of the
Grand Lodge within whose territorial jurisdiction was located the Lodge
.if his domicile.
"As a matter of law, a Masonic Lodge has, and, in the very nature
·if things can have, no jurisdiction over one who is not a Mason. It is
•oqually illogical to allege of one not a Mason that he is the material of a
1111rticular Lodge because he may happen to reside within a certain distnnce of the location of that Lodge, or for any reason. A Lodge
1cquires jurisdiction over the person of a non-Mason only by his voluntary act in filing with it a petition praying for initiation. Just as a
mmmons legally issued and served on a defendant gives to the civil
ourt jurisdiction to try and determine the issues involved in that particular case does the filing of the petition of the candidate give a Lodge
Jurisdiction over the person of the candidate, and jurisdiction to make
him a Mason. A Grand Lodge has no authority to say to one not a
Mason that he shall not be made a Mason except by a certain Lodge. It
hus jurisdiction over the Lodges of the territory embraced in its limits
11nd it may, indeed should, prescribe the conditions on which they may
make Masons ; and thus it 1s only indirectly, and through the authority
lnwfully exercises over the Lodges of its obedience, and the inhibitions
which it lays on them, that it can exercise authority over non-Masons
whose habitat may be within its jurisdiction's boundaries. It has,
1herefore, no authority to prescribe rules for the conduct of those not
Masons, or in any manner to limit or restrict them; it can only exercise
11uthority over its Lodges. This right to make laws for the government
of its subordinates, and to prescribe the conditions under which they
may make Masons, is common to all Grand Lodges and is incidental to
1overeignty.
"These premises being admitted-and we thirik that no one who
1ives them a candid thought will deny them-it necessarily follows that
any one not a Mason has been made a Mason in conformity to the law
of the Grand Lodge in whose jurisdiction is located the Lodge that
made him a Mason, he has been legally and regularly so made, and as
11 regular made Mason he is entitled to Masonic recognition by all
Masons in all Masonic Lodges, even by a Lodge which once may have
rejected him, and certainly by the Lodge and the members of the Lodge
within whose territorial boundary he may have his actual domicile
though his initiation was by another Lodge in another Grand Jurisdiction. We are forced by the. relentless laws of inexorable logic to this
·
conclusion.
"It is true, of course, that every member of a Lodge has the ri~ht,
Indeed the right is inalienable, to object to the presence of any visitor
at any meeting of his Lodge at which he may be present. This ancient
right we are not questioning. We are only contending that the legally
performed acts of every regular Masonic Lodge be recognized by every

LOUISIANA, 1912.
The One Hundredth Annual Grand Communication of the M:. w:.
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Louisiana
convened in the city of New· Orleans, at the Scottish Rite Cathedral,
on Monday morning, the 5th day of February, at 10 o'clock, John &.
Thibaut, Grand Master, presiding.
The Grand Master opens his annual address, as follows :
"It is with feelings of the deepest emotion that I welcome you to
this, the Centennial Communication of the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of
Louisiana. Unite with me, my brethren, in giving praise to Him
who, having blessed the feeble beginnings of Louisiana Masonry, sustained it with His powerful might and for His own purpose through
all its trials and vicissitudes and has fostered and prospered it. To-day
it stands before the world among the most enlightened, the most liberal
and the most active of Masonic bodies in America."
"Twin-born of our beloved State, it also has written history-a
history which brings no shameful blush to our cheeks, but,rather the
ftush of pride for the character, virtues and deeds of those who have
written it. And yet, my friends, proud as we may be of our Masonic
lineage, it is not with the memories of the past that we are to dwell.
'Its once busy existence, various sensations, fiery trials, dear-bought
triumphs, its dynasty of heroes, all of its pulses of joy and anguish, and
hope and fear, and love and praise, are with the years beyond recall.
The sleeping and the dead are but pictures. Yet, gazing on these,
long and intently, and often, we may pass into the likeness of the departed and may emulate their labors and partake of their immortality.' '
"The history of the world is a record of the rising and disappearance, like bubbles on the water, and the sweeping from the earth like
the morning dew before the noonday sun of hundreds of civilizations.
It also records the unchanging, eternal teachings of Masonry through
all the mutations of time. It witnesses its incessant efforts towards the
improvement of the sbcial order, the intellectual development of man,
the warming of men's hearts to their fellow men, and what is more
essentially its own-the inspiration of the universal world to the great
principles of human solidarity and fraternity.
. "May the dawn of this new century, radiant with its possibilities, so
inspire us with Masonry's sentiments and ideals, that we may live in the
remembrance of succeeding generations, for our gracious deeds and
our unfailing devotion to its cause-the teaching of its sublime lessons
of harmony and of love."
Five Lodges which received charters at the preceding Annual Communication were all duly constituted within the Yl!ar, and dispensations.
were issued in that time to form five new Lodges.

The Masonic Home idea meets no approval in the Jurisdiction of
1,ouisiana, the Grand Master in particular being strongly opposed .to
this method of administering Masonic relief and charity to its aged and
Infirm members and to its orphans.
We quote his utterances upon this subject in extensio because he
evidently represents the extreme view in opposition to the Home idea,
and we are constrained to the belief that his radical position in oppo1ition to the idea of the Masonic Home does not result from practical
knowledge, but rather from theory, not founded upon comprehensive
Investigation, and his classing Masonic Homes with the ordinary
Infirmary or institution of that character is hardly justifiable, and he
will find upon wider investigation that many of the Masonic Homes
throughout America have a genuine atmosphere of warmth and home,
and may not justly be characterized as "chilly institutional" affairs, and
we believe the Masonic Home not only affords comfort and shelter to a
vast number of aged and indigent Masons that would otherwise have
no homes at all, and, therefore, performs a service of inestimable value,
hut that it also promotes in those jurisdictions where the Home is a
feature charity and kindness and consideration and thoughtfulness
among the Craft generally, thereby becoming an invaluable adjunct to
character building, which is the real purpose of Masonry.
The Masonic Home has never been recommended as a money saver,
hut, as we have frequently remarked, Masonry is not primarily a financial institution, designed to assemble or hoard wealth, but it is an
organization intended for the uplift and benefit of mankind, in which
the monetary element, in this age of commercialism, happily plays only
n secondary part, and, therefore, if the Masonic Home feature of
Masonic work helps to broaden Masonic sympathy and charity it is
n good thing, and, even if it costs more than some other means of dispensing Masonic charity, it nevertheless is entitled to approval.

The following is the eloquent "conclusion" of the Grand Ma~ter's
address, voicing appreciation of the present, with its grand opportunities, and prophetic of the future, whose keynote shall be "brotherhood"
and "service," which constitute, in fact, the essence of Masonry:
"Our Masonic institution is soundly based on a fundamental human cause, the increasing sense of man's essential brotherhood. Operative Masonry today is concerned in building not alone temples and
places, but chiefly the manhood of the nation. Just as the great watchword of the eighteenth century was liberty, and the great work of the
nineteenth century was science, mechanical invention and organization;
so the great word and supreme work of this twentieth century will be,
brotherhood-service. It is an era of swift and mighty changes throughout the world. Age-old monarchies like Portugal disappear in a night
and unfurl the banners of a new republic to the light of dawn; Manchu
dynasties sacred for countless centuries are suddenly overthrown, and
liberated China awakens from its lethargy of centuries sleep, and a new
era of republican government is proclaimed to the amazed and wondering world. All progress is along the line of man's essential brotherhood.
In a quiet and unobtrusive way Freemasonry is working toward that
time prophesied by the poet :
"When the war-drums throb no longer, and the battle flags are furled
"In the parliament of man and the federation of the world."
that time dreamed of by the seer of sacred writ: "When nations shall
beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruninghooks, neither shall they learn war any more."
"Every day strengthens this bond of essential brotherhood. The
ancient prayer, 'Thy kingdom come,' is being answered by increased
peace and good-will, by daily labor for 'God and home and native land.'

"'For, with aching hands, and bleeding feet,
We toil and heap, lay stone on stone,
We bear the burden and the heat
Of the long day, and wish 'twere done;
Not till the hours of light return
All we have built do we discern,' "

MANITOBA, 1912.
The Thirty-seventh Annual Communication of the M.".. w:. Grand
Lodge of Manitoba, Ancient Free and Accepted Masons, was opened ifi
the Masonic Temple, at the city of Winnipeg, Province of Manitoba, on
Wednesday, June 12, A. D. 1912, A. L. 5912, Grand Master John
W emyss presiding.

In opening his address, the Grand Master says :
!'It is with great pleasure that I am able, like my immediate predecessors, to assure the brethren that peace and harmony prevail not
only throughout the entire jurisdiction, but also · in our relations · with
other jurisdictions, and have prevailed during my entire term. No
cloud as large as a man's hand mars the prospect for my successor. May
the kindly and brother!}' feeling which prevails not merely between individuals but also between Lodges in this jurisdiction, long continue.
That such will be the case I have but little doubt. Fraternal visits not
merely between the city Lodges, but between Lodges in adjacent towns,
are becoming more common, and over and· above the educational value
of such visits, they are producing excellent results in fostering a more
kindly feeling than sometimes prevails between the citizens of adjoining towns which are competitors for business, by bringing the brethren
of different Lodges into direct personal contact with one another, and
are establishing a bond of fraternity which cannot fail to have good
results."
That this jurisdiction happily is living in a state of harmony may
be judged from the fact that the Grand Master reports that during the
year he has not been called upon to render a decision upon disputed
points of law. He, therefore, has nothing in that line to report, and
that he has a proper conception of Masonry and the duties which devolve
upon men as Masons may be judged from the following remarks embodied in his address :

origin is lost in the mists of antiquity appeals to the human imagination

same time none of us should ever lose sight of the fact that· its mere
antiquity is not any adequate reason for its continuance-that M·asonry
must, if it is going to continue to prosper, justify its existence in the
present, and also that the ritual is merely a means to an end and not

Grand Master equalling now the length of seryice of the late King Edward VII of England, who was Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
England for twenty-seven years, occupying the exalted station of Grand
Master of Masons for a longer period of time, we believe, than any other
Grand Master in the history of Masonry, and when Brother Shryock
shall be re-elected for the twenty-eighth time, as we doubt not he will
be, he will have served in his exalted station for a greater length of
time than any other man in the history of our great fraternity.

"In conclusion, the question of whether the Home shall begin its
career of beneficence on the day when it is dedicated is one which the
brethren must settle for themselves. On that day the Craft will be the
owners of an estate fully paid for, its maintenance provided for, ready
in every respect to be of use for its destined purpose. Every dollar now
contributed will help ta. constitute a fund whose income will defray the
living expense of those who shall occupy the Home. What say you,
brethre!!? When the ceremonies which mark the completion of this
monument of charity are finished, shall we turn away from it in the
train of our Grand Master, knowing that its rooms are to be tenantless,
that the doors are to be closed, that those· who are looking to us for
refuge and shelter are to be outside its walls gazing at its darkened windows with a longing for the comfort that could so easily be given them
for the little while they are to stay among us, or shall the busy hum
of occupancy fill it with life, shall food and rest wait for those in need
of both, shall the lights of Overlook shine out over the broad valleys
which surround it to be like a beacon to the poor, and distressed; to
i>roclaim, by their radiance, their silent message to the State and the
world,. which shall tell of the good name of our Fraternity redeemed,
because we are satisfying the pledge we entered into, when we joined
ourselves together? Shall we hold fast to the tenets of our profession,
and prove our Truth by the exercise of Brotherly Love in granting Relief
to those with whom we profess to be linked together by an indissoluble
chain. of sincere affection?
"You, brethren, are the chosen representatives of the Craft, and
through you and those whom you have made our associates in this
great work of relief we look for an answer. If each will do his little
pMt, that answer. will be one we shall not be ashamed to give."

In opening his address upon this occasion, the Grand Master says :
"We have assembled here today to celebrate the consummation of
r>ur ardent hopes and desires for many years; the Grand Lodge charity,
for which many of our brethren have dreamed and prayed, has become,
by this official act of the Grand Lodge, a reality, and we have at last
In Massachusetts a Masonic Home designed for the shelter and refuge
of our unfortunate brethren and the dependent members of their families who may be eligible to take advantage of its protection.
"Homes of this character have been established in other jurisdictions,
nn<l have been satisfactorily conducted for many years, with the addition in some of them of facilities for the accommodation and education
,,f the children of deceased Masons, and the advantages here P.resented
will enable us in the days to come to make provision of a similar char11ctcr for our orphans. I anticipate with the fullest confidence that in
the years to come our brethren will not be satisfied until they have provided not only for the elderly brothers, their widows and dependents, but
nR well for the little ones, both in the nature of a home and the fitting
of these children to occupy positions in the world for which their fathers
·
would have prepared them had they been permitted to live."
R.'. w:. Melvin W. Johnson made a most thoughtful and eloquent
11ddress at the dedication of the Masonic Home, well worthy of the
perusal of every Mason, and while it is impossible to produce here the
nddress in full, there is the thought that misfortune may come to anyone in life, even those apparently most happily situated, which he implies
in the following forceful and striking manner:
"It has been said that every man is responsible for his own destiny.
No other epigram, containing much that ie· trne, ever contained more
that is false. Not that we should neglect personal endeavor or do else
than encourage it in others, but rememeerlng how enviT-0nment and surroundings have shaped our own lives, we should not too lightly con·
demn others whose lives have been in some respects failures.
"More than twenty-three hundred years ago, in a discussion between
Cyrus, the king, and Crcesus, the intimate friend and associate of Solon,
one of the wisest of the Greeks, when Cyrus was not convinced by any
argument that his plans could fail, Crtesus used these words, perhaps
suggested to him by his friend, the wise law-giver: 'Cyrus, if thou thinkest that thou are like one of the Gods and no harm can come to thee,
it may do, but I am reminded, oh, ki1tg, and take this lesson to heaf"I,
that there is a wheel on whkh the affairs of men revolve and that its
mechanism is such that it prevents any man fro1t1. being always fo1'tuKate.'
"Each of our lives revolves upon such a Greek wheel. None of them
are fortunate in all things, and it may well be that as much of our good
fortune comes from the force of circumstances, so the ill fortune of
others may likewise not be due to their own inherent fault or error.
"Are you wealthy? An earthquake or a panic may send you to the
poor-house. Are you happy 1n the love of your home and family? A

"The interior of the main house is charming. The main entrance
is in the middle of the front. Opposite the door stairs rise to the second floor, twining in both directions on a landing that is lighted by a
battery. of small windows which also afford good light to the main hall.
"On either side of the entrance door are small parlors or waiting
rooms, while a huge fireplace built of field stone occupies the left side
of the main hall. On the right is the dining-room, bright in a flood of
light from broad windows on three sides.
"Down the corridor to the left may be seen the big corner lounging room, equipped with plenty of windows and light, built-in leather
cushioned seats, field stone fireplace, and leading from it is the room
designated for an assembly room, and beyond that a smaller room
marked on the original plan for a card room.
"In the ell adjoining the dining-room are ample serving, storage
and pantry rooms, regular!)' fitted hotel kitchen with every modern
implement and equipment for easy and efficient service and results, ice
boxes, storerooms for groceries and supplies, and in short, everything
needful.
"On the second floor are fifty-two bedrooms, some single and others
en suite, all prettily Japered, some with running water, but mostly
without. On the secon floor are many baths and lavatories, while numerous toilet rooms are conveniently installed on the first floor.
"The entire inside finish is of hard wood, mostly oak, while the first
floor flooring is all of narrow oak, without a crack or warp in it. The
standing finish is also in perfect condition and of old English finish. The
finish of the bedrooms and upper halls is of white painted soft wood,
while the floors are of birch.
"The entire plant is steam heated. The laundry is a commodious
and completely equipped building, detached from the main house and
partially concealed by a grove of pines. Still further back an ample
stable and garage combined suggests possibilities for hospital uses in
case of need, as well as possibilities for enlargement in later years."

After the opening of the Grand Lodge, the Grand Master informed
the brethren that there were present distinguished visitors from the
Grand Jurisdiction of Virginia and a committee of Past Grand Masters
was appointed to retire and escort the distinguished visitors to seats· in
the Grand Lodge.

After the distinguished brethren were intPOduced, they were cordially welcomed by the Grand Master, after which a suitable response

Virginia.
When the Grand Lodge resumed labor at the afternoon session, the
Roll of Honor was called by the Grand Secretary, the Grand Lodge
standing, and the Grand Secretary was happily able to announce that

The Grand Master delivered the annual address, in which he
assured the brethren that the Grand Jurisdiction was in a prosperous

Grand Jurisdictions.
In the midst of the Grand Master's address an interruption took

Honors.

MINNESOTA, .1912.
The Fifty-ninth Annual Communication of the M.'. w:. Grand
Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of Minnesota was held
in the Masonic Temple, Sixth street -and Smith avenue, in the city of
St. Paul, commencing at high twelve on Wednesday, January 17, A. D.
1912, A. L. 5912-Grand Master Elmer A. Kling presiding.
All the Grand Officers were present. During the session 224
Lodges were represented out of 253 on the roll.
The Grand Master's address shows a year of Masonic activity in
his jurisdiction. Corner-stone ceremonies in connection with the new
Federal building at Austin, Minn., and the new High School building
in Spring Valley, Minn., and also in connection with the new Federal building at Faribault, Minn., are fully described, and the occasions
were Masonically stimulating to the places in which they were held.
The dedication of the new Masonic Hall 9f Garnet Lodge No. 166
is described, an<l the fraternity of the State is congratulated upon the
completion of such a well-appointed and beautiful Temple.
A few decisions upon Masonic law were rendered by the Grartd
Master, most of them of a purely local character.
Two of the decisions of a general nature we quote, as follows :
"Where a candidate who has been accepted, immediately before
taking the obligation of the Enteired Awrentiee degree withdrew, not
being willing to proceed, the degree fee may be returned to him. The
fee accompanying the petition for the degrees of Masonry becomes

"The residence of a petitioner for the degrees of Masonry at the

In accordance with the report of the Committee on Jurispruden~e,

may be of general interest :
. "Resolved, That Lodges be and are hereby permitted to have the
Scriptures chanted instead of read, or March Music played, during
the circumambulations in the work of the three degrees; that the
Lord's Prayer be permitted to be chanted before the Prayer at Initiation; that instrumental March Music be permitted durmg any time
the candidate is marching; that either a carpet, movable or built-in
stair, may be used in the second degree; that plain robes be permitted
for all officers and others who actively participate in the second section
of the third degree, and that a lantern or stereopticon and appropriate
music be permitted in the lectures only, as distinguished from the
'work' in all degrees."

MONTANA, 1911.
The Forty-seventh Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons of Montana was held in the
· Masonic Temple in the city of Missoula, commencing at 9 :30 o'clock
a. m. on Wednesday, September 20, 1911-J. W. Speer, Grand Master,
presiding.
The address of welcome to the members and officers of the Grand
Lodge, to the city of M'issoula, was delivered by Past Master United
States Senator Joseph M. Dixon, who said in part:
"In speaking of Masonry as an uplifting power, I may say that for
the last two or three centuries of the world's history I doubt whether
there was a more potent civil force among the nations of the globe .
than ~he. spirit embodied in Masonry, represented to-day by over 6,000
men m Montana.
"While we naturally like to go back to King Solomon's Temple for
sentimental traditions of the Order, we know that modern Masonry,
the period of its great usefulness, may be said to cover two or three
hundred years. It undoubtedly blazed the trail of human endeavor
for a betterment of existing conditions, for a philosophy of morals
and brotherly love that led the way among civilized men.
"In the history of Montana, known to all of us by tradition, Masonry has played a most creditable and· prominent part in its upbuildi_ng.
"Here on the west side, in this city Masonry I know has been a
factor only for good citizenship and betterment of local civil con·
ditions.
"We are especially proud to see the Masons meet this morning in
this our new Temple, in the erection of which we have taken some local
pride, at some sacrifice and a ~re1lt deal of ~evotion on t~e part ?f the
local membership. We all think our town 1s the best-if we did not
we would not be patriotic. We greet you and take pleasure in welcoming you to the gateway of the Bitter Root."
A fitting response to the address of welcome was made by Grand
Master Speer, after which the Grand Lodge was opened in Ample
Form.

NEVADA, 1912.
In accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, the Fortyeighth Annual Grand Communication of the M.'. w: · Grand Lodge of
Nevada was commenced in the Masonic Temple, in the city of Reno,
on the second Tuesday of June (being the 11th day of the month),
A. L. 5912-Herman Davis, Grand Master, presiding.
· The Grand Master, in his address, states that while the Grim Reaper
did not, during the preceding year, invade the official circle of the
Grand Lodge, yet was busy among the Craftsmen of the various Lodges,
and he pays a just tribute to their memory.
He recounts the work of the preceding year, ;i.nd refers to the
present condition of the Craft in his jurisdiction. He is glad to observe
that a substantial increase in membership had been achieved, but
sounds a note of warning because of certain loose methods which he
believes are in vogue in certain Lodges of inquiring into the qualifications of those who seek admission to the fraternity, and feels, also, that
there is danger of drifting away from the ancient landmarks by· the
adoption of convenient and elastic interpretations of their meanings, and
absorbing customs and ideas from certain modern societies of mushroom growth, thereby manifesting tendencies absolutely foreign to the
spirit of Ancient Craft Masonry.

NEW BRUNSWICK, 1911.
The Forty-fourth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
the Ancient and Honorable Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons
of New Brunswick was held at Freemasons' Hall, in the city of St.
John, on Tuesday, the 22d day of August, A. D. 1911, A. L. 5911M.'. w:. Henry Seabury Bridges, Ph. D., in the East.

In opening his address the Grand Master says :
"It is my privilege and pleasure to report that peace and harmony
have prevailed throughout every part of this jurisdiction, and also that
there has been unusual activity in the Subordinate Lodges throughout
the Province during the past year. The reports of these Lodges will
show a substantial increase in our membership. But, my brethren, it
Is well to remember that it is not the number of those who wear the
lamb skin that has given to our fraternity the proud position that it has
always held in the world's estimation, but. rather the internal qualifications and exemplary conduct of each individual Mason. No anxiety
therefore to increase the membership of our Lodge should ever lead us
to permit those to join our ranks who do not maintain that high moral
standing which should always characterize good Masons. If we wish to
preserve the high standing of our noble fraternity, we must never lose ·
sight of that well known maxim, 'Guard well the outer door.'"
His address is a business-like statement of his activities during
the year.
He dwells particularly upon the great pleasure he received from
his visitations to the subordinate Lodges of the jurisdiction.
He mentions, also, his acceptance of the cordial invitation extended
by the Grand Master of the District of Columbia to be present with
him on the occasion of the celebration of the lOOth anniversary of the
Grand Lodge in the city of Washington, and of the great pleasure which
the acceptance of that invitation gave him.
From the reports of the Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary the
information is afforded that the finances of the Grand Lodge are in a
sound condition, and that there was, during the year, a substantial
increase of membership, the total membership at this Communication
being 3,061.
T he Committee on Foreign Relations made the following report,
which was apparently adopted.

ns

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

"The negotiation, movement, action, or whatever it may be termed,
between the Freemasons of France as represented by the Grand Orient
and those of Germany has not, your Committee find, made sufficient
progress to justify the declaration that the breach which has for a long
time existed between the members of the Craft in the two countries has
been healed, although some progress has been made in some of the
Grand Lodges of Germany towards removing the impediments which
stand in the way of a more satisfactory relationship than now exists.
The difficulties appear to have begun in 1871. out of the Franco-Prussion war, or rather out of the events or circumstances connected with that
war, and they were extended or perpetuated by the action of the Grand
Orient of. France in regard to what is known among the Fraternity as a
removal of one of the ancient landmarks, the extinction of one of the
Great Lights, and which action of the Grand Orient of F rance has mater.ially affected the attitude towards it of, practically, the whole Craft in
America as well as in some parts of Europe, notably those in which the
English language is used.
"The progress of time, the constantly improving relationship between
the people of France and of Germany have disposed a great many of the
German Masons to endeavor to put an end to the unsatisfactory relationship between the Craft in the two countries, and some of the German
Grand Lodges have so declared themselves; but there is not the unanimity
of feeling in the matter which Brother Kruger anticipated when he made
his appeal to us. Indeed the whole matter has created a great deal of
feeling among the Freemasons of Germany. So apparently, prudence
and care will be most necessary in the endeavor to bring about a final
settlement. Your Committee share in the hopes that this whole business will eventually be amicably settled, and that the Grand Orient of
France will so far recollnize the strong desire of the Craft in many
countries for a restoration of harmony and a cessation of the troubles
·
which have been created by the action referred to above.
"Your committee remind Grand Lodge that there are in France two
supreme authorities over the Craft Lodges, and that these two bodies
are in harmonious relations with each other. The doctrine of exclusive
Jurisdiction does not hold in that country to the extent to which it 'is
held in America. One of these bodies is the Grand Orient ; the other. is
the Grand Lodge of France which has under its control over one hundred and twenty Lodges, fifty of which are in Paris and its suburbs.
Your Committee can see no verr strong reason against friendly relatidnship and fellowship with this Grand Lodge. It often happens that a
member of the Craft from this Province seeks, when in France, to visit
the fraternity there. Our relations or want of them with the Grand
Orient practically prevents this. The brother does not seek the Grand
Lodge of France, for he knows nothing of it. Yet it is a le~itimate authority, admitted to be so, by the Grand Orient, and its certificates and balustres are issued in the name of the Grand Architect of the Universe;
and its membership is a satisfactory one. The Committee is of the opinion that the Grand Lodge of New Brunswick might open negotiations
with it looking for an interchange of representatives, pending the final
settlement of all the difficulties which now exist between the Grand
Orient of France and the governing bodies of the Craft elsewhere; and
they so recommend."
R:. w:. Henry S. Bridges, St. John, re-elected Grand ·Master.
R:. w:. J . Twining Hartt, St. John, re-elected Grand Secretary.

NEW HAMPSHIRE, 1912.
A Special Communication of the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of the
Ancient and Honorable Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of New Hampshire was held in the city of Portsmouth, on
fhursday, June 22, A. L. 5911, A. D. 1911, for the purpose of participating in the celebration of the one hundred and seventy-fifth anniveraary of St. John's Lodge No. I-Charles H. Wiggin, M:. w:. Grand
Master, presiding.
The celebration of the one hundred and seventy-fifth anniversary
of St. John's Lodge No. 1 was indeed a notable event, participated in
by a large number of the eminent Masons of New Hampshire.
The celebration extended over the afternoon and evening of June
22d, the principal literary feature of the afternoon being a historical
address by the M:. w:. Frederick W . Sawyer. It was characterized
by all as a remarkably fine production, and while necessarily exhaustive
in its scope, it was neverthele$S followed very closely, so we are told,
by the immense audience who heard it.
A pleasing incident of the address was the announcement made by
M:. W:. Brother Sawyer, that of the Grand Officers who were present and participating in the one hundred and fiftieth anniversary of St.
John's Lodge No. 1, held in 1886, eleven were on the platform, and as
their names were called they in turn arose, and received hearty greetings from all present.
At the evening celebration an elaborate program was rendered,
in which there were a number of addresses by distinguished Masons,
and at the conclusion of the day it was the universal opinion that the
anniversary celebration was most successful and that the Portsmouth
brethren were entitled to great praise for their splendid management
of the affair, and all agreed that "it was a grand affair, grandly observed."
Another Special Communication of the Grand Lodge was held on
July 24, 1911, for the purpose of attending the Centennial Annlnrsary
of Humane Lodge No. 21, and also of dedicating their new Masonic
Temple.
Still another Special Communication of the Grand Lodge was held
on November 7, 1911, for the purpose of cjedicating the Hall of Cube
Lodge No. 10.

The one hundred and twenty-third Annual Communication of the

The Grand Master, in his annual address, after a few brief words
of introduction, devotes considerable space to the subdivision "Necrology,'' in which he fittingly refers to the lives and characters of certain members of the fraternity who had in the preceding year been
called to their reward.
Concerning conditions of peace and harmony within the jurisdlc- •
tions, he has this to say :
"Masonically the year has been void of strife, contention or serious
infraction of our regulations. Peace and fraternal good-will, to the best
of my knowledge, prevail in all Lodges; none of the ancient landmarks
of the Craft have bee·n dimmed or obliterated; numerically we are
stronger by one hundred and twenty-two than one year ago. I do not
feel that there has been diminution of interest or failure to investigate
carefully the character, habits and Masonic worth of those who have
sought admission to our fraternity."
Among his decisions we find the following:
"Question-A petitioner, after receiving a clear ballot and before
the conferring of any degrees, was objected to by a member of the
Lodge to the Master privately. Afterwards the objections were withdrawn. Will another ballot be necessary or can the petitioner receive
his de~rees at once provided he returns his fee and still wishes to
enter?'
"Answer-See Grand Constitution, page j5, Article XIV, section
117. The withdrawal of the objections cannot be considered any more
than the withdrawal of a negative ballot cast in open lodge. The petitioner stands rejected."
This, as we know, is not the rule in California. If the objection is
withdrawn within sixty days, the case proceeds as if no objection had
been made, and it is only in cases where the objection is not withdrawn
in sixty days that it has the effect of a blackball.
Concerning the celebration of the one hundred and seventy-fifth

all of you. I have them to spare, and, besides, the kind with which I
am infected are extremely prolific. They are truly microbes worth

Two decisions on Masonic law were rendered in the year, one of
which was as follows ·:
"Where the ballot has been spread on the petition of a candidate,
and the result has been announced in the south and west, can the Master
destroy the ballot if but one black ball or cube appear?
.
"Ruled-That where the ballot has been spread for the, election or
rejection of a petitioner, and the result has been announced in the south
and west or m the south only, the Master cannot destroy the ballot,
but must' declare the petitioner elected or rejected as the ballot may
decide."
New Jersey still appears to' hold the record, so far as the question
of "visible physical defects" are concerned. Ninety-seven cases of this
chatacter were submitted to the Grand Master, and each received his
closest scrutiny ; he granted ptrmlssion to receive petitions in 62 cases ;
he refused permission in 29 cases, and he states that there are 6 cases
still pending.
That certainly Is "going some" in the Depattment of "v. p. d."
There is one paragraph in the "conclusion" of the Grand Master's
address that, while it is of possibly no particular importance, is difficult to understand. He states that one day of every seven has been
devoted to "executive matters," entailing a weekly journey of over
t,200 miles, or a total of more than 62,000 miles during the year. This,
like "v. p. d.," is difficult to figure out.
