NEW YORK, 1912.
Number of Lodges, 808.
Number of Masons, 173,713.
The One Hundred and Thirty-first Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of New York
was opened in the Gra.nd Lodge room, Masonic Hall, city of New York;
on the afternoon of May 7, A. D. 1912, A. L. 5912, at 2 o'clock-M.". w:.
Robert Judson Kenworthy, Grand Master, presiding.
·
In the introductory part of his annual address the Grand Master
refers to the apparent indifference to Masonry of such a large percentage
of the membership,

124

REPORT ON · CORRESPONDENCE. ·

This indifference, however, in our opinion, is more apparent than
real; because even among the vast numbers of Masons .who do not
attend Lodge frequently, there nevertheless is a very warm· regard for
the institution and a genuine interest in its welfare and progress, and
the failure to manifest a more open interest is frequently the result of
other duties which demand such a tribute of time. However, the Grand
Master's remarks upon this subject are of interest, and are as follows:
"It seems to me we ought to reach out in earnest for that seventyfive per cent. inactive part of our membership. Among them ar~ nui;ierous influential worth-while men. The roster of the Craft will disclose the name~ of many prominent in all walks of life, who have
attained honor and distinction in their respective callings; men who
delight in association with their fellow-citizens and are sought ?n every
notable public occasion; yet th~ Craft leaves them alone, to 4nf~ from
its influence-and so the prestige of many a strong personality is lost
to us. In the face of such conditions can we honestly claim our Fraternity is 'progressing' numerically? I feel it is worth our thought to
try and meet this situation, and I urge you men of today-take the subject home with you, study its possibilities. When .we ha".e lea.med how
to cement the membership we already have and mfuse mto 1t the red
blood of interest, then will Masonry truly come into its own."
The Grand Master fittingly refers to "The Fraternal Dead," enumerating the list of those prominent in the jurisdiction who, within the year
preceding, had been called to their reward.
·
The Grand Master enumerates the public ceremonies conducted in
the year by the Grand Lodge, making a special report of the dedication
of the Daniel D. Tompkins Memorial Chapel at the Masonic Home at
Utica, N. Y., on Sunday, June 25, 1911.
The occasion certainly was an inspiring one, and the addresses were
of a high order.
Governor Tompkins was one of the historical characters of the
early portion of the last century, and some of the remarks of the
Grand Master concerning Governor Tompkins will no doubt b<; of
general interest, and we, therefore, quote a portion of the Grand Master's address, as follows:
"In 1812 Governor Tompkins prorogued the Legislature for the
first time in the history of the State as a last resort against the favorable reception of numerous petitions f?r the incorporatio,n of sun~ry
banking companies, accompanied .by the influence ?f corruption and .bribery, and projecting a system "".h1ch threaten~d evil to the community. .
"At this time the declaration of war with England was made and
the Govern0r was charged with the additional duties of State and national defense without the aid of a cordial Legislature.
'He organized the militia, expending his large means in adyan~ing
money in all directions to ena?!e the war to be prosecuted; mam~amed
by his personal means the M1htar:y Academy at West Pomt, paid for
recruiting in Connecticut, and sustained t~e workmen wh? .IT!anufactured
arms at Springfield, Massachusetts ; equipped 40,000 m1htia and sent
them to the defense of Plattsburg, Sacketts Harbor, Buffalo, and other

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

,. 125

points, and sustained the credit of the United States government with
hb own private funds at a time when the banks of New York refused
to loan to the government on its treasury notes without his personal
endorsement.
"President Madison held Governor Tompkins in such high esteem
that he tendered him the portfolio of Secretary of State, which was
declined by Governor Tompkins with the explanation on his part that
he could serve his country better as Governor of the State of New York
than as a member of the President's Cabinet. His resulting popularity
la testified to throughout the country by many counties, towns and
1ocieties which have perpetuated his memory by adopting his name.
"In 1816 Governor Tompkins was a candidate for the Presidency
of the United States, and it it is interesting to know that it was largely
his opposition to slavery that prevented his nomination. He accepted
the Vice-Presidency, however, under President Monroe, and early in
the following year resigned the Governorship to go to Washington.
"It was then that the cruel and totally unfounded accusation was
made against him of having misused the State funds, when, as a matter of fact, he had practically placed his entire private fortune in the
State treasury and used it for the defense of his country and the honor
of his State. Broken in health, broken in fortune, and, we may well
believe, broken-hearted, this renowned patriot, splendid American, and
noble Mason went home to Staten Island to die.
"In relation to thoughtful, patriotic, straightforward, and successful
administration in elective office, Masons have always given a good
account of themselves. Governor Tompkins was one of the most striking instances in the history of our Order and in the history of our
nation of a man in office subjected to the bitterest opposition, the most
difficult political obstacles, and, finally, the vilest slander, who yet pursued the even tenor of his way, planning and working steadily and
incessantly for the welfare of his city. the State, and the people.
''Unusual rewards were his during his active career, yet he died
in disappointment and in poverty; and it remained for posterity, for his
fellow Masons, to record his name permanently in our annals of honorable life and good deeds.
. "Fifty-one years old is too young for a robust and active man to
die; and when such a man dies at fifty-one, as Daniel D. Tompkins did,
broken in health and bankrupt, after the honest accumulation of a
large fortune, which he spent for his country, and after an extraordinary
career of unremitting hard work, devoted to his country, there is in that
man's character a brilliant exemplification of what we mean by
Masonry.
"Governor Tompkins attained the 33d degree while he was still
in the thirties-a young man. He was Grand Secretary of the Grand
Lodge of New York in 1801 to 1805, beginning his term when he
was but twenty-seven years old. During 1820 and 1821 he was Grand
Master of Masons in the State of New York. Before that, in 1813,
he had been made Grand Commander for life of the SuJ,>reme Council
of the Thirty-third Degree for the Northern Masonic Jurisdiction of
the United States of America."

13L

This is what the Grand Master has to say under the heading of
decisions:
"I have seen fit to put down very few decisions, those being the
ones which were not covered by the present Masonic Law. One exception, however, to this I will make. It seems that there has been so
much misunderstanding as to laws bearing upon ballot that I will give
a resume of them. Whenever a petition is received it must be balloted
upon. When it is balloted upon and a candidate is rejected, another
ballot may be taken for fear a mistake has been made. In no case can
more than two ballots be taken, nor can another ballot be taken on the
same petition at any subsequent time. The petitioner must wait one
year before he ciln petition again. The ballot is secret and sacred. The
Worshipful Master, Senior and Junior Warden, and Senior Deacon
have no right to disclose how the ballot stood if rejected. No man
has a right to question the ballot nor to ask anyone how he voted on
the ballot. No man has a right to tell how he voted. Thus, you see the
strongest laws are thrown around a ballot in order to keep it secret.
Any brother who is a member of the Lodge can demand another ballot
on passing or raising and can stop the Entered Ap{lrentice by objecting
thereto. A man was elected to degrees in Edenton Lodge six years aR"O,
initiated in Ranah Lodge, was made an Entered Apprentice at Danville,
Virginia, passed in Concord Lod!le at Tarboro and raised in Eno Lodge,
Durham, but has not signed the By-laws of Edenton Lodge, what is his
position ?-That of a non-affiliated Mason.''
·
The Grand Master particularly urges upon the Masons of the
iurisdiction the duty of carrying forward to a successful conclusion
the project which is under consideration of a Masonic and Eastern
Star Home.
The Oxford Orphan Asylum still claims the affectionate interest
of the fraternity and is regarded, in many respects, as the model institution of its kind in America. Three hundred and sixteen children
are sheltered there and are heing trained and educated to fit them in a
proper manner to battle with the world successfully and to make
good, high-minded, useful citizens.

"Your Committee on 'Good .o f the Order' begs leave to direct the
11ttention of this Grand Lodge, and the members of constitutent Lodges,
briefly to two subjects which appeal to us as just now demanding the
1ympathetic support of all men who believe in the betterment of humanity. Certainly if the principles of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth
have any practical application, it may be expected that Masons would be
Interested in these topics.
"The first of these topics is 'The Peace Movement in its various
activities;' the other, 'The Burden of Tuberculosis and its Prevention.'
Both of these movements have progressed far beyond the field of speculntion. They are organized, and we expect th.e next ten years will see
more progress made toward their solution than has been made in the
pnst fifty.
"There was a· time when might made right, when a nation coveting
n hit of territory, or feeling its interests or its honor trenched upon,
resorted immediately to the sword as the only way of bringing about the
rlesired settlement. Those days, we hope, have gone by, yet it is within the
memory of every man in this room to realize how easily and quickly war
has been resorted within the past ten or fifteen years. There is a
glamor about military trappings; the marshal spirit frequently seizes
a people. The splendid appearance of the man in the ranks, the dash
of the officers, the blare of the bugle and the ·rattle of the drums, are
apt to outweigh temporarily the agony of death in battle or in the
hospital, the sorrow of fatherless children and widowed mothers, the
destruction of property and all the terrible costs of war. General Sherman said : 'War is hell.' This expressfon fits the case. We conceive
of nothing which approaches nearer to the ordinary conception of the
'inferno' than such a battle as Gettysbttrg. We believe that we are beginning to realize that war is a crime, yet we go on as a· nation spending our money in preparation for wars that are to be.
"We direct your attention today as impressively as we can to the
fact that this nation which spends more than a billion dollars a year
for its maintenance, that it is spending more than half that amount, more
than 500 millions annually upon the up-keep of its army and navy and
in the payment of pensions to those who fought the battles of the past;
and this, in a nation which maintains proportionately the smallest standing army in the world. We are spending annually more than $5.00 a
head on wars past and future for every man, woman and child in this
country of ours. We are spendin~ more in this way than is spent in
the maintenance of all the educational institutions of the land. What
we spend is less than that spent by several of the great powers of
Europe.
"England has 73 first-class hattleships, representing an expenditure of more than a half billion dollars, United States 37, Germany 36,
France 32, Japan 24, Italy 15, Russia 12, and all of these nations are
building warships just as fast as the money can be raised by taxation or
bond issues and the ship-yards can turn them out.
"We may well ask, what means all this feverish activity, all this
bu rden of taxation, all this waste of productive · activity. The statesmen
of all nations see the folly of it; the financiers and economists see
fi nancial ruin staring many nations in the face as the result of it. We
may also ask: where is our boasted Christian civilization; where is our
much vaunted ide~ of brotherhood? Yet let us not be discouraged.
There have been two Hague conferences. There have been serious questions which twenty-five years ago would have meant war in fortyeight hours settled by arbitration. There are now many treaties of

OHIO, 1911.
A group picture of an "unbroke~ line" of twenty Past Grand Masters of the M. ·. W. ·. Grand Lodge of Ohio, F. and A. M., forms
the frontispiece of the Proceedings.
From an examination of this picture one is justified in the belief
that the group, from the standpoint of intelligence and character, will
compare favorably with any group of men of like number which
might be assembled anywhere on earth.
The group contains the picture of William B. Melish, Grand Master
of Ohio in 1896, and now the Grand Master of the Grand Encampmeat
of Knights Templar of the United States, and Barton Smith, Grand
Master in 1897, and now Sovereign Grand Commander of the Supreme
Council of the Thirty-third Degree for the Northern Jurisdiction of the
United States.
..
The Grand Lodge of the Most Ancient and Honorable Fraterqity
of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Ohio convened in the
Masonic Temple, Dayton, Ohio, at 10 o'clock a. m., Wednesday, October
18 1911-Brother H. S. Kissell, Grand Master, presiding.
' The Communication was graced by the attendance of all of the
living Past Grand Masters, all of the Past Deputy Grand Masters and
representatives from 508 out of 520 chartered Lodges.
This showing we believe to be unprecedented in the history of
Grand Jurisdictions as large as that of Ohio.
The Grand Communication was welcomed to Dayton by Bl'other
Edward Burkhardt, Mayor of the city, and by M.'. W.'. Brother Horac~
A. Irvin, on behalf of the Masons of Dayton.
'
To these addresses M.'. w:. Brother A. P . Sperra made response
on behalf of the Grand Lodge in suitable and expressive language.

..

"As we survey the year which has just closed, w~ cannot, I am
quite sure, but distingui~h a. splendid advance in all h~es of thought
and action. Corruption in high places, unscrupulous business methoqs,
unfair dealing between employer and employee, th~ great moral and s~cia1

morally socially and economically, and I believe that the teachings of

Four dispensations were granted to form new Lodges. These dis111•nsations were granted only after most careful investigation, for,

The Grand Master states that "the day was replete with many
pleasant incidents, and every courtesy was shown the brethren from
Ohio."
That there is a tendency in Ohio, as well as in other Grand
Jurisdictions, to interpolate matter into the ritual that does not belong
there, with a view of promoting the dramatic effect, etc., of the "work,"
may be judged from the following quotation from the Grand Master's
address:
"I find that not a few of the Lodges are adding quite a little
work which is not contained in the Ritual or Standard Monitor. A
long soliloquy is being Used in one of the Lodges at least; a dialogue
has also been added which pertains to the conspiracy; several of the
Lodges have very elaborate drills; and I have seen and heard of other
matters which I fear will, if continued, destroy the effort which has
been made to secure uniformity in the work.
.
"When the attention of the Master has been called to Resolution
10. found on page 84 of the Code, the reply has been that they 'conform
to' the Ritual and Monitor by not omitting any of the prescribed work,

The M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge, A. F. and A. M., of the State of

In opening his address, Grand Master Eddleman says :
"It is my pleasure to be able to tell you that peace and harmony
have prevailed throughout this grand jurisdiction; that but little discipline has been required; that the great work of building and maintaining our Masonic Home, was neither a dream nor a spasm, but a living
idea, and that it thrivt:s and grows in the hearts of the brethren, and
that they may be safely trusted to rally to its support and meet its requirements. We realized in the beginning that a hard year was before
us, and the tax upon our resources heavy, but the brethren have stood
by their guns, and have said by their actions, the Home must and shall
succeed."

Among the decisions rendered by the Grand Master we quote th'e
following:
"Question-Eighteen months ago, petitioner was rejected by the
Lodge in a neighboring town. Since then, he removed to this city and
has been a resident here for about twelve months. Recently he petitioned
this Lodge for the degrees, but the Lodge of his former jurisdiction
which had previously rejected him refused to waive jurisdiction. Has
that Lodge perpetual jurisdiction over him so long as he remains in
this Grand lurisdiction, or can this Lodge take jurisdiction and either
..
admit or reject as it may deem it?"
"Answer-We have abandoned perpetual jurisdiction. The Lodge
which rejected the petitioner only has jurisdiction for six months thereafter. In cities where two or more Lodges have concurrent jurisdiction,
the jurisdiction over rejected material continues for twelve months.
" Held-In case of the death of the Worshipful Master of the Lodge,
the duties of that office devolve first upon the Sr. W. and in his absence
upon the Jr. W. The Lodge cannot elect a Worshipful Master for the
unexpired term nor can the Grand Master authorize same by special di.spensation. In rendering this decision, I reversed myself, but did so
after the examination of Masonic authorities."

The Report on Foreign Correspondence is by W.'. Thomas
Chauncey Humphry.

Of the Masonic Home the Grand Master says:
"This is the apple of our eye, the core of our hearts. We are
proud of our Home and we have the right to be. We are faithful and
loyal to it and God grant we ever shall be. In this institution, we are
building for time and eternity. As Freemasons of this generation, w~
are erecting a monument more durable, _more creditable, than the finest
marble shafts that wealth can purchase. Generations yet unborn will
rise up to call us blessed. We have made, are making, and will continue
to make, sacrifices for the Home, but brethren, we can well afford to
make them. Think of it! The children of our deceased brothers
snatched as brands from the burning, cared for, educated and equipped
for the battles of life, they go forth full grown men and women, a credit
to themselves, to the community and to us."

OREGON, 1912.
A Special Communication of the Grand Lodge assembled on May
11, 1912, in the Masonic Temple, Portland, Ore., for the purpose of
laying the corner-stone of Reed College, a public edifice in the near
vicinity.
The Sixty-second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge,
Ancient Free and Accepted Masons, of the State of Oregon, was open~d
in the Grand Lodge room, Masonic Temple, city of Portland, on the
morning of June 12, A. D. 1912, A. L. 5912, at the hour of 10 o'clock
a. m.-Thomas M. Baldwin, Grand Master, presiding.
In opening his address, the Grand Master says:
"Brethren, I congratulate you upon the close of a year of prosperity,
as evidenced in the report of our Grand Secretary, whose labors have
contributed largely to this happy result. This report will show the
greatest material gr.o wth for any like period in the history of the Craft
in this State.
"I fear we are in danger of becoming 'purse proud.' Rather let us
extend the beneficent influences of Masonry as far as our means and opportunities will permit. We will thus best serve the great purposes of
our Fraternity and more clearly demonstrate our usefulness as a factor
in the scheme of civilization.
"Our chief aim should be to exert the greatest amount of practical
good possible. To apply the principles of a speculative science to the
practical needs of humamty; indeed, the preservation of our ancient landmarks is quite consistent with a complete adaptation to present . needs.
for the needs of humanity today are the needs of yesterday, and of all
time. These ends are not to be attained by a careful memorizing of
the ritual alone, by proclaiming aloud our virtues or by delving amid
the ruins of an age whose splendor and glory have long since passed
away. These are interesting and important in their way, and afford
stimulus for further exertion, but after all is said, we discover they are
only means to an end, and so, the question of the hour is, 'How can we
make Masonry to be in actuality, all that it can be as a force for good?'
Find the answer. You know it."

The Grand Master bespeaks "reverent attention" while he alludes
to the "fraternal dead" of his own and other jurisdictions.
His report in a straightforward, business statement of his activities
during the year, which consist in part of the constitution of the six
Lodges which received charters at the preceding Annual Communication; of the issuance of dispensations to form five new Lodges; of the
placing of corner-stones of several public buildings; of the dedication
of a number of Masonic Halls, etc.
From his "opinions" we make the following quotation:
"Question-ls it permissible to take more than one candidate at a
time through the E. A., F . C. or the first part of the M. M. degrees ?
"Answer-No, except the second section of the Fellow Craft degree
and the lectures of the several degrees. The ceremonies should not
be abridged for the sake of saving time. They should be made as im~
pressive as possible, and no careless, slipshod work should be permitted."
"Question-is it a violation of any Masonic law to allow the ladies.
of the Eastern Star, as an organization, to take part jointly in the
funeral service by occupying one side of the hollow square at the grave
and depositing the flowers into the grave after the Masons have depos•
ited the sprig of acacia?
"Answer-I would grant to the Eastern Star' every privilege not inconsistent with the law and established customs of Masonry, but as the
burial of a brother is strictly Masonic work, and as the Lodge is at labor during the whole service, it is not proper or permissible to permit
anyone not a Mason to take part in the funeral ceremonies, except the'
clergy.
"I hold that a Subordinate Lodge conducting a funeral service may
invite (or permit to join in the funeral procession) other societies. or
appendant orders, to act as escort, whose position shall be assigned by
the Lodge conducting the ceremonies. The Order of the Eastern Star
might be invited to join in the procession and to render its beautiful and
impressive funeral service at the close of the Masonic ceremonies."
"Statement-Charges were preferred against a brother by the Jun"
ior Warden of the Lodge at a Stated Communication, charging conduct
unbecoming a Mason. The trial commission appointed in pursuance
of this action, in due time reported its find ings in tl;te matter, its verdict
being guilty, and the sentence reprimand in open Lodge. The brother
gave immediate notice of appeal to the Grand Lodge, which appeal, by
mutual consent, was subsequently dismissed. The brother has not ~t
any time appeared before the Lodl{e to submit to the sentence of reprimand, nor has he at any time indicated his intention to do so
"Question, 1-What was the brother's standing after the dismissal
of his appeal by the Grand Lodge?
"2-To restore himself to good standini;r, must he submit himself
to the sentence of 'reprimand in open Lodge'?
"3-Before such action on his part, can the Lodge accept payment
of dues tendered?
"4--Would such acceptance restore him to good standing?"
"Opinion !-His standing as a member of the Lodge was not :i-ffected by dismissal of his appeal by the Grand Lodge. beyond rendering
him subject to the penalty imposed by the trial commission.

From the report of the Grand Secretary we obtain the informati~n that there are in the jurisdiction at this time 127 chartered Lodges,
with a total membership of 11,410, and that the Grand Jurisdiction is
growing at the rate of about 900 members a year.
There is on hand at the present time in the hands of the Grand
Treasurer, Grand Lodge assets to the value of $137,276.92, from which
it may be seen that financially the Grand Jurisdiction of Oregon is in
exceedingly sound condition.
The Grand Orator, w:. Brother Stephen A. Lowell, delivered the
annual address, largely historical in character, which was greatly appreciated by the Grand Lodge and ordered printed in the Proceedings.
On the second day of the Communication a delegation of ladies
from the Grand Chapter of the Eastern Star favored the Grand Lodge
with a visit; mutual felicitations were exchanged, and in the report of
the function we read :
'.'The Gran~ Matron, Mrs. Pauline Riley, thanked the Grand Lodge
for .1s fraternahsm and the courtesy of allowing the visitation and, in
closing, .Presented Mrs. Nellie Baldwin who, in a few well chosen and
appropriate remarks, presented to the Grand Lodge and the Grand Master, ~er husband, a large bouq.uet of red carnations.
. The Grand Master received the bouquet, and bestowed upon his
wife the fond embrace of love and affection amid the cheers of the
'
Grand Lodge and its visitors."
Our opinion has not been asked concerning these functions but
if it were we would venture to say that a body of females in a Grand
Lodge of Master Masons is out of place and that the "fond embraces of
love and affection" are more in keeping with the atmosphere of the fireside and hearthstone than in the mixed presence of a large body of
strange men, assembled from the four quarters of an American commonwealth like Oregon.
Our opinion, however, as stated, has not been asked, and the
above remarks may be considered obiter dictum.
The Grand Lodge was honored in the second day of the session
with a visit of M.' · w: · Fred J. Mock, Grand Master of Idaho. The
honorable brother was duly received ; he was welcomed by Grand
Master Baldwin and conducted to a seat in the East.
The election of Grand Officers resulted in the choice of Brother
George H. Burnett of No. 50 as Grand Master, and the re-election of
Brother James F. Robinson of No. 11 as Grand Secretary.

A Quarterly Communication was held at Philadelphia, December
6, 1911. Four hundred and thirty-th.ree Lodges were represented.
At this Communication reports of the various charity and financial
boards were rendered, examination of which discloses the fact that the
Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania is possessor directly and indirectly of
properties that aggregate in value $3,887,910.SS.
A full and complete report was rendered at this time by the Committee on Masonic Homes.
The corner-stone of the principal building in the Masonic Home
aroup of buildings was laid' by the Grand Lodge at the time of the celebration of the one hundred and twenty-fifth anniversary of the founding
of the Grand Lodge.
The contract for this building called for an expenditure of about
$400,000, and from the report of the Committee on Masonic Home it
nppears that excellent progress is being made and that the establishment
will be open for the reception of guests of the Grand Lodge probably
within the year.
The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge was held December 27th.
Grand Master Guthrie, in his annual address, severely rebukes the
use of Masonry for political purposes, as will appear from what he says
upon this subject, as follows:
"In the late political campaign, some members of the fraternity, forgetful of their obligations, attempted to make use of their Masonic connection to promote their political interests.
"In some of the cases the candidates advertised their membership
in Symbolic Lodjles and in other Masonic bodies, in circulars which
they themselves distributed to the public; in others, while the adver·
tisement was as objectionable in form, the candidates gave me theit
personal assurance that the publication was made by their supporters,
without their knowled!le or authority.
" In one case in Susquehanna County, and in another in Berks
County, the candidates issued and distributed printed circulars, in
which the names, addresses and locations of the various Masonic
bodies to which they belonged were fully recited.
"When these circulars were called to my attention I notified the
candidates that they must be immediately recalled, and instructed the
District Deputy Grand Masters in the respective counties to visit each
Lodge under their jurisdiction and instruct the brethren that such conduct was unmasonic and deserved the condemnation of every sincere
Mason.
.
"Almost immediately after this occurrence, my attention was called
to publications in three papers in the city of Philadelphia, in which
in different articles recommending certain candidates to support their
Masonic connections were set forth at lenp;th.
"One of these publications was in a 'Masonic' paper, in which a
whole page was devoted to the advocacy of the interest of a certain
candidate, his Masonic relations and character being specially dwelt
upon.

152

REPORT ON CORRESPOND..!NCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

"The others, in two papers, both published in West Philadelphia,
were equally objectionable.
.
"Any member of the fraternity whose Masonry is more than a
name knows that such conduct as this is unmasonic.
"It is not permissible for a Mason to use his Masonic membership
to promote his personal interests either in ·business or in politics.
"A brother convicted on a charge of attempting to use the fraternity for any such purposes could, and should, be expelled from Masonry; and every earnest, faithful Mason should show his condemnation of such conduct by every means in his power.
"We cannot be too vigilant and severe in checking such attempts to
use the fraternity improperly.
"If we permit the fraternity to be used for any selfish purposes,
particularly if we permit to to be dragged into the bitterness of partisan politics, we invite the condemnation of all right-thinking men.
"To permit such actions to go unrebuked will furnish a precedent
for further abuses, and will inevitably do more to injure our ancient and
honorable fraternity than years of faithful and unselfish devotion can
rectify.
"When the improper act is done by unwise supporters, without.
the personal knowledge or consent of the candidate, of course he cannot be held personally responsible ; but it is his duty promptly to repudiate the action, so that the guilty parties, if Masons, shall receive
the punishment which their offense deserves."

was the advent of His Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught
Canada's first Royal Governor. The people of Canada appreciate high
the fact that he is the son of the ever-to-be-revered Queen Victoria.

to him a most loyal and cordial greeting."

Concerning R.". w:. Brother William J. Hughan, deceased, ~he

"R.". w:. Brother William J. Hughan, England's famous historian,
and an honorar:v Past Grand Senior Warden of this Grand Lodge, died
at his home in Torquay, England, in May last. His death is a de<lide,.
loss to the Craft the world over. His life was spent in tracing out. the

Quebec, which was delighted to do him honor thirty years ago."

RHODE ISLAND, 1911.
An excellent picture of Henry W . Rugg, Grand Master, forms
the frontispiece of the Proceedings.
.
An Emergent Communication of the Grand Lodge of Rhode Island
was convened in Freemasons' Hall, Providence, Monday, July 25, 1910,
and was opened by the R .'. W.' . Deputy Grand Master, Brother James
B. Gay, presiding in the East.
Concerning this Special Communication, the Grand Secretary says':
"The R.'. w : . Deputy Grand Master announced that the Grand
Lodge had been called together in Emergent Communication for -the
purpose of paying the last tribute of respect to the memory of our
Brother Henry Warren Rugg, . M.'. w:. Grand Master of Masons.
He stated further that Brother Rugg had expressed the wish that there
should be no unnecessary display at his funeral. His wishes were that
the officers of the Grand Encampment of Knights Templar of the
United States, of which body he was the M.'. E . '. Grand Ma~ter, should
perform the Knights Templar funeral service over his remains and
that the officers of the Grand Lodge of Rhode Island would render the
Masonic burial office at the grave.
"Brother Gay spoke feelingly of the active, useful life which the
Grand Master had lived, and of the great loss which had come, not
alone to our fraternity but to the church and the entire community as
..
well, by his death.
" Past Grand Master Presbrey also spoke of the life and character
of the deceased, after which the service for the Lodge room was read.
"The procession was formed and the brethren passed to the street, .
where they took carriages and were conveyed to the Church of the
. Mediator, the church over which Brother Rugg had been the l?astor
for so many years previous to his retirement from active service in
the ministry and to which his mortal remains were now brought pre- '
vious to their being consigned to the grave.
"Religious servies were held, conducted by Rev. Henry I. Cushman,
pastor emeritus of the First Universalist Church, and Rev. Dr. ~. W,
Hamilton, president of Tufts' College, of which institution Brother Rugg
·
was at the time of his death the secretary.
"The Knights Templar service for the dead was impresslvel7 rendered by Brother William B. Melish of Cincinnati, Ohio, It. . E.'
Deputy Gradn Master of the Grand Encampment of Knights Templar
of the United States."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

In opening his annual address, the Grand Master says :
"It is a pleasure to me to announce that this Grand Lodge continues
to prosper. The increased membership of the past year has been astonishing, and I am led to believe that with but few exceptions, the very
best men in the Province are being received into our institution. I
believe that the moral teachings of Masonry are having an effect on
not only the Masons of our Province, but on the citizens as well. It
is not to be wondered that Masonry is increasing in our great country,
and apart from Masonry our Province is increasing and developing with
greater strides than" any other part of the Dominion. It must be g·ratifying to us to know that we are living in such a favored section of the
Universe, and we trust that while our prosperity continues we will not
forget those who are in need of our aid and benevolence.
"Last year we had a total of 83 Lodges, 65 under charter and 18
under dispensation. We now have a total of 94 Lodges, 77 under charter, and 17 under dispensation. Our membership last year was about
4,000. It is at the present time 4,500, and it should be gratifying to the
Grand Lodge to know that we are making such rapid progress."

Lodges may be judged from the following paragraphs from his review
of California:
"One Lodge asked that it be made lawful for any Lodge to exercise
its option as to whether wines, etc., might be used at Masonic banquets,
which request was refused.
"In our remarks we have frequently objected to Grand Bodies
encroaching on the rights of private Lodges, and to our mind, this is
a case in point. Personally, we are opposed to the use of any liquor
at such functions, but we deny the right of any Grand Lodge to compel by Legislation."

From the following paragraph, taken from the report of the Committee on Charters and New Lodges, we judge that Masonry is going
ahead at a rapid pace ·in the jurisdiction of Saskatchewan:
"Twelve dispensations have been issued during the last year for new
Lod~es. Eleven of these have been instituted. Six dispensations were
continued from last year, making seventeen under dispensation at the •
present time."
The Report on Foreign Correspondence is by R.'. W .'. Brother
Arthur S. Gorrell, elected at this Communication Grand Master. It
contain·s a review of California, 1911.
Concerning the charity work in California, as shown in the reports
of the various Boards of Relief, the reviewer comments as follows :
"The reports of the Boards of Relief reveal the fact that the practice of unostentatious charity continues, and the necessity and reason for
their existence thereby demonstrated. No practical illustration of the·
universality of Masonry could be more apparent than the statements
in the reports of the various boards showing the diversity of territory
from which come many of the recipients of relief. This labor of love
has been mostly admirably performed, and reflects honor and glory
upon the workers and upon our fraternity."
That the chairman of the Correspondence Committee believes in a
larger measure of local self-government as applied to subordinate

Brother Gorrell's report throughout shows a marked degree of
ability in the comments which he frequently makes and discrimination
in selections for quotations.

SCOTLAND, 1912.
A Quarterly Communication was held at St. Cuthbert's Hall, Edinburgh, February 1, 1912-the M.'. H.". the Marquis of Tuillibardine,
Grand Master, on the throne.
The Grand Master, in his address, refers to the death of Brother
Dr. W . Dashwood Kingdon at the age of ninety-eight years. Brother
Kingdon was initiated in Lodge Canongate, Kilwinning, Edinburgh No.
2, on March 7, 1837, and he states that Dr. Kingdon was probably the
oldest Freemason in the world, having been a member of the Craft for
nearly seventy-five years.
There is a living Past Grand Master, Brother Mitchell, of the
Jurisdiction of Michigan, who is now ninety-six years old, and we trust
will at least reach a hundred and surpass Dr. Kingdon in the years of
his Masonic membership.
The following amendment to the Constitution was proposed·
"No brother of any Lodge on the roll of the Grand Lodge of Scotland, or whose diploma as a Master Mason issues from Grand Lodge,
shall take part in or be concerned with the working or promulgation in
any manner of way of any degree, or rite, or order, purporting to be
Masonic, which is not .authorized by Grand Lodge, or by one of the
other. Masonic Grand Bodies with whom Grand Lodge is in amity; and
any brother acting in breach hereof, or who shall join or countenance
any body or society, purporting to be Masonic, not sanctioned by Grand
Lodge or other Masonic Grand Body in amity with it, shall be liable
to suspension or expulsion either at the instance of his Lodge'" or at the
instance of Grand Committee."
The estimated income and expenditures for the present year, as
reported by the Grand Treasurer, is as follows:
"Income : Half of half of free income of Grand Lodge for year
ending November 30, 1911, £1,469, lls. lOd. ; interest on investments,

If it be true that the total annual income of the Grand Lodge of
Scotland is only slightly in excess of £4,000 (about $20,000), the juris-.
diction does not take high rank financially.
The system of dispensing assistance in the form of what are termed
"annuities" has much to commend it. It is exceedingly economical, so
far as administration is concerned, and, besides this, annuitants are permitted a degree of personal freedom which is impossible in connection
with the Masonic Home systetr1, and the annuitants also are permitted'
to exercise a latitude of choice in their manner and method of living,
impossible in connection with the institutional method.
The Grand Secretary submits a list of 248 annuitants as of October·
1911, receiving in the aggregate £2,7-45, equivalent to about $15,000.
'
It is interesting to observe that, while the Grand Lodge of Scotland
has its Lodges distributed all over the world, drawing tribute from all
of them, yet of the 248 annuitants receiving the beneficence of the Grand
Lodge all but ten of them reside in Scotland.
There appears to be on the membership roll of the Grand Lodge
of Scotland 763 Lodges, of which 425 are in Scotland proper and 338
scattered throughout the world.
For instance, India has 55 I.,odges; Queensland 74, New Zealand
12, Western Australia 38, The Transvaal 38, and anywhere from one to
eight Lodges in the following remote places: Rhodesia, Mauritius,
Jamaica, Bermuda, Newfoundland, Gibraltar, Peru, Chili, Nicaragua,
China, Japan, Egypt, Fiji Islands, Syria, Panama, Malta, British East
Africa, West Coast of Africa, Straits Settlements, Straits of Magellan,
Philippine Jslands, Korea, Turkey, Siam, .etc.
Anybody's charter fee or annual per capita to the Graqd Lodge
looks good to Scotland, and, as noted above, Scottish thrift is manifested when it comes to disbursements, and evidently the doctrine of
kteping enrything possibte at home is prudently carried out, for, as
stated, of the 2-48 annuitants, beneficiaries of the Grand Lodge of Si:otland, 238 of them rei;ide in th.e land wher.e the Grand Lodie js domi~iled, while one each 11re r~ted as livipg in India, Queensland, ~ ew
Zealand, China, British Central America, and two in Australia and three
in Cape Colony.

nble to dispose of most of the questions presented by reference to the
lly-laws or former decisions. A <limit was issued to a brother and it
nfterward appeared that he did not intend to·apply for it. He returned
the dimit requesting that it be canceled and his membership restored.
I directed that his request be complied with. All questions as to physical qualifications have been answered by reference to former decisions,
leaving the responsibility with the Lodge.''
He reports that he received invitations to visit the Grand Lodge of
to attend its One Hundred and Twenty-fifth Anniversary; to the Grand Lodge of Louisiana to attend its One Hundredth

an active one, he having performed a vast number of official acts,

ceremonies in connection with laying corner-stones, dedications of halls,
etc., and under the heading of "visitations" says:

been unable to visit as many of the Lodges as I desired b~t those visited
have not disappointed me, and I am very thankful for the royal and
cordial treatment extended the office of Grand Master, and also to me
personally. Rest assured, brethren, I will always cherish these visits
'
and only wish they could have covered a broader scope."

Speaking of the Widows and Orphans' Home, the Grand Master
says :
"This institution reflects not only the spirit, aims and purposes of
Masonry, but its splendid success and increasing usefulness have been
the means of exalting our profession and ·of commending our principles
to the world. It has filled not only the hearts of those in official position, in our ranks, and those who projected and labored for It, but it
is the pride and glory of every individual Mason. Therefore, it should
r eceive a generous and unstinted support ; it should never be hampered
·for the want of sufficient funds, but be cared for liberally."
And concerning the same institution, the Board of Control, at the
conclusion of its report, states :
"On December 10th, next, the Home will have rounded out twenty
years of existence. During that time 476 widows and orphans have
been sheltered, clothed, and educated within its waI1s. Many of them
a re today occupying positions of responsibillty and trust, and exceedingly rare is an instance of where one has not reflected credit upon the
institution. They, themselves, are proud of such a record; this Board
is proud of it, and we know that this Grand Lodge is proud of it.
Where is there a work that not only Masonry, but mankind in general
is doing today that surpasses it ?-the moulding of character, relieving
of want ;ind distress, and kindling the fire of hope within the bosom
of those helpless ones, each of whom, were so near and so dear to a
brother who has gone before us."

The method of compensating the Grand Treasurer by commissions
upon the money handled by him seems to be in vogue in Tennessee, and
in this matter he received for his services during the preceding year

$965.04.
That seems rather extravagant compensation in a jurisdiction
whose total income appears td be less than $40,000.
California, with an income more than double this, pays its Grand
Treasurer $200, which sum, we believe, represents about the average
amount received by Grand Treasurers throughout the United States.
West Virginia and Tennessee appear to be upon the comm1ss1on
basis, very much to the financial disadvantage, we would say, of the
Grand Lodge.
This jurisdiction is one of the several that passes the so-called
"Signet Ring" from one Grand Master to another, and the ceremony
of the presentation of the "Signet Ring" took place just before the
closing of the Grand Lodge, with suitable words from the retiring
Grand Master, Brother John R. Rison, addressed to the recently
installed Grand Master, Brother J. Leon Bachman. The Grand Master
accepted the charge, responding in gracious and appropriate language.
From an inspection of the Grand Secretary's report, it appears
that the Master Masons in good standing January I, 1912, number
25,589, a net increase for the year of 787.

Henry A . Chambers.
In his "introduction" he says in part :
"Probably the most important thing of general Masonic interest in
the United States during the time covered by .the Proceedings we have
examined, is the proposition to erect at Alexandria, Va., a Memorial
to George Washington as a Mason. Most of the Grand Lodges that have
taken action in this matter, especially in the Eastern and Middle States,
seem strongly in favor of the Memorial. The Grand Masters of a number of the Grand Lodges have met at Alexandria and helped to formulate a plan and have urged its acceptance by other Grand Lodges. One
Southwestern Grand Lodge, however, took the view that while Washington deserved and should receive high honor as a soldier, statesman
and patriot yet he was not so active and prominent a Freemason as to
be entitled to a special Masonic Memorial."

interests of others. 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least
of these, my brethren, ye have done it unto Me.' 'All things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them.' How
changed would the whole world be if these two thou~hts were kept constantly in mind and practiced in our daily walks of hfe I
"The heart is longing as never before, the world is calling as never
before, the age is demanding as never before men with big, unselfish
natures, who exemplify at all times, and under all circums~ances, the
principle of the Golden Rule, of the Good Samaritan, whose hearts are
filled with love and sympathy for humanity and its frailties. Let us,
my brethren, stand ready to satisfy this longing, and respond nobly to
this call while time and opportunity offer.''
"Love for humanity, preached and practiced, would lead us all to
feel that we are in a peculiar way our brother's keeper. And what is
this love of humanity? It is that sentiment of affection that puts underneath our weaker brother the strong arms of support and protection,
cloaks his follies and foibles, whatever they may have been, with tht
mantle of charity, whispers into his listening ears the words of friendly
counsel. lifts him to his feet, and a cheery smile sends him on his way
rejoicing. That sentiment that . provides comfortable and happy homes
for the widow and orphan, the aged and unfortunate. That sentiment
that no matter how dark and troubled the present hour may be through
hope whispers the promise of brighter and more peaceful davs, and of
rich and ample compensation of every affliction and grief. That sentiment that lifts the feet from the valley of despair· and plants them on
the glorious heights of opportunity and service. That sentiment that
thrilled the breast of the meek and lowly Nazarene as two thousand
years ago he toiled up J udean hills or sailed Galilean seas, which found
its highest expression in the agony of Gethsemane and the sorrows of
the Via Dolorosa. That sentiment that in the end will exalt every
brother who is faithful 'to the glorious companionship of that undissolving Lodge where the designs upon the Trestle Board will be seen completed, where the adoration of the twelfth hour will be the everlasting
joy, where the noontide of bliss will eternally shine, where the scales
of doubt and darkness shall fall from our eyes and the wise purposes
of the Divine Architect be displayed in all their splendor.
"The love and sympathy the world needs today is not, perhaps, of
that heroic mold which characterized the long ago, but of that finer
fiber that smooths the wrinkled brow of care, wipes bitter tears from
sorrowing eyes, binds up the wound.s of broken hearts, writes the faults
of our brothers in the shifting sand and their virtues on tablets of love
and memory: cheers the despondent in his lonelv hour, sentinels the
approach of doubt and dangers, cements ties in relations almost sacred,
and when time for our brother is no more, performs the last sad rites,
and in after years 'commemorates with freshening tears the memory of
loved ones who have shifted their places from the narrow .confines of
this life to a seat upon that stage which has all time and space for its
boundaries and the stars for its footlights.'"

The Report on Corerspondence is by Past Grand Master Thomas
M. Matthews, Sr. California, 1910, is fully and favorably reviewed.
His . reference to the oration of Brother Charles A. Adams is as follows:
"Brother Charles A. Adams delivered a sensible, plain nad practical
address upon the subject, 'Masonry in Business and Politics.' It is both
unique and refreshing, because it differs markedly from the addresses
usually heard upon like occasions, and in that it is wholly devoid of the
'highfalutin' platitudes and glittering, sky-scraping generalities which
nearly always characterizes such effusions. It points out clearly what
a power for good Masonry could and should exert in every day business and politics, and what a potent factor the true Mason might become
in elevating and purifying both, if only he would be true to his principles
and duty as they are taught him. We would that every true and rightthinking Mason had the opportunity to, could and would read and act
upon it. As an evidence of what those who heard the address tnougbt
of it, we make note that 10,000 extra copies were ordered to be printed
for distribution among the members of the Lodges."

Temple, Salt Lake City, Tuesday, the 16th day of January, A. D. 1912,

presiding.

reward:
"We have with us today two of those men, and they are just as

Christopher Diehl, who, with the exception of the first few months,
when he was Assistant Grand Secretary, has been continuously the

well known to all, and he will ever remain the bright and shining star
of Masonry in Utah. Then comes our M.'. w:. Brother, Louis Cohn,
the first Deputy Grand Master, and the third and now oldest living Past
Grand Master of this jurisdiction. We all know his good work, and
the inspiration he has ever been to the younger brethren. May they be

Concerning dispensation for new Lodges, the Grand Master says:
"February 14th, 1911, I received a petition signed by forty-one Master Masons, requesting a dispensation to establish a new Lodge in Salt
Lake City, to be known as Acacia Lodge, U. D. The petition was accompanied by the recommendation of the three Lodges of Salt Lake City.
Believing it to be for the best interests of the Craft in this city, I
ordered the issuance of a dispensation, February 16th.
"Ma rch 17th, 1911, I received a petition signed by fifty-two Master
Masons, requesting a dispensation for a new Lodge in Ogden; to be
known as Unity Lodge, U. D. The petition was accompanied by the
recommendation of Weber Lodge No. 6. Believing the same conditions to exist in Ogden as in Salt Lake, I granted the request and
ordered the issuance of a dispensation.
"At the institution of Acacia Lodge, which occurred February 25th,
every Grand Lodge Officer and over two hundred brethren were present, and I know all joined in wishing the new Lodge 'Godspeed' in its
future work.
"On April 24th, I instituted Unity Lodge at Ogden. On this occasion I was accompanied by most of the Grand Lodge Officers and about
fifty brethren from Salt Lake City. The new Lodge starts out under
the brightest auspices, and will, I believe, do much for Masonry in ,
Ogden.
·"This is the first time in the history of the Grand Lodge that two
dispensations have been issued in one year for the formation of new
Lodges, and shows that Masonry is progressing in Utah. I might state
that over two-thirds of the petitioners were non-affiliates."
Concerning the condition of Lodges and the general work of
Masonry in the jurisdiction, the v:. w:. Grand Secretary, Christopher'
Diehl, says :
"Brethren, we have again reason to rejoice and to offer thanks to
the Grand Master on High, who has showered His blessings upon our
Lod11;es and the Craft in our jurisdiction during the past twelve months.
During no year has the accession of Lodges and members been so large
as during 1911. We have gained two new Lodges and 205 members;
total membership, 1984. And that the Lodges are very careful in the
selection of new timber is shown by the fact that 77 petitions for the
three degrees were rejected. Besides that, the returns prove that a verv
lar11;e percentage of the candidates are young and intelligent men, who
will be devoted Masons, and practice the teachings of the Craft in the
daily walks of life. Again, Brethren, let us rejoice and be thankful."

The M: . w:. Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
•ltate of Vermont convened in its rooms in the Masonic Temple, city
of Burlington, on Wednesday, the 12th day of June, A. L. 5912, at the

presiding.
Out of the 103 Lodges, 76 were represented at this Communication. The percentage of unrepresented Lodges, it would appear to an
nbeerver, is rather large.
In opening his address, Grand Master Ballou says :
"It is with satisfaction that we view the usefulness of our Institution. Working ofttimes in ways unknown to those outside its pale, it
has nevertheless been a potent factor in molding the life of our State.
lta work has largely been associated with the fountain of all life, the
human soul. By its symbolism, its constant reiteration of the great
1piritual truths in its ritual and charges, Masonry has been working
most profoundly, though silently to the outside world, in bringing a

better day for our Commonwealth. As quietly and as powerfully it has
worked on the hearts of its votaries as have the mighty forces of nature
that brought the spring and the summer out of the winter. The results
have been most marked though the agency has been hidden. The unloosing of ice-streams, the banishment of snow and cold, the bursting out
of ·pastures and forests and fields into green, · the clothing of gardens
and orchards with blossoms, are some of the brilliant results of springtime; but the cause and beginning have not attracted attention. It is
in the silent sunbeam and the gentle caress of the south wind. It is
hidden among the silent forces, as quiet and unobtrusive as the breath
of a child.
"So our Lodges have been quietly at work, the rough ashlars becoming perfect ashlars, polished and prepared for the temple beautiful.
Character has been developed to an extent little realized by the uninitiated. From our Lod11;e meetings the brethren have gone forth to affect
society profoundly. Like all sublime achievements and important results
strength has been conceived ·in the brooding places of silence. The
greatest tornado that ever swept over the sea was insignificant compared to the power over the ocean's depths exercised by the silent; ·
unheralded influence of the moonbeams that lift millions of tons of
water from the bed of the sea and hurls it along the shores of the continents. Thus has heen the influence of Masonry. It is silent, nevertheless it worketh like the leaven in the lump and the moonbeam on the
tide and its power for good is felt in every department of our civic life."

Of the condition of the Craft and the high standing Vermont

The following paragraphs are quoted from the "conclusion" of the
Crand Master's address:
"I believe that Masonry is worth while; that it stands for something.
I believe that it is as enduring as the hills and that in the upbuildfog
of our institutions and in the advancement of our civilization its influence has been and will be a strong agency in the constructive order
of things that are of real value. Masonry, if it is anything, is a constructive institution, and if it would advance with the advancing civilization it must develop into a strong constructive force, and form into
nctive operation the growing mind of to-day, which will be the ruling
force to-morrow. We must impress upon every neophite not only the
5igns and secrets of this institution, but also impress upon his mem,ory
and inspire into his life and into the life of every individual the principles of Masonry which are contained within the extended points of the
compasses, and place upon the trestle board of life designs which should
and must govern every man who enters its portals, and inspire every
person with whom we may come in contact.
"We are constantly reminded in every admonition that is given us
from the time we enter the threshold of Masonry that our first duty
is to God; our next to our country, our neighbor and ourselves. We
are repeatedly reminded of our duty to the widow and the orphan, and
to protect the chastity of the family of our brother. What greater
service can Masonry do as a constructive force than to assist the
rotmg and growing mind? There is a great opportunity for Masonry
111 this jurisdiction; ye, in the world.
The boy of to-day is the man
of to-morrow, and as the mind of the boy is trained so will the man be.
The future of our sacred institution and of our country depends upon
the boy and the girl of to-day.
"Masonry is not a kindergarten, nor a reformatory, nor is it primarily an institution of charity, but is an institution for character
building. an institution whose object is to make its votaries wiser and
hetter men, and the points of whose compasses extend beyond the
limits of active membership. What greater can a Mason do than to
he alive to the welfare of the growing boy and lend this additional
influence in guiding the destinies of the world?" Here there is great
need, and much can be done to add to the strength, beauty and adornment of our civilization."

From Brother Chadwick's "conclusion" we quote:
"Mindful of changing conditions, I would add another word : To
the student who can look back over the orogress of the race, the light of
history reveals an ever-seething cauldron of human emotion. Man by
nature is dissatisfied. If to this fault we may attribute our troubles, we
may find consolation in the thought that out of it has come our material
progress. The finished steel is the fruit not only of the upheavals of
nature, but also of the refining processes of man. In nature the rocks and
rivers become the parents of our fertile valleys; and so with men. Out
of the grindings of human thought and emotion civilized government'has
come.
"It. is so to-day ; we are in a period of transition, a revolution' as
distinct and as certain as any to · be found in the tomes and volumes
which treat of other generations. This revolution is and will be
bloodless; but its r'e snlts will be more important to humanity than all
of those which. have gone before. In it every Mason has a part to
elay. Between the extremes of thought there is a middle ground where
Justice must walk, blind, unmindful of the selfish demands of either
side. To walk by her side and to sustain her, to see that demagoguery
does not' destroy logic, and that selfishness-that selfishness that would
fatten upon the wants and necessities of men and of women and of li'ttle
children-does not shackle the lives and souls of men, is the duty of the
hour. Masonry profasses to put man above the dollar; let it be so, for
the revolution now upon us comes from an unrest which is, as it seems
.~o me, the natural outgrowth .of the unequal distribution of wealth."

It will be with general regret that Masonic circles will learn of the
withdrawal of Brother Chadwick from the corps of reviewers of
Masonic reports, because in this work he has displayed marked ability.
llis comments have always been illuminating and his contr.ibutions .of·
the highest order of merit.
We quote his concluding words as follows:
"I conceive the work to be too imoortant to slight; and however
flattering the remarks of my fellows have been, I feel that I have
not done my best work; therefore I have insisted that this work be put
upon another.
"To those noble men whose words have inspired me to nobler deeds
and higher thoughts, I can say but little:
" ' 'Twixt such friends as we few words suffice.'
"If, in the heat of discussion, I have said ·aught that has given
offense, I pray that it be forgiven and foq~·otten. I have endeavored
to be just in my judgments and fair in my criticisms. If I have praised,
it was because I thought praise was due; if I have condemned, it has
hcen for the sake of the Masonic institution as I conceive it to be, and
not from any desire to be captious or malicious. I have not willfully
watered my words with flattery or tinctured my speech with the bitterness of acrimon)'. ·~ ···
"I shall not dwell upon the accomnlishments of the living; but to
one who has lived in a Masonic atmosphere since childhood, it is not
out of place to say that to have received Masonic instruction at the
hands of Drummond, Cunningham, Robbins, Vinci!, Hodson, Inglesby,
Barlow, Hedges, Wait, and men of like character, is a reward far greater
than can be measured ·in money or in words.
"I have personal acquaintance with but two correspondents; but the
older members of our guild, those who were here when I came, are well
known to me. So frank and open are the natures of these men that,
though the flesh be far away, their spirits have shared my moods when
following their words and works.
"I can say with Vincentio:

" 'There is a kind of character in thy life
That to the observer doth thy history
Fully unfold. Thyself and thy belongings
Are not thine own so proper, as to waste
Thyself upon thy virtues, they on thee.
Heaven doth with us as we with torches do,
Not light them for ourselves; for if our virtues
Did not go forth of us, 'twere all alike
As if we had them not.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

On the subject of laying the comer-stones -of churches the Grand
Master says:
"I have issued several proxies for the laying of corner-stones of
churches, but confess I have had my doubts about my power to do it,
but, as the Grand Masters who have preceded me have done it, I have
not felt justified in refusing these requests.
" It will be remembered that Grand Master Showalter refused to
issue a dispensation to a Lodge to attend divine service, and I followed
in his footsteps in that particular, but the question as to whether or
not we should lay a corner-stone of a church is a matter which presents cr nsiderable difficulties. We are supposed to lay the cornerstone of public buildings, and a church is not, in my opinion, such a
public building for which we are justified in laying corner-stones. We
are never asked, as far as I know, to lay the corner-stone of a Jewish
synagogue, or a Catholic church, but we lay the corner-stones of Methodist, Baptist and other churches. As I understand it, a public building
is one in which every person has the same rights, and this is not true
o f a denominational church-an Episcopalian has no business in a Presbyterian church, nor has a Baptist any right in a Methodist church.
Therefore, I should suggest that this Grand Lodge express its opinion
in regard to the matter and settle this question for all time, mx view
being that a church is not such a public building as we are allowed by
the landmarks of the Craft to supervise the laying of a corner-stone.
If we cannot attend divine service, and the Grand Lodge has held 'fie
cannot, why should we lay the corner-stone of an edifice in which services are held ?"

the Eastern Star, and that they be forbidden to meet in our Lodge
rooms. It is just as much an independent order as that. of the Odd
Fellows or the Knights of Pythias, but we allow them to meet in our
Lodge rooms in the same manner as if they were a branch of the
Masons."
"The Committee on Foreign Correspondence of Western Australia,
in commenting upon Oregon, gives a pretty fair history of the Adopted
Rites in the following:
" Until we read Brother Hodson's report, we had always looked upon
the Eastern Star 'fad' as merely an amiable weakness of our American brethren. We know his fondness for 'conventions' when he takes
his womankind along, and there are short business meetings and
long intervals for amusements ; and we had looked upon the Eastern Star business as a sort of excuse to associate with ladies in a
so-called lodge, for the ·reason that they could not be accepted into
the Craft.
"We take this opportunity to fraternally · but thoroughly disabuse
the minds of all American brethren of any hope that the Eastern Star
'fad' is likely to secure a home here. We are thorough believers
in the 'no women' landmark, and the mere suggestion that Grand
Lodge should call off to receive a delegation of Grand Matrons from
an unmasonic body, such as the Order of the Eastern Star, would be
howled down, and if persisted in would raise rebellion. For the information of the brethren in this State we may say that the Androgynous
Institution (institution for both sexes) known as the Order of the
Eastern Star was invented by Rob Morris in 1855. It consists of five
•
degrees.
"l. Jepthah's daughter, or the daughter's degree.
"2. Ruth, or the widow's degree.
"3. Esther, or the wife's degree.
"4. Martha, or the sister's degree.
"5. Electa, or the Christian Martyr's degree.
"It is not only in America that attempts have been made to introduce Androgynous Masonry (Masonry for both sexes).
"For nearly 200 years attempts have been made from time to time
to introduce women into speculative Freemasonry. France has been
one of the greatest sinners. About 1730 they introduced what they
called 'Meconnerie d' Adoption,' because each female or adoptive lodge
was obliged to be adopted or appended to an ordinary Craft Lodge.
"In Paris, about 1743, was formed 'L' Order des Felicitaires.' The
name speaks for itself. The female members were supposed to be
on a voyage to the Island of Felicity, in ships navigated by the brethren.
"Other similar societies sprang up, and eventually arose the System
of Lodges of Adoption. The Grand Orient of France assumed protection of these lodges about the end of the eighteenth century, but I do
not know whether any of them now exist. There is in France a system
called co-Masonry, which admits women, and which has no connection with Freemasonry, and is regarded as bogus and disreputable,
and so the adoptive rite has appeared from time to time, wherever
brethren have been weak enough to be led away by it, until at last it
seems to have settled in America, where our good brethren seem to
have a severe attack of the adoptive rite malady, which, like other
fevers, will no doubt take its deoarture in due time, leaving the patient
weak and debilitated."

Upon general principles he is opposed to granting dispensation to
reballot, and upon this subject says·
. "I have h<;td two applications for the recirculation of the ballot upon
r ei ected c~nd1dates, and have refused both of them. This is, really,
a very serious matter, and unless there are good grounds showing that
there is a mistake, do not think a dispensation for that purpose should
be granted.
"In the first place, should the man who has cast the black ball aisclose the fact, he is guilty of a Masonic offense, and, in the second
place, should he not do so, he may sign the petition for a recirculation
in order to hide the fact that it was he who did it, or he may be so
terrorized by his brethren that he will admit a man against whom there
is a valid objection."
Of the use of Lodge rooms by other organizations, we quote . the
Grand Master as follows :
. " I find that very few of the Lodge rooms are used by any organizations except Free Masons and concordant bodies, but have discovered
the fact that the Ladies' Shriqe meets in the Lodge room of the Temple at Wheeling. They are supposed' to he the daughters and wives
of the members of the Mystic Shrine, but have been repudiated by the
Mystic Shrine, and have no standing in Masonry, and I should, therefore. SU!!'gest that they be forbidden to meet in the Masonic Temple
at Wheeling, and that this matter he taken up at once.

Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Wisconsin was opened in

streets, in the city of Milwaukee, at the hour of 2 o'clock p. m., on

Master, presiding.
The Grand Master, in his address, states that a condition of harmony exists in the jurisdiction and that only minor differences, which
have been adjusted, have occurred.
He mentions the death in the year of Dr. D. McL. Miller, Past
Grand Master, and states that he requested Brother David B. Greene,
R. ·. W . ·. Deputy Grand Master, to prepare a memorial for Brother
Miller.
A number of decisions of a local character, touching the construction of the Constitution and Edicts of the jurisdiction, are mentioned.
The Grand Master reports the issuance during the year of 59
special dispensations, 49 of them being for the purpose of waiving certain · articles of the Constitution.
Wisconsin occupies a unique position, so far as its Constitution is
concerned, inasmuch as the Grand Master has power to waive certain
sections of the Constitution upon payment of certain stipulated fees.
Sundry Special Communications of the Grand Lodge were held for

WYOMING, 1911.
A portrait of M.'. W.'. Brother Harold Banner, the newly elected
Grand Master, forms the frontispiece, and the Proceedings are also
embellished with the portrait of the Grand Secretary, who is likewise
chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, the R. ·. w. ·.
W. L. Kuykendall.
The Grand Lodge, A. F. and A. M., of Wyoming, met in Annual
Communication in Cheyenne, Wyo., September 6 and 7, 1911-Grand
Master Hugh Hynds presiding.
The Grand Master, in opening his address, says :
"The year which has passed has been marked with many substanti;l
benefits to us as members of our great brotherhood, whose universality
is as extensive as the world itself, and whose influence and power are
only limited by the confines Qf civilization. It gives me pleasure to
announce to you that peace and good fellowship has prevailed througbout this jurisdiction, and that, although we have not advanced with
great strides still we are increasing in numbers and influence. We have
laid our Masonic foundation good and strong, and are building the superstructure upon it with care and deliberation, and upon the broad principles of morality, virtue and truth. Our financial condition and memhership continue to improve and we may by economy and thrift confidently look forward to the accomplishment of some Masonic undertakini< which will prove of lasting benefit to the membership of this
Grand Lodge and Grand Jurisdiction."
Under the heading "Necrology" the Grand Master enumerates with
profound sorrow the list of brethren called during the year "from
labor here to everlasting refreshment above."
Grand Master Hynds reports the laying of three corner-stones
under Masonic auspices, viz: the new high school building at Laramie,
the high school building at Buffalo and the Masonic Temple at Laramie.
The Grand Master rendered a number of decisions, upon purely
local questions; he made a dozen or more official visitations to subordinates during the year; he recommends the adoption of an official
cnrd receipt and that it be made uniform throughout the jurisdiction.

Grand Secretary Kuykendall introduces his annual report as
follows:
"For the twenty-fifth time I submit my annual report as ·your Gr;~md
Secretary. During all that time I have endeavored to do my duty faithfully as a man, a Mason and as an official of this Grand Lodge. I have
labored early and late to give this Grand Jurisdiction prestige with all
others which I believe has been accomplished. In all this work every
act of 'mine has been guided by what I have believed, after due investigation in all cases, to be right, just and for the best interest of our fraternity locally and as a whole, and now, at the close of this quarter
of a century of such work, it is a pleasure to submit this report for
such action as may be deemed necessary thereon."
As evidence of the esteem in which Grand Secretary Kuykendall is
held, the following is quoted from the report of the Proceedings of the
Grand Lodge :
"At this stage of the proceedings, and during a lull in business,
Past Grand Master C. N. Potter, on behalf of Past Grand Master E. F.
Cheney, for the Grand Lodge, in a very eloquent and touching manner
and speech, presented to W. L. Kuy~enda,11, the Grand S~cretary, a fine
scarf pin and sleeve butto~s, set with d1~mond~, to which . the Grand
Secretary, with great emotion, responded in f~eling and fitting expressions of appreciation and thanks for the tangible tokens of confidence
and good will of the members of Grand Lodge.

thanks of the Grand Lodge, but that certain recommendations 'made
therein looking to the termination of fraternal relations with certain
Grand Bodies that recognized the Lodges in the Philippine Islands,
chartered by the Grand Orient of $pain, says :
"In our opinion here was a chance to have opened the way through
the adoption of said special report and resolutions for drawing the
line definitely between regular, irregular and clandestine Masonry. It
is too bad that every regular Craft Mason in the United States cannot read said special report and resolutions. which would without a
doubt be approved by a large majority upon a referendum vote or
upon Lodge instructio n. We agree with nearly every argument and
finding in said special report, especially the unanswerable statement
of fact admitted to be such by every Grand Lodge in this country,
that no Supreme Council or any man ever connected with Scottish
Rite Masonry ever had any right or power to confer or authorize the
conferring of the t 'ree 1...raft or Symbolic degrees anwhere. It is
admitted by nearly if not every Masonic student and writer that no
such power ever existed. Certainly if it legally exists in any country
we have no right to deny it in this country. The supreme height of
inconsistency is reached when a Grand Lodge declares against the
existence of such power and at the same time admits its existence
through recognizing as Masons men upon whom said degrees were
conferred in Scottish Rite Lodges chartered by Supreme Councils.
The insidious arguments advanced by a few on this question, coupled
with such recognition granted by a few of our Grand Lodges, has
laid the foundation for the claim recently made in several quarters
that under the word universality we should accept and recognize
every brand of so-called Masonry, whether clandestine, irregular or
under ban. We hope said report and resolutions will be called up
again and be adopted, thereby opening the way for the supremacy of
our regular Masonry without any half-breed entanglements or by mix!'
ing up with the latter hecome as they are, political machines, and iii
great measure unmasonic, as most of them are well known to be."

be legally conferred by any other Rite. Therefore, the granting of
such charters and conferring of said degrees has been assumed by
other Rites in foreign countires without any authority whatever, so far
as our knowledge of any evidence worthv the name is concerned. In
support of our contention the two regular Scottish Rite bodies of this
country do not claim that they have any right or power to grant Lodge
charters or to confer said degrees. Such being the case, certainly the
same Rite elsewhere has not and never possessed such power, and yet
the Grand Lodge of Craft Masonry have been and are being importuned
continually to grant recognition to Grand Lodges and Grand Orients
organized by such illegal Lodges. We regret to say that the argument
is used that they should be recognized because they represent the dominant Rite in some foreign countries and that a few of our Grand Lodges
have listened to the voice of the siren by granting recognition to such
illegal bodies, thus endorsing the unlawful assumption of powers nonexistent. We are not questioning the action of any Grand Lodge in this
matter, as we have no right to do so, but it does seem that committees,
instead of diligently seeking for something to recognize, should carefully
investigate the parentage of Grand Bodies from a legal standpoint, based
upon Craft Masonry, before recommending recognition, especially when
grief is liable to be the outcome in doses or as a whole eventually. As
a member of the Scottish Rite we claim to be as loyal thereto as any
member, and as ready to fight the battles of the two regular bodies
thereof in this country. They are now in a position to take care of
themselves through having a great field of material to draw upon, and
if recognizing of other bodies of the Rite or anything emanating therefrom is absolutely necessary they are the proper organizations to grant
such recognition as applying to themselves alone, thereby leaving Grand
Lodges of Craft Masonry to only consider the legitimacy of applicants
for recognition belonging to the latter. They are separate and distinct
rites and should so remain, except upon the ground existing between
them in this country, and we are of the opinion that a few Scottish
Rite Masons who, as reporters, committees on correspondence and
writers, are advocating and recommending the recognition of illegal,
so-called Grand Bodies directly in opposition to the well-defiried position
of both Rites in this country to which they owe obedience, are making
a grave mistake, which will result eventually in endless trouble and
complications detrimental, if not absolutely dangerous, to the supremacy
of Craft or York Rite Masonry in controlling the conferring of the
Craft degrees, which we are unalterably opposed to srurendering, either
directly or indirectly, to any other Rite in this country or elsewhere.
''The question of any regular Grand Lodge having recognized an
in<lividual Mason or man claiming to be such through official action
before recognizing his Grand Lodge, has never been attempted but once
within our knowledge. The result of such action is well known, and yet
we /ind a few high in the councils of the Craft advocating the heresy
that they are above Grand Lodges in having the right to recognize and
fellowship with any man claiming to he a Mason who they may choose,
irrespective of whether or not his Grand Lodge has been declared to be
regular and has been recognized by their Grand Lodges or not, and who,
if we mistake not, have in their travels in Europe, South America and
elsewhere visited Lodges which have not been recognized as regular by
their Grand Lodges, even going so far as to fraternize with Masons
and Lodges of the Grand Orient of France, which their Grand Lodges
have declared non-intercourse with. On this see South Carolina and
others in this report. If we as regular Masons are going to retrograde

Brother Kuykendall's views on Ancient Craft Masonry are of
unquestioned soundness and orthodoxy, and we quote the larger pore
tion of his "conclusion," the ideas therein set forth being of interest to
Masonic students, even though some may not agree fully with bis
position:
" On the first question it will probably not be disputed that se.veral
brands of regular and also of so-called Masonry exist, divided into
and known as rites, only two of which we consider as having any
standing, namely Ancient Craft Masonry, dubbed the 'York Rite,' with
which the Chapter and Commandery organizations claim connectioµ,
and the 'Scottish · Rite.' That Ancient Craft Masonry great!~ antedates all other brands will also probably not be disputed. That it
established the first Grand Lodges or organized bodies which rightly
claimed sole control over speculative Craft Masonry because of organizing same and the granting of Lodge charters and the sole right to
confer. the Craft degrees has never, to our knowledge, been successfully denied. Such being the case, reason and common sense dictate
that, having assumed such power and control, no agreement would be
or ever has been legally entered into with anv other Rite for a division
thereof whereby Lodge charters could be granted or the Craft degrees

REPORT ON CORRESPONDltNCE.

and go back to the go-as-you-please style of operative Masonry, when
no Grand Lodges existed and chaos instead of a well-formulated system
of government with Sovereign Grand Lodges as the supreme power, then
let us get there as quickly as possible, for that it what the heresy of
such personal recognition of individual Masons and Lodges as first promulgated and advocated by Brother Upton means. With such a doctrine generally accepted, Grand Lodges will be figure-heads and a useless expense and in the way, opened for individual recognition of clandestine negro Masons, as Upton advocated and intended should be
accomplished, and the great millennium day of universality will have
dawned with the blind leading the blind, who cannot or will not see that
a great army of Masons in this countrv will not travel. with them down
the road to Masonic destruction for universality of the brand and composed of the elements advocated, or any other impossibility. Such individual recognition of Masons and Lodges and advocacy of universality
for a purpose are the rocks upon which the bark of regular Masonry will
be wrecked unless better counsels prevail. When leading Masons here
and there begin to openly advocate such individual recogn.ition of
men as Masons, and their right to visit any Lodge they please, it is,
in our opinion, about time for all other Masons and especially reporters,
to open up a crusade against such a heresy, as well as against the kind
of universality emanating in certain quarters in Europe for a pflrpose
well known to themselves and a few sympathizers and abettors, in this
country. We believe there is more danger to our Craft Masonry in
said theoretical doctrines and the promiscuous recognition of so-called
Grand Lodges and Grand Orients than in all other questions confronting
our fraternity. So believing, we shall, alone if necessary, continue t-0
combat said doctrines in their infancy and not pass them up for others
to fight in the future when they have arrived at maturity and have
become a dangerous menace to Craft Masonry. Relating to all this we
call the attention of our readers to England, Quebec, Montana, Louisiana,
Florida, Massachusetts, District of Columbia and others in this report."
Harold Banner, Casper, elected Grand Master.
W. L. Kuykendall, Saratoga, re-elected Grand Secretary. ·
